content:
Members received
and considered the report of the Director of Resources which
provided an update on the draft Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn
position for 2025/26, the updated Capital Programme and proposed
Flexible Capital Receipts Policy. The report also provided an
update on progress against the 2025/26 savings targets. 
 
The Revenue Budget
(RB) and Capital Programme (CP) statements were summarised at
Appendices A and B to the report respectively and a review of the
agreed savings targets for 2025/26 was contained within Appendix C
to the report. The proposed Flexible Capital Receipts Policy, which
was an update to the previously adopted Productivity Plan and
facilitated the use of the Government’s Directive to extend
the ability to use capital receipts flexibly, was contained within
Appendix D to the report.
 
The RB draft
outturn position was an overall deficit of £1,331,000 against
the approved budgeted drawdown from Reserves of £694,000.
This position incorporated the previously reported losses on the
Hermes investment and the write off for capital schemes previously
reported. 
 
The 2025/26 RB
included anticipated savings totalling £1,084,424; the
budgeted savings listed in Appendix C had been RAG rated (Red,
Amber, Green) to show levels of assurance. £422,627 of the
savings were rated Green to indicate that they had been achieved
and delivered in full in year, £208,213 were rated Amber
indicating they were partially achieved and £453,584 were
rated Red as they were not deliverable in year.  Achieved savings totalled £473,328,
representing 44% of the target, leaving an underachievement of
£611,093, mainly due to planning fee income which was
affected by the broader economic climate. Some ‘green’
savings areas outperformed their targets in year, offsetting
£239,851 of the gap.
 
The main variances
were outlined in the report and summarised in Appendix
A.  These included: additional staffing
costs (agency staff and costs relating to Local Government
Reorganisation (LGR)); underspend due to staff vacancies;
underspend in respect of numerous supplies and service budgets such
as stationery, computer services and licences, hired and contracted
services; overspend in relation to external fees paid to the
Council’s External Auditor, Grant Thornton, in respect of
charges made in 2025/26 that related to previous financial years; a
temporary accommodation deficit primarily due to reduced placements
from a housing provider; increase in rental income; transfers to
Earmarked Reserves required at year end in respect of funds
received but not yet utilised; costs associated with the
devolvement of assets works (to be funded from Flexible Capital
Receipts); adverse impact because of voids and leases; net
underspend in Neighbourhood Services which included £516,000
additional grant received for the Government Extended Producer
Responsibility for packaging grant funding towards food collection
sources; and reduced income from planning fees, although an
improvement on the previous year.
 
Further income had
been generated in year from loans to the Rother DC Housing Company
(RDCHC), the total anticipated payable for 2025/26 being
£1.870m but not incorporated currently into the overall
revenue outturn position. This would be ahead of the final
financial statements being drafted and allocated to an Earmarked
Reserve.  The Net Cost of Services also
incorporated an adverse variance to the revenue position in respect
of a loss on the Hermes Investment of £423,000 and
£759,000 of capital costs written back to revenue in year
primarily in respect of the Town Hall Renaissance project and Old
Lydd Road Housing project. 
 
On 1 April 2025,
the General Fund Reserve stood at £5m and the budget
anticipated a drawdown of £694,000. During 2025/26, the total
drawdown from the General Fund was £1.33m. The General
Reserve at year end was therefore forecast to be
£3.67m. 
 
The total Capital
Budget for the CP set in February 2025 was £165m, with
£44m having been spent in previous years, and a projected
2024/25 outturn of £40m. New business cases had been brought
forward and approved as detailed in the report and the draft CP
outturn as at 31 March 2026 was now
£42m. The current projection for spend from 2026/27 through
to 2029/30 was c£87m. The updated total capital budget was
now £196m, which was an increase of c£31m compared to
the position in February 2025. The overall position of the CP was
summarised in Appendix B to the report, having been adjusted for
slippage based on the 2025/26 outturn position.
 
There was a new
emerging risk relating to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East,
which was having a negative impact on inflation, with living costs
rising and both bank and mortgage rates forecast to increase. If
interest rates increased, this would also have a negative impact on
the Council’s interest payments in respect of borrowing.
 
Inflationary
pressure could increase construction and material costs but would
not be an issue for those contracts that were already tendered and
agreed. There were, however, a number of
significant schemes still to be tendered over the coming year. The
position would continue to be monitored.
 
In March 2025, the
Government confirmed that the ‘Flexible use of capital
receipts: direction’ was to be extended through until 2030;
this would enable the Council to use capital receipts from the sale
of its own assets to help fund the revenue costs of transformation
projects and release savings.
 
Cabinet considered
an update to the Productivity Plan in July 2025 (adopted by full
Council in September 2025), which outlined the Council’s
intentions to utilise those flexibilities.  A summary was provided within the report of where
Flexible Capital Receipts had been used. Appendix D to the report
outlined the proposed use of Flexible Capital Receipts for 2026/27
and 2027/28, for Members’ consideration.  This document would be subject to some refinement
ahead of Cabinet’s consideration of it. 
 
Members were given
the opportunity to ask questions and the
following points were noted during the discussion:
 

•     Members were
pleased to note the surplus on the operational budget;

•     the savings
programme should not now include anticipated income as this was not
in the control of the Council. The savings programme would be
different in the next year and
discussions were due to commence earlier than last; and

•     there was
uncertainty about household income and interest rates, but this
would eventually settle.
 
The Council
remained in a challenging financial position; however, the outturn
position was an improved picture with lower anticipated draws from
reserves, through the in-year monitoring.  Some of the gains experienced in year would not
recur in future financial periods, so careful financial management
would be of importance as the Council progressed through 2026/27,
to ensure that it was able to effectively manage the resources
available to it. 
 
RESOLVED:
That:
 

1)   the proposed amendments to the
Capital Programme and the Flexible Capital Receipts Policy be
recommended to Cabinet for onward approval and adoption by full
Council; and

 

2)   the draft revenue and capital
outturn position, be noted.
topline: The UK council has recommended amendments to the Capital Programme and the Flexible Capital Receipts Policy, while noting the draft revenue and capital outturn position.

In certain

given delegated authority to issue the decision of the Planning
Committee once the requirements of the Committee have been
satisfactorily complied with.  A
delegated decision does not mean that planning permission or
refusal will automatically be issued. 
If there are consultation objections, difficulties, or negotiations
are not satisfactorily concluded, then the application will have to
be reported back to the Planning Committee.  This delegation also allows the Head of Planning
to negotiate and amend applications, conditions, reasons for
refusal and notes commensurate with the instructions of the
Committee.  Any applications which are
considered prior to the expiry of the consultation reply period are
automatically delegated for a decision.

below.

content:
This
application had been called in by one of the local Ward Members
(Councillor Osborne) for the following reasons, local interest,
highway and drainage issues and effect on the High Weald National
Landscape (HWNL).
 
The Planning Committee had visited the
site.  The proposal sought to demolish
The Garden House and construct 70 dwellings with access from Main
Street, including parking, landscaping, open space and
infrastructure.  The site was located
within the HWNL, adjoining the development boundary, and was
identified in the Peasmarsh
Neighbourhood Plan (PNP) as a potential long-term residential
site. 
 
The Planning Officer’s
opinion was that the development was not ‘major
development’ under Paragraph 190 of the National Planning
Policy Framework (NPPF) and overall, the scheme’s adverse
impacts would not significantly and demonstrably outweigh the
benefits under Paragraph 11(d) of the NPPF.  The proposal delivered a well-designed mixed
housing development with much needed affordable homes in a
sustainable location, incorporating energy efficient products such
as air source heat pumps and electric vehicle charge
points.  Existing planting would be
retained and enhanced with new landscaping and improved public
access, alongside upgrades to bus stops, pedestrian links, and a
financial contribution to bus services via a Section 106
Obligation.  Plus,
the new dwellings would contribute towards the Council’s lack of a
5-year housing supply.
 
The Planning
Committee heard from a representative of Peasmarsh Parish Council (PPC), who raised objections to the scheme,
particularly regarding drainage and sewerage.  They also heard from the Applicant’s Agent
and the local Ward Member (Councillor Osborne), who expressed
reservations (as outlined above). 
Consideration was also given to the comments made by the statutory
and non-statutory consultees, as detailed within the report,
along with the
update sheet circulated before the meeting, which included
additional submissions from the Applicant and one further
objection.
 
Members asked a series of questions in relation to several
issues and commented as follows: site susceptible to potential
severe flooding and sewage issues; gardens of the surrounding
properties were currently susceptible to flooding in adverse
weather conditions; current discharge of raw sewage into the River
Rother; disappointment was expressed by the limited evidence
received from Southern Water (SW) and the Lead Local Flood
Authority (LLFA), and by the lack of comment from the Environment
Agency (EA); scheme not in accordance with High Weald Housing
Design Guide (HWHDG); level of harm to the HWNL; density / massing
of the site, close compact / crammed dwellings (increased from 45
to 70 properties) causing urbanisation in a village location;
increased population of a rural village (change dynamic); urban
creep; increased traffic movements on a multiple speed limit road;
limited infrastructure (doctors and schools); close proximity to
two applications previously resolved to approve (Pippins and Pond
Cottage); narrow access road; huge attenuation pond in comparison
to the size of the houses; size of the gardens (small –
subjective preference); and substandard design (open to
criticism).
 
Regarding the increased number of properties, Members were
advised that the PNP requirement was for smaller units (1 and
2-beds), therefore the number of dwellings was increased to help
toward achieving this and to maximise the use of the
site.  A suggestion was proposed to add
the EA and PPC as consultees to Condition 3 and the EA to Condition
5 and add the wording “to prevent water pollution, having
particular regard to the sensitive drainage situation within the
village of Peasmarsh and concerns over
discharge of more sewage to the River Rother”, to the Reason of Condition
3.
 
During the debate, the Planning Committee considered the
Planning Officer’s view that the scheme did not constitute
‘major development’ but as the decision maker, Members
considered it to be major development (for the purposes of the
NPPF) that had the potential to have significant impact upon the
HWNL.  They referred to objections from
the High Weald Unit, which stated that the layout and design was a
“wholly unacceptable” response to the HWHDG and would
conflict with Objective 2 of the High Weald (Area of Outstanding
Natural Beauty) Management Plan, thereby exacerbating the adverse
impacts on the HWNL.  The Development
Manager referenced Paragraph 190 of the NPPF.
 
Councillor Mier moved the motion that the
scheme be considered to be a major development in the HWNL, this
was seconded by Councillor Grohne.  The
motion was declared CARRIED (5 for / 3 against).
 
After a thorough and robust debate, the Planning Committee
agreed the site was suitable for redevelopment but could not
support this application in its current form.  They resolved to defer the application so Planning
Officers could discuss a revised scheme with the Applicant,
reducing the number of dwellings and improving property design,
including the layout and density. 
Members considered that a smaller scheme would still harm the HWNL,
but if designed appropriately and in line with the HWHDG, would not
do so unacceptably.  They also required
further information from the EA, SW and LLFA on sewage
issues.  If the Applicant chose not to
engage with the Council, REFUSAL would be delegated to Planning
Officers, in consultation with the Chair of the Planning Committee,
on landscape impact and design grounds.
 
Councillor Mrs Barnes moved the motion to DEFER, and this was
seconded by Councillor Gray.  The motion
was declared CARRIED (8 for / unanimous).
 
RESOLVED: That planning application
RR/2025/1499/P be designated as major development in the High Weald
National Landscape for the purposes of Paragraph 190 of the
National Planning Policy Framework.
 
DECISION: DEFERRED TO CONSULT WITH
THE APPLICANT TO DISCUSS A REVISED SCHEME, REDUCING THE NUMBER OF
DWELLINGS AND IMPROVING PROPERTY DESIGN, INCLUDING THE LAYOUT AND
DENSITY IN LINE WITH THE HIGH WEALD HOUSING DESIGN GUIDE, AND
FURTHER INFORMATION TO BE RECEIVED FROM THE ENVIRONMENT AGENCY,
SOUTHERN WATER AND LEAD LOCAL FLOOD AUTHORITY ON SEWAGE
ISSUES.  IF THE APPLICANT CHOOSES NOT TO
AMEND THE SCHEME, THE DECISION OF REFUSAL BE DELEGATED TO PLANNING
OFFICERS, IN CONSULTATION WITH THE CHAIR OF THE PLANNING COMMITTEE,
IN RESPECT OF LANDSCAPE IMPACT AND DESIGN GROUNDS.
topline: The Planning Committee has deferred a decision on the construction of 70 dwellings in the High Weald National Landscape, citing concerns over drainage, sewage, and landscape impact.

purpose:
To update the Climate Change Steering Group on
Green Team activities to support sustainable waste practices within
the council.
content:
In 2023, the
Council completed a Waste Audit at the Town Hall and Amherst Road
buildings, which lead to recommendations being implemented to
reduce waste, improve recycling and cut contamination.  A follow-up audit carried out in September 2025
assessed their impact, alongside the introduction of commercial
food waste collections.
 
Waste items recorded in the 2025 audit (excluding
food waste) were 38% lower than in 2023, including 53 fewer paper /
card and 150 fewer plastic items, with reductions in tissues and
paper towels.  Contamination improved,
particularly for glass and batteries, though Tetrapaks, soiled tissues and paper cups were still
incorrectly disposed of.  Overall, waste
volume fell by 29.9% with reductions across both recycling and
general waste, indicating improved recycling rates, though
contamination issues remained.  New
signage was displayed advising of what could and could not be
recycled.
 
Other initiatives carried out in the year
included clothes and Christmas gift swap events, promotion of
Plastic Free July, plus a book and jigsaw exchange in the staff
canteen.  To further improve waste
practices, staff would be encouraged to use reusable bottles and
mugs, share food, plant swap and join a Gardening Club to grow
herbs/vegetables on the staff canteen patio.
 
During the discussion the following was
noted:
 

·      
Members were advised that the water fountain paper
cups supplied at the Town Hall offices would be phased out, and
staff and Members would be encouraged to bring their own cups or
bottles.  It was agreed to place signs
by each water fountain stating that the cups provided were not
sustainable.

·      
All green hints and tips messages were promoted on
the intranet, website and published on ‘MyAlerts’.
 
RESOLVED: That the findings and
recommendations be noted.
 
ACTION 7: That signs be
placed by each water fountain stating that the cups provided were
not sustainable and encourage staff and Members to bring their own
cups or bottles (Head of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood
Services / Climate Officer).
topline: The council has decided to implement recommendations to reduce waste and improve recycling in their buildings.

purpose:
This report sets out the progress made against
the climate action plan from 1st April 2025 up to 31st March
2026.
content:
The
Climate Strategy and Climate Action Plan (CAP), adopted in December
2023, outlined the Council’s approach to reducing emissions
across five key areas: Buildings and Energy Efficiency; Transport;
Resource Consumption and Waste; Biodiversity; and Energy
Generation.  The Climate Officer’s
report at Appendix A summarised progress made between 1 April 2025
and 31 March 2026 against the five objectives set out in the
Climate Strategy.  Highlights were, as
follows:
 
Buildings
and Efficiency

·      
Promoted building retrofit and low-carbon housing
(launched Homewise tool in June
2025).

·      
£350,000 improvements made to 18 private homes
in Rother through Warm Homes Grant to fund energy upgrades and low
carbon heating in worst quality, low-income and privately rented
homes (to be continued for the next two to four years).

·      
Supported the development of regional Housing
Retrofit Strategy for East Sussex, led by East Sussex County
Council (ESCC).

·      
Reviewed and improved the Council’s
operational buildings (Energy Performance Certificates rated C or
above).  Refurbished Camber Welcome
Centre was rated 3A.
 
Transport

·      
Worked with partners on transport and air
quality.

·      
Shared events and information to promote sustainable
travel e.g. health walks etc.

·      
Encouraged residents to switch to electric
vehicles.

·      
55 of 154 Council’s Taxi fleet were electric
(hybrid) vehicles.

·      
Reduced the Council staff’s travel emissions
(joined Easit scheme [transport
initiative to promote sustainable commuting and reduce
congestion]).

·      
On schedule to achieve ‘Gold’ Carbon
Literacy status.  Once achieved,
training will be offered to the parish and town councils
(P&TCs).
 
Resource
Consumption and Waste

·      
Encouraged and enabled the sustainable use of
resources.

·      
Promoted sustainable food practices (joined Sussex
Six campaign in September 2025).  The
Head of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services confirmed
that progress on the Sussex Six campaign was being monitoring by
the Regeneration Team; statistics and an update would be presented
at a future meeting.

·      
Improved the Council’s organisation waste
practices (decreased waste by 30% since 2023).
 
Biodiversity and Land Use

·      
Strengthened the Council’s support for nature;
two motions were passed on the rights of rivers and trees in
September 2025.  A Nature Emergency was
declared in December 2025; the Council was committed to tackling
investment in nature-based solutions to climate change.

·      
Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG): Progress over the
period 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2025 was available on the
Council’s website, 
Our Biodiversity Duty – Rother District
Council.

·      
Supported partners to improve the health of water
environments and land management practices.

·      
Promoted and funded action for nature e.g. Dark Sky
Week and No Mow May.

·      
Three community orchards were planted across the
district, plus a micro wood of 1,000 trees at Bulverhythe Recreation Ground.
 
Energy
Generation

·      
Funded renewable projects for community buildings
e.g. The Pelham in Sidley and Brightling Village Hall.

·      
Promoted the take-up of domestic
renewables.

·      
Supported local community energy
opportunities.
 
Appendix B to the report detailed progress achieved against each
action in the CAP.  The following minor
changes were proposed for 2026/27:
 

2.2.3    
Use On-Street Residential Chargepoint
Scheme (ORCS) funding to install Electric Vehicle (EV) charging
infrastructure in Council owned public car parks: Amended following
the removal of ORCS funding: Install EV charging infrastructure in
Council-owned car parks at no capital cost.

2.2.11   Pool EVs
made available for staff use: Removed, the Council had no plans to
introduce pool vehicles.

3.1.2    
Promote Rother Reduce, Reuse, Recycle Grant to fund community
initiatives: Removed, superseded by the Rother Community Grants
Scheme, run by Sussex Community Foundation.

4.1.5    
Develop a natural / open spaces asset management plan which
designates a minimum 10% of Council owned natural assets to
‘wilding’ and nature recovery, with consideration to
BNG and creating Habitat Banks: Reworded: Develop a Management Plan
for Open Spaces, designating a minimum 10% to nature recovery, with
consideration given to creating Habitat Banks.

5.2.4    
Work with partners to explore feasibility studies for geothermal
heat networks in the district: Removed, as no local partners were
known to be progressing geothermal heat extraction
locally.
 
Completed Actions 3.1.3, 3.1.4 and 3.2.5 would be
removed.
 
During the discussion
the following was noted:
 

·      
It was suggested that separate press releases with
photos be published to share positive news stories, including all
those who were involved in the projects / events e.g. District
Councillors, P&TCs, relevant stakeholders and organisations
etc.  Members were reminded that all
information was uploaded to the website.

·      
Members requested site visits to successful
projects, particularly those that had received grant funding, e.g.
Organic Farm.

·      
Members requested guidance on the appropriate
methods of glass disposal / recycling; advice would be sought from
the Neighbourhood Services Team and Waste Team.

·      
An update on on-street EV charging points was
requested; it was understood that a contract was still to be agreed
/ signed by ESCC.

·      
Members requested advice on slow drainage methods in
urban settings; advice would be sought.

·      
A motion was passed on 18 May 2026 which opposed the
Government’s National Planning Policy Framework reforms,
noting the Council’s higher BNG target (20% or higher)
compared to the Government’s 10%. 
It was suggested that 20% remained in the Council’s Local
Plan.

·      
Clarity was sought on several BNG issues, including
credits achieved at land at Hoads Wood, through planning
applications, and the process for calculating credits on
Council-owned land.  Advice would be
sought from the Climate Officer, Estates Team and Head of
Planning.

·      
Members requested that the Food Partnership be
revived with Rother Voluntary Action (RVA).  The Head of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood
Services agreed to contact RVA.
 
RESOLVED: That progress against the
Climate Action Plan achieved in 2025/26 be noted.
 
ACTION 1: An update on the
progress of the Sussex Six campaign to be presented at a future
meeting (Head of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services /
Climate Officer).

 
ACTION 2: That separate press
releases with photos be published to share
positive news stories including all those who were involved in the
projects / events (Head of Corporate, Strategic and
Neighbourhood Services / Climate Officer).

 
ACTION 3: A site visit to the
Organic Farm be arranged for Members of the Climate Change Steering
Group (Head of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services /
Climate Officer).
 
ACTION 4: To seek advice on slow
drainage methods in urban settings (Head of Corporate, Strategic
and Neighbourhood Services / Climate Officer).
 
ACTION 5: To seek advice on BNG
credits from the Climate Officer, Estates Team and Head of Planning
(Head of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood
Services).
 
ACTION 6: To contact
Rother Voluntary Action regarding the Food Partnership (Head of
Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services / Climate
Officer).
topline: The Council has approved the progress made against the Climate Action Plan in 2025/26.

content:
Consideration was
given to the report of the Head of Environmental Services,
Licensing and Community Safety concerning the Council’s
Licensing Policy 2026.  The Committee
had previously considered the Policy in January 2026 and agreed to
recommend to Council that it go out to consultation for six
weeks.
 
Rother District
Council (RDC) was required to have a Licensing Policy that set out
how the Council would generally approach the licensing of premises,
persons and events where there was the provision for the sale
and/or supply of alcohol, regulated entertainment and late-night
refreshment.  The Council’s
Licensing Policy had been developed in accordance with the
Licensing Act 2003 and also with
statutory guidance issued under section 182 of the Act. 
 
The Council had
consulted the responsible authorities (Sussex Police, East Sussex
Fire & Rescue Service etc.) and the Director of Public Health
about any changes required to be made to the Policy. No major
changes were proposed, but the Policy had been amended to reflect
the consultation responses received from the fire and rescue
authority, the local planning authority and the Director of Public
Health, to reflect current regulations. (Amendments were
highlighted in the Policy attached at Appendix A to the
report.)
 
The Policy also
included a statement taken from the revised Government guidance:
“The Authority recognises the important role which pubs and
other licensed premises play in our local communities by minimising
the regulatory burden on business, encouraging innovation and
supporting responsible premises”.
 
The Policy could be
reviewed at any time; if a request for an amendment was received,
it would be reported to the Committee for consideration. Major
changes would be subject to consultation with premises licence
holders and the public.
 
Officers confirmed
that uptake of schemes such as ‘Ask Angela’ were not
monitored by the Council, although the Police Licensing Unit would
often check with premises whether they were in place. Where issues
were experienced at premises that led to a licence review, adoption
of such schemes could be required as a condition of the
licence.
 
If a premises was
subject to a food hygiene inspection, compliance with licensing
conditions would also be checked at the same time; non-food
premises were checked by the Police. The Council would carry out
licensing checks on premises where a complaint had been received
and could ask the Police Licensing Unit to carry out checks on any
new, high-risk premises. Regular meetings took place between the
Council and the Police Licensing Unit.
 
Members were
supportive of the Licensing Policy 2026 being approved.
 
RECOMMENDED:
That the Licensing Policy 2026 be approved.
 
(Councillor Hayward
declared a Non Registerable Interest in this matter in so far as he
was a paid member of the Town Square Social Club, Bexhill and in
accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct remained in the
meeting during the consideration thereof.)
topline: The Licensing and General Purposes Committee has decided to approve the Council's Licensing Policy 2026.

content:
Members received
the report of the Head of Environmental Services, Licensing and
Community Safety concerning a consultation to be run to increase
hackney carriage fares. The Council set the maximum fares that
could be charged by hackney carriages (that could ply for hire at taxi ranks); drivers were free to
accept a lower fare, but meters had to be set to the
Council’s fares. There was a cost in calibrating meters and
issuing new fare cards and therefore fares were not altered too
frequently. Hackney carriage fares were last increased in April
2023.
 
The cost of diesel
had increased by 19% over the previous three years. Taking this
into account, together with the rate of inflation, an increase of
10% from October 2026 was recommended to be consulted on, the
results of which would be reported to the Committee.
 
If no objections to
a table of fares or variation were made within the 14-day
consultation period, or if all objections were withdrawn, the table
of fares or variation would come into operation at the end of the
14-day period.
 
If objections were
made and not withdrawn, the Council would set a further date, not
later than two months after the first specified date, on which the
table of fares would come into force with or without modifications,
after consideration of the objections. This two-month rule
effectively meant the fare increase could not take place until
October 2026.
 
The current fare
card was attached at Appendix A and fare cards of other authorities
at Appendix B to the report for Members’ information. Members
were requested to consider whether to consult on increasing fares
this year.
 
Setting of Hackney
Carriage fees was an executive function as confirmed at Paragraph
10.1 of the Taxi and Private Hire Vehicle Licensing Best Practice
Guidance for Licensing Authorities in England (November
2023).  Members were supportive of
Cabinet being requested to agree to the consultation being carried
out and fares being increased in accordance with recommended
timescales.
 
RESOLVED:
That:
 

1)   Cabinet be requested to agree
that consultation be carried out to increase hackney carriage fares
by 10%  from
October 2026;

 

2)   subject to no objections being
received, to increase fares from the end of the 14-day consultation
period; and

 

3)   any objections received will
be reported to the Licensing and General Purposes Committee for
consideration and the table of fares shall come into force, with or
without modifications, not later than two months after the first
specified date.
topline: The Licensing and General Purposes Committee has decided to approve recommendations to increase hackney carriage fares by 10% from October 2026.

purpose:
For Council to confirm the designation of
Philip Baker as this Council's Monitoring Officer and Solicitor to
the Council.
content:
Following the departure of the Council’s previous
Monitoring Officer (MO) and Solicitor to the Council, it was
necessary to make alternative arrangements for the statutory post
of MO.  It was proposed that Philip
Baker, MO and Deputy Chief Executive, Governance Services at East
Sussex County Council (ESCC) be designated as this Council’s
MO and Solicitor to the Council with effect from 19 May
2026. 
 
In
the context of heightened delivery pressures and the additional
demands associated with preparing for potential Local Government
Reorganisation (LGR), both authorities had identified opportunities
to strengthen capacity and resilience through structured
staff-sharing arrangements.  A Section
113 agreement provided a well-established legal mechanism to
support such arrangements by placing at the disposal of the latter
authority the services of officers employed by the former
authority.
 
The
Council and ESCC had a history of working collaboratively, and the
proposal would expand on this and benefit both organisations and is
particularly timely given LGR.
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)    
Philip Baker, Deputy Chief Executive, Governance
Services at East Sussex County Council be designated as this
Council’s Monitoring Officer and Solicitor to the Council
with effect from 19 May 2026;
 

2)    
a wider reciprocal Section 113 framework arrangement
be put in place between East Sussex County Council and Rother
District Council to enable either authority to place the services
of other officers at the disposal of the other authority (and vice
versa), where this supports service resilience, programme delivery
and Local Government Reorganisation preparedness, with each
individual placement to be approved in accordance with each
authority’s internal governance and Human Resources
processes; and

In

to the Motion moved by Councillor Field and seconded by Councillor
Gray on the National Planning Policy Framework.
 
Whilst a formal amendment was not made to the Motion, it was
suggested and agreed that should the Motion be carried, the Leader
of Council be authorised to include within his letter to the
Secretary of State the application of greywater reuse in water
systems.
 
In
accordance with Council Procedure Rule 17.5(a) a vote by roll call
was requested by four Members, as follows:

Barnes, Biggs, Bradley, Burton, Clark, Mrs Cook, Creaser, Drayson,

Thomas, Timpe and Winter.

Chowdhury, Coleman, Delany, Legg and McCourt.
 
The
Motion being put forward was declared CARRIED.
 
RESOLVED: That Rother District
Council:
 

1)    
objects to the proposed National Planning Policy
Framework changes regarding Biodiversity Net Gain and Net Zero
Construction;
 

2)    
calls on the Government to empower councils to
protect and restore nature and to set ambitious energy and
sustainability standards for new developments, through local plans
processes;
 

3)    
endorses the letter, coordinated by the Town and
Country Planning Association and signed by over 60 local
authorities, businesses and Non-Governmental Organisations, on this
issue; and
 

4)    
requests that the Leader of the Council writes to
the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local
Government on this matter.

content:
The
2025/26 Community Grants Programme (CGP), totalling £100,000,
plus £13,000 management contribution, was administered by
Sussex Community Foundation (SCF) under a Service Level Agreement
(SLA).  The CGP ran from 15 September
2025 to 31 October 2025.  Overall, 52
applications were received from Voluntary, Community and Social
Enterprise groups and parishes, requesting £462,843;
£98,913 was awarded to 15 groups and partnerships as detailed
in Appendix A to the report.
 
It
was proposed that delegated authority be granted to the Member
Community Grants Panel (MCGP – Terms of Reference detailed at
Appendix C) to ensure applications were processed within the grant
window.  As most applications came from
parish councils, a “Top Tips for Parishes” guidance
information sheet, at Appendix B to the report, was produced and
published on the Council’s website to clarify the CGP
criteria.  It was noted that some
applicants had confused the Council’s Community Grants Scheme
(CGS) with the main SCF CGP, highlighting the need for clearer
signposting and communications to emphasise that organisations
could apply to the Council’s CGS while also holding an SCF
CGP grant.  Feedback was given to
unsuccessful applicants, and SCF had confirmed that they would
offer telephone consultations.  Future
applicants would be directed to contact SCF with application
queries.  It was noted that a webpage
detailing all various grants that were available was being compiled
and would be available shortly.
 
The
report highlighted the next steps for the 2025/26 funding round
which included visits to selected funded projects with Councillor
involvement and promotional activity; monitoring of all funded
projects by SCF within six to 12 months of funding award; and
production of a summary report by SCF in January 2027, highlighting
successful projects and lessons learned to inform the
Council’s annual report.  For the
2026/27 funding round, it was proposed that the process be reviewed
to reflect lessons learned; the funding round be launched in June
2026 with a closing date in early to mid-July 2026; and the MCGP to
meet in September 2026, with applicants notified of outcomes by
October 2026.
 
It
was noted that advice was being sought regarding the Rother
Community Lottery and how it would operate following Local
Government Reorganisation; Surrey authorities were in a similar
position and seeking advice which would be made available to Rother
District Council as soon as it was available.  It was confirmed that the £100,000 fund was
substantially larger than the revenue generated by the Lottery
income.
 
Cabinet thanked SCF for timely application processing and
supported continuing the partnership for 2026/27 and 2027/28,
noting alignment with East Sussex County Council.  They agreed to delegate project selection to the
MCGP, the Leader of the Council to appoint its membership, and the
Head of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services to agree
the SLA at the same funding level with SCF for the next two
municipal years.
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)    
the projects funded through the Community Grants
Scheme for 2025/26 be noted;
 

2)    
the proposed next steps, as set out above, based on
lessons learned from review of the 2025/26 programme, be
approved;
 

3)    
delegated authority be granted to the Member
Community Grants Panel to select successful projects through the
scheme going forward, selected against agreed criteria;
 

4)    
the Leader of the Council to appoint up to five
Members to the Community Grants Panel, to ensure optimum
representation;
 

5)    
the Community Grants Scheme be funded for 2026/27
and 2027/28 at the same funding level, via a Service Level
Agreement with Sussex Community Foundation; and
 

6)    
delegated authority be granted to the Head of
Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services to agree the
Service Level Agreement with Sussex Community Foundation to
continue administering this programme in 2026/27 and
2027/28.
 
(Councillor Delany declared an interest in this matter in so far
as he was a paid employee of the Bexhill Foodbank, a recipient of a
community grant, and in accordance with the Member’s Code of
Conduct, remained in the room during the consideration
thereof.)
topline: The Cabinet has decided to continue funding the Community Grants Programme for 2026/27 and 2027/28, delegating project selection to the Member Community Grants Panel.

purpose:
To provide an update to Members on the
acquisition of Temporary Accommodation.
content:
Cabinet considered the report of the Head of Housing and
Strategic Assets which provided an update on progress and financial
performance of the Temporary Accommodation Programme (TAP), Local
Authority Housing Fund (LAHF) grant and funding changes to meet
Afghan Resettlement (AR) obligations, whilst maximising grant
opportunities to reduce reliance on high-cost temporary
accommodation (TA).
 
Since 2019, the TAP had expanded the Council’s TA
portfolio, which delivered annual revenue cost avoidance of
approximately £975,000 while providing stable
accommodation.  Ongoing participation in
the LAHF remained key to securing external grant funding and
supporting both general needs TA and homes for households under the
AR Programme.  It was the Housing
Delivery Team’s (HDT) responsibility to deliver the TAP,
supporting the Council’s ambition to increase direct housing
supply, with financial oversight retained by the Corporate
Development Team.
 
Annual TA expenditure was £2.7m.  Demand remained high, with around 264 households
in TA or move-on accommodation, with approximately 70% reliant on
costly third-party interim provision, which placed increased
pressure on the Council’s Revenue Budget.
 
In
April 2024, the TAP was increased by £12m to deliver 50
additional Council-owned TA homes.  To
date, 25 properties had been acquired. 
The Council owned 75 high quality TA and move-on properties across
the district (mainly in Bexhill, with some in Rye); 69 were
occupied and the remainder were being refurbished ready to
let.  It was noted that purchasing TA
within the rural areas was difficult due to accessibility and
management, however the market towns and larger villages could be
considered.  
 
A
further 25 TA homes were required to meet target, including 14
properties part-funded through Round 4 of the LAHF.  Under revised LAHF conditions, a proportion of
these homes must support AR for use as settled accommodation for a
minimum of three years before reverting to general needs use, if
and when an AR household vacated it. 
Two properties were still to be acquired under LAHF Round 3,
including one for AR, with a further TA property under
offer.  All three were expected to be
completed in Quarter 1 2026/27, which completed the Round 3
programme.  It was noted that properties
would continue to be brought through street purchases.  The HDT would also develop proposals for a
small-scale new-build programme and seek additional external
funding.  Further details would be
reported at a future meeting.
 
To
date, the Council had invested £25m in the TAP, including
£5.3m in external grant (c£7.7m expected). £16.6m
had been spent, including £6.9m since the last
update.  Approximately £8.9m
remained to deliver the final 25 properties, subject to a funding
commitment under LAHF Round 4 (£1.8m assumed to be
met).  The programme was expected to
deliver a return on investment of approximately 5.2%.  A £2.3m LAHF Round 4 grant, exceeding the
original assumption, required a £566,020 increase to the TA
Capital Programme, bringing the total to £25.6m and enabling
the acquisition of the remaining 25 homes, including larger family
properties.
 
The
report outlined the purpose of the LAHF, established in 2022 to
support local authorities to acquire TA with a proportion
ringfenced for Afghan and Ukrainian resettlement schemes,
highlighted key differences between fund rounds, and Appendix 1 to
the report referenced the timelines showing how LAHF rounds aligned
with varying accommodation demands.  The
Council had received £3.74m through LAHF Rounds 1 to 3 to
acquire 28 properties, 14 for Afghan and Ukrainian resettlement,
which would revert to general needs housing once resettlement was
complete.
 
It
was noted that a full comprehensive report concerning the Town Hall
complex would be coming forward later in the summer to bring
forward a range of options.  It was
hoped that the Social and Affordable Homes Programme and the
£39 billion that had been earmarked by Government would
provide a significant boost in the coming months and years, in
terms of delivering affordable homes across the
country. 
 
Cabinet supported the budget amendment, noted progress on the
TAP, and agreed it strengthened the Council’s housing supply,
reduced exposure to volatile private sector TA costs, and improved
the sustainability of homelessness provision.
 
RECOMMENDED: That an amendment to the
Temporary Accommodation Capital Programme to reflect the confirmed
£2.3m Homes England Local Authority Housing Fund Round 4
grant award, resulting in a net increase of £566,020 to the
approved programme budget, be approved.

progress of the Temporary Accommodation Programme,
including financial performance under the Local Authority Housing
Fund Rounds 1–3 be noted;

the revised Local Authority Housing Funds Rounds 3
and 4 funding conditions, which support the provision of settled
accommodation for Afghan arrivals, ensure compliance with Afghan
Resettlement Programme commitments, and optimise grant funding to
deliver additional temporary accommodation be noted; and
 

3)    
the Local Authority Housing Funds Round 4 allocation
of £2.3m (subject to terms) to support the Temporary
Accommodation Programme to deliver 14 properties between
2026–2030, comprising five Afghan Resettlement Programme
homes, and nine general needs Temporary Accommodation homes, in

*The

procedure under Rule 16 of the Overview and Scrutiny Procedure

purpose:
To seek Cabinet approval to provide licences
to occupy public conveniences to Bexhill-on-Sea Town
Council
content:
It
was noted that the report contained an inaccuracy as Rye Town
Council (RTC) did not currently operate Lucknow Place or Station
Approach toilets, it only operated Gun Gardens and the Strand
Quay.
 
Since 2025, Bexhill-on-Sea Town Council (BTC) and RTC had
managed eight of the Council’s public toilets, as detailed
within the report, ensuring that they remained open during peak
summer periods and holidays.  At
present, no formal legal agreement was put in place, leaving both
parties exposed to risk. 
 
Legal licences had been drafted to formalise the arrangements
and allow BTC and RTC to continue to operate and maintain the
facilities for 12 months as an interim arrangement, pending
devolution or commercial leasing.  If
neither occurred within that period, the licence could be renewed,
rolled over, or ended.  The facilities
would continue to operate on a peppercorn rent, with BTC and RTC
responsible for internal works and the Council retaining
responsibility for structural repairs and maintenance.  It was noted that whilst there were other public
conveniences across the district that were closed and / or
derelict, the Council had worked with those town councils that had
wished to keep certain toilets open.
 
If
the Council did not agree the licences, operations would continue
without a formal agreement, increasing risk if issues arose, and
BTC and RTC would have no obligation to keep the facilities
open.  The only alternative was closure,
which was not in the public interest, or direct operation by the
Council, which had previously been found to be financially
unviable.
 
It
was considered that none of the Bexhill Special Expenses collected
by Rother District Council (RDC) covered any of these public
conveniences; should any other community assets within Bexhill and
Rye where RDC had collected a special expense for 2026-27 transfer
before the end of the financial year, the Council would reconcile
the spending on those assets and come back to Members to determine
what would happen with the funding that had been
collected.
 
Cabinet approved the licence agreements, supporting the
continued availability of public conveniences in Bexhill and Rye.
The Cabinet Portfolio Holder, Councillor Timpe, wished to place on
record her thanks to BTC and RTC for the way that they had worked
with RDC to keep these toilets open.
 
RESOLVED: That the Council enters into
licenses for eight public conveniences in total, six to
Bexhill-on-Sea Town Council and two to Rye Town Council, to
continue their ongoing operation and management; the licenses being
for 12 months, commencing from their signing in May 2026 or
thereafter, as follows:
 

·          
Bexhill-on-Sea Town
Council: Coast Road, Normans Bay, East
Parade (De La Warr Parade), Ninfield Road, Sidley, Peartree Lane
(Roundabout), Litte Common and West Parade.

·          
Rye Town Council: Gun
Gardens and Strand Quay.
 
(Councillor Timpe declared an Other Registerable Interest in
this matter in so far as she was a Member of Bexhill-on-Sea Town
Council and a Trustee of the De La Warr Pavilion and in accordance
with the Member’s Code of Conduct, remained in the room
during the consideration thereof.)
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve license agreements for public conveniences in Bexhill and Rye, ensuring their ongoing operation and management.

purpose:
This report sets out the Council’s
proposed strategy for its service and commercial investments;
treasury management activities and capital strategy for the 2026/27
financial year.
content:
Consideration was given to the Director of Resources’
report that set out the Council’s proposed strategy for its
service and commercial investments, treasury management activities
and capital strategy for the 2026/27 financial year.
 
The
CIPFA 2021 Prudential and Treasury Management Codes required the
Council to produce a Capital Strategy Report (attached at Appendix
1 to the report).  The Strategy provided
a high level overview of how capital expenditure, financing and
treasury management supported service delivery, how risks were
managed, and the implications for long term financial
sustainability.  It was intended to give
Members a clear overview of the Council’s approach and to
ensure capital investment plans were affordable, prudent and
sustainable. 
 
Following confirmation of Local Government Reorganisation and
the implementation of a Section 24 Direction, the incoming shadow
authority was unlikely to change any decisions made prior to the
implementation of the Section 24 Direction. A Section 24 Direction
was a legal mechanism issued by the Secretary of State that
prevented outgoing predecessor councils from making significant
financial commitments without the consent of the incoming shadow
authority, once the Section 24 Directive was in place.
 
The
Council was also required to receive and approve a minimum of three
main treasury reports each year to include: Prudential and Treasury
Indicators and the Treasury Strategy; a Mid-Year Treasury
Management Report; and an Annual Treasury Report.  Quarterly reports were also produced at the end of
June and December.  Whilst not reported
to full Council, they were scrutinised by the Audit Committee and
included Treasury and Prudential Indicators, with updates where
applicable.
 
The
Treasury Management Strategy (attached at Appendix 2 to the report)
for 2026/27 covered the following two main areas, which ensured
compliance with the relevant Guidance and Codes:
 

·          
Capital issues including capital expenditure plans
and the associated prudential indicators and the Minimum Revenue
Policy.

·          
Treasury Management issues including the current
treasury position; treasury indicators; prospects for interest
rates; borrowing strategy; policy on borrowing in advance of need;
investment strategy; creditworthiness policy; and the policy on use
of external service providers.
 
The
Annual Investment Strategy (attached at Appendix 3 to the report)
focused only on financial investments and covered matters such as
appropriate credit worthiness of counter parties; terms of
deposits, transaction limits and roles and responsibilities
held.
 
The
strategies and interest rate forecasts aligned with the assumptions
used in the 2026/27 Revenue and Capital Budgets, with treasury
costs funded within the 2026/27 Revenue Budget.  Approval provided the Council with an operating
framework for the next 12 months. 
 
Members were reassured that despite the challenging financial
landscape in terms of interest rates and inflation as a result of
the continuing war in Iran, these were all kept under review and
reported quarterly to the Audit Committee, as well as through the
Corporate Programme Board in terms of impact on capital
schemes.
 
It
was noted that in relation to the Council’s asset management,
as detailed within the Capital Strategy, the Council was in a very
positive position to fill the majority of the small kiosks within
the refurbished Colonnade, in Bexhill by the start of the summer
season.  A report would be presented to
the next Cabinet meeting setting out the options for the lease of
the larger restaurant unit.
 
RECOMMENDED: That the:
 

1)    
Capital Strategy as set out at Appendix 1 to the
report be approved and adopted;
 

2)    
Treasury Management Strategy as set out at Appendix
2 to the report be approved and adopted;
 

3)    
Annual Investment Strategy as set out at Appendix 3
to the report be approved and adopted;
 

4)    
Minimum Revenue Provision Policy Statement 2026/27
be approved;
 

5)    
Prudential and Treasury Indicators as set out within
the report be approved; and
 

6)    
authorised limits set out in the report be
approved.
 
(Councillor Timpe declared an Other Registerable Interest in
this matter in so far as she was a Member of Bexhill-on-Sea Town
Council and a Trustee of the De La Warr Pavilion and in accordance
with the Member’s Code of Conduct, remained in the room
during the consideration thereof.)
 
(Councillor Field declared an Other Registerable Interest in
this matter in so far as she was a Trustee of the De La Warr
Pavilion and in accordance with the Member’s Code of Conduct,
remained in the room during the consideration thereof.)

purpose:
To consider and agree proposed amendments to
the Articles of Association of Rother DC Housing Company and direct
the Board of Directors to amend the Articles of Association
accordingly.
content:
When the
Shareholder Executive Committee (SEC) was first established in July
2025, it was anticipated that amendments might be proposed to the
Articles of Association of Rother DC Housing Company (RDCHC), in
due course.
 
Following a
detailed review, as a result of
amendments made to the Company Articles of Association and
Shareholders Agreement in November 2023, and the approval of the
Development Facility Agreement (and associated supporting
agreements), it was no longer considered necessary by officers to
propose any further amendments at this time. 
 
When combined, the
agreements in place represented a comprehensive suite of documents,
providing the Council with the control and oversight required to
protect its interests as both 100% shareholder and funder.
 
Members
acknowledged that, since the establishment of the SEC, the
oversight and understanding of both RDCHC and the Tapestry
development at Blackfriars had increased significantly, as had the
detailed reporting regarding RDCHC’s operations.  This had brought about improved collaborative
working arrangements and engagement with RDCHC, whilst increasing
transparency and oversight.
 
RESOLVED:
That the officer conclusion that as the Council has the protections
and control required across the various legal agreements in place
to provide sufficient oversight in respect of RDCHC in its role as
both 100% Shareholder and funder, no amendments are required to the
Articles of Association or any other agreements at this time be
noted and endorsed.

purpose:
To provide Members with an update regarding
Rother District Council Housing Company (RDCHC), and to enable the
Shareholder Executive Committee to monitor the performance of RDCHC
effectively.
content:
Consideration was
given to the report of the Director of Resources that set out the
performance position for the Council’s wholly owned company,
Rother DC Housing Company (RDCHC) for the period to March
2026.  The report also addressed one of
the recommendations made within the recent Housing Company
Governance audit (detailed at Confidential Appendix A) being
considered separately by the Audit Committee at its June
meeting. 
 
The report set out
the notable highlights and key issues
and the following were brought to Members’ attention:
 
Ø 
in February 2026, RDCHC won an award from the Local Authority
Building Control (LABC) Warranty provider, which recognised
’the quality of the site wide
workmanship and management’ of the scheme, primarily an award
acknowledging the work of the contractor Greymoor; this was a significant achievement
supported by various press and social media releases;
 
Ø 
Greymoor had been able to complete
a number of the housing clusters
significantly ahead of the original anticipated completion dates,
leading to early transfer of some plots to Places for People(PfP), which would
have a positive impact on the cashflow; this would also help to
mitigate against any delays to the open market sales units;
 
Ø 
dates contained within the Joint Contracts Tribunal (JCT) contract
were on track to complete as expected; the first phase of
completions were released in March 2026, with the whole scheme on
track to be completed by September 2027; and
 
Ø 
the latest cashflow position in April 2026 highlighted peak debt of
£38m being reached this month.
 
The Key Performance
Indicator data provided by RDCHC had been RAG (Red, Amber, Green)
rated to consider current risks against overall progress of the
Blackfriars programme, as detailed in the report and Confidential
Appendix A to the report.   
 
It was noted that
profit, debt and revenue metrics were all now rated as green; there
had been a change from the previous debt metric due to the
agreement RDCHC had reached with PfP
and the acceleration of the delivery programme by Greymoor.  The updated
Funding Drawdown Efficiency summary indicator position showed an
underspend of £0.45m against a drawdown of £4.6m, which
was a reduced variance of 10% against the target and was a positive
improvement since the last reporting period.
 
The report also set
out the main risks associated with both the delivery of the housing
and the provision of the loan to RDCHC, with the two issues being
fundamentally connected.  The £40m
loan provision represented a significant financial risk to Rother
District Council and was the single largest item of expenditure
within the Council’s £191m Capital Programme. Two of
the key risk factors were the ability to deliver the housing at the
rate required in line with the JCT construction contract and the
ability to sell at the rate required and for the values
assumed.  There were also new emerging
risks related to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, in terms
of inflation, living costs and bank and mortgage rate
increases.  The Council’s Risk
Register was included within Confidential Appendix B, which
included a number of risks specific to
the Blackfriars development and also
some wider corporate risks in respect of the Council’s
position as 100% shareholder and lender.
 
The Shareholder
Executive Committee moved into confidential session to consider the
contents of the Confidential Appendices (Agenda Item 10) and
Members asked a number of questions in
relation to sales and marketing and possible incentive schemes that
might be used to ensure sale completions.
 
Members were
reassured that RDCHC was proactively looking at all possible
avenues to increase sales, within the current systemic challenging
housing market.  Members were
particularly pleased to note that Greymoor had won an award from the LABC Warranty
provider and requested that RDCHC passed on the Council’s
congratulations to Greymoor.     
 
RESOLVED:
That:
 
1)    
the RDCHC Board arrangements (as contained within exempt Appendix A
to the report) be considered and agreed as acceptable;

 
2)    
the skills and knowledge of the non-executive directors (as
contained within exempt Appendix A to the report) be considered and
agreed as acceptable;

 
3)    
Shareholder Executive Committee (SEC) request that RDCHC complete
an annual audit of Board skills and effectiveness, to be completed
by the end of 2026, for review by the SEC in early 2027 (as
contained within exempt Appendix A to the report); and

 
4)    
the contents of the report be noted.
 
(Appendices A and B
to this report were considered exempt from publication by virtue of
paragraph 3 of Schedule 12A of the Local Government Act 1972, as
amended).
topline: The Shareholder Executive Committee has decided to review and approve the performance of Rother DC Housing Company, addressing achievements, risks, and financial implications.

In certain
circumstances the Planning Committee will indicate that it is only
prepared to grant or refuse planning permission if, or unless,
certain amendments to a proposal are undertaken or subject to
completion of outstanding consultations.  In these circumstances the Head of Planning can be
given delegated authority to issue the decision of the Planning
Committee once the requirements of the Committee have been
satisfactorily complied with.  A
delegated decision does not mean that planning permission or
refusal will automatically be issued. 
If there are consultation objections, difficulties, or negotiations
are not satisfactorily concluded, then the application will have to
be reported back to the Planning Committee.  This delegation also allows the Head of Planning
to negotiate and amend applications, conditions, reasons for
refusal and notes commensurate with the instructions of the
Committee.  Any applications which are
considered prior to the expiry of the consultation reply period are
automatically delegated for a decision.

the Planning Applications be determined as detailed

content:
The
application had been called in by Councillor Stanger for the
following reasons, the impact on the living conditions of
neighbours and conservation.
 
The
Planning Committee had visited the site and heard concerns from Councillor Bayliss who spoke on
behalf of the local Ward Members.  Comments from statutory and non?statutory
consultees, as detailed in the report, were also
considered.
 
The
application sought retrospective permission for a shepherd’s
hut in the front garden for use as a holiday let and a yurt in the
rear garden for a small wellbeing business.  Amendments limited the yurt’s temporary
usage from March to October (dismantled the rest of the year), with
a maximum of 10 students across four courses, and no drumming or
wood burning.  The site was within the
Bexhill development boundary and the Bexhill Old Town Conservation
Area, in a sustainable location close to local amenities and the
Manor Gardens car park.  Both structures
were well screened, not readily visible in the wider street scene,
and had a neutral impact on the Conservation Area.  Tourism and small businesses were supported by
local and national policy, and officers considered the proposal, as
conditioned, would not harm neighbouring residential
amenities.
 
Members were disappointed that the Applicant had not consulted
neighbouring properties prior to erecting the structures, and that
the business had been operating for approximately one
year.  Planning Officers advised that
the yurt could have been erected under permitted development if
used solely for personal purposes, and that toilet facilities would
be provided within the main dwelling. 
Located in an urban area, where some noise was audible from events
at the nearby St. Peter’s Community Centre.  Therefore, sympathy was expressed by Members
towards the neighbouring properties regarding noise and smoke
nuisance.  However, it was noted that no
environmental health complaints had been received. 
 
Councillor Stanger moved the motion to REFUSE (Full Planning
Permission) and seconded by Councillor Gray for the following
reasons, harm to the Conservation Area, inadequate parking and
impact on the neighbouring residential properties.  Following advice from the Head of Planning that
these were inadequate material reasons (potentially undefendable at
appeal in this case), Councillors Stanger and Gray withdrew the
motion.
 
After further deliberation, the Planning Committee supported the
Planning Officer’s recommendation but agreed to grant
permission on a temporary two-year basis, with the impact on
neighbouring properties to be assessed before any permanent
permission was considered.
 
Councillor Drayson moved the motion to GRANT (Temporary Planning
Permission for two years) subject to planning conditions and this
was seconded by Councillor Creaser.  The
motion was declared CARRIED (6 for / 3 against).
 
DECISION: GRANT (TEMPORARY PLANNING
PERMISSION FOR TWO YEARS)
 
SUBJECT TO
CONDITIONS:
 

1.       
The use and related development hereby permitted
shall be discontinued and the land restored to its former condition
on or before the 16 April 2028 in accordance with a scheme of work
submitted to and approved in writing by the Local Planning
Authority. 
Reason: The
use is potentially detrimental to the amenities of the occupiers of
the adjacent properties, and this permission is granted temporarily
to enable the Local Planning Authority to monitor and assess the
effects of the proposal, having regard to the criteria set out in
Policy OSS4 (ii) of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy.

 

 2.    
The development hereby permitted shall be carried out and retained
in accordance with the following approved plans and
details: 
Location
Plan, dated 21 May 2025
Drawing No.
1 001 01, dated 15/05/2025 – Block Plan
Drawing No.
2 001 01, dated 15/05/2025 – Proposed plans and
elevations (shepherd hut)
Drawing No.
2 001 02, dated 15/05/2025 – Proposed pans and
elevations (yurt)
Design
& Access Statement, dated 4 July 2025
Email dated
24 March 2026 with Agent
Reason: For
the avoidance of doubt and in the interests of proper
planning.

 

3.      The Shepherds Hut hereby
approved is to be occupied for holiday purposes only and shall not
be occupied as a person’s sole or main place of
residence.
Reason: To
ensure that the approved holiday accommodation is not used for
unauthorised permanent residential occupation, in accordance with
Policies OSS4 (iii) EC6 and RA3 of the Rother Local Plan Core
Strategy and Policy DEC2 of the Development and Site Allocations
Plan.

 

4.      The owners / operators shall
maintain an up-to-date register of the names of all occupiers of
the Shepherds Hut as a holiday unit on the site, and of their main
home addresses, and shall make this information available at all
reasonable times to the Local Planning Authority.
Reason: To
ensure that the approved holiday accommodation is not used for
unauthorised permanent residential occupation in accordance with
Policies OSS4 (iii) EC6 and RA3 of the Rother Local Plan Core
Strategy and Policy DEC2 of the Development and Site Allocations
Plan.

 

5.     
The Shepherds Hut as hereby approved for holiday purposes shall not
be occupied for more than 56 days in total in any calendar year by
any one person.

         Reason: To
ensure that the approved holiday accommodation is not used for
unauthorised permanent residential occupation in accordance with
Policies OSS4 (iii) EC6 and RA3 of the Rother Local Plan Core
Strategy and Policy DEC2 of the Development and Site Allocations
Plan.

 

6.     
The Yurt shall only be located within the rear garden between
the months of March and October in any calendar year and be used
for a maximum of four training courses per calendar year between
March and 30 June, with each course not to be run for more than two
consecutive days in any calendar month, with a maximum of 10
students at any time and organised and run only by the
Applicant, Rachel Streeter. The Yurt shall only be used
for personal purposes by the Applicant and family between July and
October. 
Reason: To
ensure that the approved business remains limited in its extent and
to protect the residential amenities of the neighbouring properties
at Church Farm and Chantry Farm and noting that the Yurt can only
be assembled and disassembled during the months of March and
October, in accordance with Policy OSS4 (ii) of the
Rother Local Plan Core Strategy and Paragraph 198 of the National
Planning Policy Framework.

 

7.      No
use of drums or amplified music shall take place at the site
and use of the Yurt for the courses hereby approved, shall only
take place between the hours of 9.00 and 16:00 on
weekdays, Saturdays and Sundays but not at any time on Bank or
Public Holidays.
Reason: To ensure that the approved business remains
limited in its extent and to protect the residential amenities of
the neighbouring properties at Church Farm and Chantry Farm, in
accordance with Policy OSS4 (ii) of the Rother Local Plan
Core Strategy and Paragraph 198 of the National Planning Policy
Framework.
 

NOTE
 

1.       
The Applicant is reminded to positively encourage
customers visiting the site to use the nearby Manor Garden car park
or public transport to access the site.

 

NATIONAL PLANNING POLICY
FRAMEWORK: In accordance with
Paragraph 39 of the National Planning Policy Framework (2024), the
Council has worked in a positive and pro-active way with the
Applicant and has negotiated amendments to the application to
enable the grant of planning permission with conditions.

content:
RM
DECISION: GRANT (FULL PLANNING
PERMISSION)
 
The
application had been called in by one of the local Ward Members
(Councillor Coupar) if the recommendation was for REFUSAL for the
following reason, that the proposal was a small, hobby / employment
space that would have no impact on the High Weald National
Landscape (HWNL).
 
The Planning Committee had visited the
site.  The proposal sought to erect a
standalone private artist’s studio on an existing concrete
slab in a rural field east of Cottage Lane (within the land holding
of the Applicant).  A previous similar
application had been withdrawn following Planning Officer
advice.  The site was in the countryside
and HWNL, and the proposal was unrelated to agriculture or
tourism.  Planning Officers concluded
that it did not meet any exceptions for countryside development,
offered no economic benefit, lacked access information, and would
harm the character and appearance of the countryside and HWNL due
to its location and domestic appearance.
 
The Planning Committee heard from the Applicant and
one of the local Ward Members (Councillor Coupar) who supported the
scheme.  Comments from Westfield Parish
Council, as detailed in the report, were also
considered.
 
Members asked a series of questions in relation to several
issues and commented as follows: previous application for a stable block and access
track was approved in 2000, with the foundations to this laid and
thus the permission was extant; impact on the
HWNL; protection of the countryside; isolated location / distance
of the concrete slab in relation to the residential curtilage (if
nearer to the main dwelling the application might be acceptable);
concern that the building would be converted into a domestic
dwelling; further planning permission would be required should the
Applicant want to use the building for commercial purposes; reduced
carbon footprint; provided a dedicated workplace; important not to
set a precedent for the countryside; as the site was not
overlooked, it was considered an excellent location for an
artist’s studio; materials were considered acceptable and
appropriate for the setting; wooden screens covering the glazing
would protect the dark skies; the scale and design was acceptable;
the concrete slab was an eyesore; concrete access path had been
installed by the previous owner; noted the Applicant’s plans
to re-landscape the site by planting more trees; and supported home
working opportunities. 
 
After deliberation, the Planning Committee accepted that,
although the site was outside the defined development boundary and
within the HWNL, the harm to the countryside would be
minimal.  They noted the
Applicant’s intention to work from home using the building as
a private artist’s studio and emphasised that it must not be
converted into a domestic dwelling. 
Members agreed that the existing concrete slab was an eyesore and
considered the scale and height of the proposal comparable to an
approved agricultural building.  It was
also noted that there was an extant permission at the site for a
similarly sized building.  Subject to
conditions controlling landscaping and protection of dark skies,
the Planning Committee granted full planning permission contrary to
the officer recommendation, with relevant planning conditions
delegated to officers.
 
Councillor Gray moved the motion to GRANT (Full Planning
Permission) and this was seconded by
Councillor Grohne.  The motion was declared CARRIED (7 for / 2
against).

and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004).

High Weald National Landscape in accordance with Policies OSS4(iii)
and EN1 of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy and Policies DEN1
and DEN2 of the Development and Site Allocations Local
Plan.  

 

4.       
No development above ground level shall commence
until an Ecological Design Strategy (EDS) addressing ecological
enhancement measures, has been submitted to and approved in writing
by the Local Planning Authority.  The
EDS should be in line with best practice and shall include the
following:

a)   
Purpose and conservation objectives for the proposed
ecological works;

b)   
review of site potential and constraints;  

c)   
detailed design(s) and / or working method(s) to
achieve stated objectives;  

d)   
extent and location / area of proposed works
on appropriate scale maps and plans;  

e)

and

works, where relevant.  
The EDS
shall be implemented in accordance with the approved details, and
all features shall be retained in that manner
thereafter.
Reason: To
ensure that the measures considered necessary to enhance the site
are provided as required by Policy EN5 of the Rother Local Plan
Core Strategy; Policy DEN4 of the Development and Site Allocations
Plan and Paragraphs 187 and 193 of the National Planning Policy
Framework. 

 

5.       
Prior to any use of the building hereby permitted,
details of measures to protect dark night skies shall be submitted
to and approved in writing by the Local Planning
Authority.  The approved measures to
protect dark night skies shall be installed prior to any use of the
building and thereafter retained in accordance with the approved
details.
Reason: To
prevent light pollution and to protect the dark night skies and
local ecology of the surrounding countryside and High Weald
National Landscape, in accordance with Policies EN1 and
EN5 of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy and Policies DEN1, DEN2
and DEN7 of the Development and Site Allocations Local
Plan. 

 

6.       
No floodlighting or any other external means of
illumination shall be provided, installed or operated at the
site.
Reason: To
safeguard the dark night skies and ecology of the High Weald
National Landscape and visual amenities of the locality and living
conditions of the neighbouring property in accordance with Policies
OSS4(ii)(iii), RA2(vi), RA3(v) and EN1(i) of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy and
Policies DEN1, DEN2 and DEN7 of the Development and Site
Allocations Local Plan. 

 

7.       
No development above ground level shall take place
until a landscaping scheme, incorporating native tree planting, has
been submitted to and approved in writing by the Local Planning
Authority.  The landscaping shall be
carried out as approved and within one year of the approval of
these details.
Reason: To
ensure a high-quality landscape setting taking account of the
characteristics of the area within the High Weald National
Landscape, in accordance with Policy EN1 and EN3 of the
Rother Local Plan Core Strategy and Policies DEN1 and DEN2 of the
Development and Site Allocations Local Plan. 

 

8.       
There shall be no insertion of any additional
mezzanine floor within the building including the roof
space.
Reason: To
enable the Local Planning Authority to properly consider and
control the development in terms of access, parking and impact to
neighbour’s amenity, having regard to Policies OSS4 (ii &
iv), TR3 and TR4 of the Rother Local Plan Core
Strategy. 

 

9.       
The premises shall be used as a
private artist’s studio for a single
individual and for no other purpose (including any other
purpose in Class E of the Schedule to the Town and Country Planning
(Use Classes) Order 1987 (as amended, or in any provision
equivalent to that Class in any statutory instrument revoking and
re-enacting that Order with or without
modification). 
Reason: To
enable the Local Planning Authority to properly consider and
control the development in terms of access, parking and impact to
neighbour’s amenity, having regard to Policies OSS4 (ii &
iv), TR3 and TR4 of the Rother Local Plan Core
Strategy. 

 

10.    
The building hereby permitted shall not be occupied
as self-contained residential accommodation or overnight sleeping
accommodation. 
Reason: To
ensure that the approved building is not used or occupied as an
unauthorised residential dwelling within the countryside in
accordance with Policies OSS4 (iii), RA2 and RA3 of the Rother
Local Plan Core Strategy.
 
NOTE: 
 

1.       
Please be advised that permitted development
rights as set out under Part 1, Schedule 2 of the General Permitted
Development (England) Order 2015 (as amended) do not apply to this
development as it would not be within the curtilage of a
dwellinghouse.  
 
NATIONAL PLANNING POLICY FRAMEWORK: In accordance with Paragraph 39 of the National Planning
Policy Framework, the Council has worked in a positive and
pro-active manner and has imposed planning conditions to enable the
grant of planning permission.
