RM
DECISION: SUBJECT TO A SEQUENTIAL
FLOOD TEST BEING COMPLETED TO THE SATISFACTION OF THE COUNCIL, TO
GRANT (FULL PLANNING PERMISSION) SUBJECT TO APPROPRIATE PLANNING
CONDITIONS AND A SECTION 106 LEGAL AGREEMENT TO BE DELEGATED TO
PLANNING OFFICERS IN CONSULTATION WITH THE CHAIR OF PLANNING
COMMITTEE
 
This
application had been called in by one of the local Ward Members
(Councillor Osborne) if the recommendation was for REFUSAL for the
following reason, that the proposal offered positive contributions
regarding housing type, economic uplift and social
value.
 
The Planning Committee had visited the
site.  The proposal sought to build a
detached two-storey building containing 10 affordable apartments,
together with associated works and change of use to Grade II Listed
Pond Cottage, on land situated outside the development boundary and
within the High Weald National Landscape (HWNL).  The scheme required the removal of mature trees
and loss of an historic routeway. 
Planning Officers concluded that it would introduce a large, modern
contemporary development, which failed to secure policy compliant
affordable housing, would impact the character and appearance of
the HWNL and cause harm to the setting of the Grade II Listed
Building.
 
The Planning Committee heard from the Agent who
confirmed that the Applicant would be willing to enter into a
Section 106 Agreement.  They also heard
from one of the local Ward Members (Councillor Osborne) who
supported the scheme given its benefits.  Comments from statutory and non?statutory
consultees, as detailed in the report, and an update sheet
including pre-application advice were also considered.
 
Members asked a series of questions in relation to several
issues and commented as follows: located in a sustainable area next
to a supermarket including car park and petrol station within the
HWNL; was a green buffer between the approach to Peasmarsh and the
supermarket; would require the removal of a significant number of
trees, reducing the openness of the corner plot, although some
replacement planting was proposed; lack of evidence submitted to
demonstrate that the level of affordable housing would meet
specific local housing need; social rental units not viable; close
proximity to the Grade II Listed Building, however in relation to
its setting, the development would be disproportionately large;
site susceptible to significant flood risk; sequential flood test
completed, but not passed as there were potentially other sites
within Peasmarsh that were not at risk of flooding; Romney Marshes
Area Internal Drainage Board had been consulted (no response
received); not readily visible from eastern approach, as a high
soil bank reduced the perceived height of the development;
disappointment aired that pre-application advice was not
incorporated, which included design and materials guidance; scheme
not in accordance with High Weald Housing Design Guide; use of
uncharacteristic building materials (e.g. stone); Community Hub
would deliver public benefits to the wider community (e.g.
healthcare and social events); locally supported scheme;
opportunity for older residents to downsize, freeing up larger
family homes in Peasmarsh; and would contribute towards the Council’s lack of a
five-year housing supply.
 
After debate and deliberation, the Planning Committee concluded
that the public benefits (in particular the 100% affordable
housing, the delivery of housing and securing the community use of
Pond Cottage) outweighed the harm to the character and appearance
of the area, including the landscape and scenic beauty of the HWNL
and the less than substantial harm to the setting of the Grade II
Listed Building.  The site was
considered sustainable, adjacent to a supermarket and not readily
visible from the eastern approach.  The
scheme would deliver much needed affordable housing supported by
Peasmarsh Parish Council, restore the Grade II Listed Building for
use as a Community Hub, and contribute to addressing the
Council’s five-year housing supply shortfall.  Subject to a Section 106 Legal Agreement and a
sequential flood test being completed to the Council’s
satisfaction, the Planning Committee granted full planning
permission, contrary to officer recommendation, with relevant
planning conditions and Section 106 Legal Agreement (including but
not limited to, securing 100% affordable housing and the community
use of Pond Cottage) be delegated to officers in consultation with
the Chair of the Planning Committee.
 
Councillor Stanger moved the motion to GRANT (Full Planning
Permission), subject to planning conditions and a Section 106 Legal
Agreement and this was seconded by Councillor Creaser.  The motion was declared
CARRIED (9 for unanimous).

purpose:
To consider the sale of land at the King Offa
site.
content:
In July 2025,
Cabinet agreed that officers progressed options for a sale of
residential land at the King Offa site in Bexhill for affordable
housing tenures and report back.  
Officers prepared Sales Particulars and sought offers from six
Registered Providers (RPs) who operated within the district at this
scale and with this type of project.
 
Following this
work, officers were recommending acceptance of a Conditional
Purchase, Subject to Planning, to a RP, as detailed within the
report, which would provide 100% affordable housing tenures. Terms
of the conditional offer, the valuation report and funding were set
out at confidential Appendices B, C and D to the
report. 
 
The RP would seek
planning permission once contracts were exchanged and, following a
grant of satisfactory planning permission, the RP and the Council
would then complete the purchase of the site according to the terms
contained within the Agreement.  It was
proposed that a budget of £30,000 be approved for the legal
agreements required for this element, to be funded from capital
receipts, as legitimate costs incurred as part of the disposal.
 
There was a risk
that any unspent Brownfield Land Release Funding (BLRF) provided by
One Public Estate (OPE) and Ministry of Housing, Communities and
Local Government, awarded to the Council in relation to the King
Offa site would need to be returned; however, some of this funding
had been used to prepare the site for development, so not all would
be lost.  The Council had been in
continual contact with OPE regarding the BLRF, who had agreed that
the remaining BLRF could be retained as long
as the timescales within the July 2025 Cabinet paper were
met.
 
It was noted that
whilst an open market sale would likely generate a higher offer,
the proposed disposal was considered a very credible offer from a
RP who was well positioned to deliver on the commitments made. The
proposed sale would facilitate the delivery of approximately
45–49 additional Affordable Homes, alongside a financial
payment for the land.  It was
acknowledged that in reality, this
payment would likely be made to the new unitary authority, as given
the timescales involved in submitting and achieving planning
permission, it was unlikely to be within two years. 
 
Cabinet was pleased
to agree that the offer, taking the combined benefits of affordable
housing and a capital receipt, without the planning risk,
represented the best consideration reasonably obtainable and
therefore complied with the Council’s obligations under
Section 123 of the Local Government Act 1972 in terms of best
value. 
 
RESOLVED:
That:
 

1)   the Chief Executive be granted
delegated authority in consultation with the Leader and Cabinet
Portfolio Holder for Housing, to agree final terms, prepare and
exchange contracts for the Conditional Sale of the land known as
King Offa for the delivery of Affordable Housing; and

 

2)   a budget of up to
£30,000 be approved to allow the necessary legal agreement(s)
to be drafted and entered, to be funded from capital receipts.
 
(Appendices B, C
and D to this report were considered exempt from publication by
virtue of paragraph 3 of Schedule 12A of the Local Government Act
1972, as amended).
topline: The Cabinet has decided to accept a Conditional Purchase for the sale of land at the King Offa site in Bexhill for affordable housing.

purpose:
To consider the implications arising from the
The Renters Rights Act
content:
Under the Renters
Rights Act (October) 2025, the Council was required to enforce
updated housing legislation covering assured tenancies, possession
grounds, rent matters, pet ownership, discrimination and rent
increases.  This necessitated a revised
Enforcement Policy and updated civil penalty powers under the
Protection of Eviction Act 1977.  An
overview of the Act was provided in Appendix A to the report, and
its provisions would be implemented in stages over the next decade;
the provisions of the Act would bring about a significant culture
change. 
 
Government (New
Burdens) funding had been provided in 2025/26 and the same level was expected in
2026/27, but would not be sustained into
the future.  It was likely that
additional enforcement staff would eventually be needed, funded
through income from the civil penalties. 
 
Appendices B and C
to the report set out the updated Private Sector Housing
Enforcement Policy 2026, prepared by the Association of Chief
Environmental Health Officers in conjunction with the Justice for
Tenants organisation, and a revised Civil Penalties Policy 2026,
prepared by the Justice for Tenants organisation
respectively.  After implementation, a
rise in “illegal evictions” was anticipated, which
would require the Council to take enforcement action.  An increase in complaints about property standards
and a potential reduction in private sectors lettings might also
drive higher demand for homelessness services.
It was noted that
whilst the abolition of section 21 “no fault” evictions
on 1 May 2026 might lead to a short-term increase in evictions,
raising demand for homelessness advice and temporary accommodation,
it was challenging to predict the likely impact on the
Council’s finances and housing teams and often, following
changes in legislation, the impact was less than predicted;
officers would keep the level of impact under review.
 
Cabinet was pleased
that the Government had introduced this much needed legislation
that would help to address the power balance between landlords and
tenants, with the abolition of Section 21 “no fault”
evictions.  However, there were capacity
concerns, which would hopefully be addressed by using the civil
penalty income to recruit additional environmental health staff and
the amalgamation and strengthening of teams through Local
Government Reorganisation.
 
Cabinet supported
both policies and agreed under the Act that delegated authority be
granted to the Chief Executive, Director of Governance and
Community Services, Head of Housing and Strategic Assets and Head
of Environmental Services, Licensing and Community
Safety.  It was also agreed to delegate
authority to the Chief Executive and Director of Governance and
Community Services, in consultation with the Cabinet Portfolio
Holder for Housing, to amend the policies in response to
legislative updates or minor administrative changes.
 
RECOMMENDED:
That the Private Sector Housing Enforcement Policy 2026 and the
Civil Penalties Policy 2026 be approved and adopted.
 
AND
 
*RESOLVED:
That:
 

1)   under the Act, delegated
authority be granted to the Chief Executive, Director of Governance
and Community Services, Head of Housing and Strategic Assets and
Head of Environmental Services, Licensing and Community Safety;
and
 

2)   delegated authority be granted
to the Chief Executive and Director of Governance and Community
Services, in consultation with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder for
Housing, to amend both policies following legislation or minor
local administration changes.
 
*The
RESOLVED parts of this Minute are subject to the call-in
procedure under Rule 16 of the Overview and Scrutiny Procedure
Rules by no later than 4:00pm on 23 April 2026.
 
(Councillor Bayliss
declared an Other Registerable Interest in this matter as a
leaseholder and in accordance with the Members’ Code of
Conduct, remained in the room during the consideration
thereof.)
 
(Councillor Osborne
declared Disclosable Pecuniary Interest in this matter as a
landlord and in accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct,
left the hybrid meeting room during the consideration thereof.)
 
 
(Councillor Prochak
declared Disclosable Pecuniary Interest in this matter as a
landlord and in accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct,
left the room during the consideration thereof.)

content:
Cabinet considered
the confidential report of the Director of Resources that sought
approval for the Council to act as guarantor for the
Council’s Housing Company, Rother DC Housing Company (RDCHC),
for the Local Authority Building Control (LABC)
Warranty.  The Chief Operating Officer
from RDCHC, Neill Tickle, joined the meeting remotely to assist
Members in their deliberations. 
 
LABC had confirmed
that, due to the limited financial strength of RDCHC, they were not
able to offer a 10-year warranty without the Council, as 100%
shareholder and funder, acting as guarantor.   Having the warranty in place would enable
RDCHC to transfer and sell the 200 homes and repay the funding owed
to the Council.  The financial and legal
implications were set out within the confidential report, together
with the risks. 
 
Members were
satisfied, on balance, that the proposed recommendation represented
the most responsible and pragmatic course of action. It offered a
clear path forward that supported the Council’s strategic
objectives whilst being mindful of the challenges ahead.
 
RESOLVED:
That the Council acts as guarantor for the Rother DC Housing
Company Local Authority Building Control warranty (Option B),
required to be put in place for the development at Blackfriars,
known as "Tapestry".
 
(This matter was
considered exempt from publication by virtue of paragraph 3 of
Schedule 12A of the Local Government Act 1972, as amended).
topline: The Cabinet has decided to act as guarantor for the RDCHC Local Authority Building Control warranty at Blackfriars.

purpose:
To consider amendments to the Constitution
arising from the Constitution Review Steering Group in relation to
the Formal Hybrid Committee Meeting Protocol and the Member /
Officer Protocol
content:
The Constitution
Review Steering Group (CRSG) had been reconvened to review
amendments to the Officer Scheme of Delegations and other matters
within the Constitution.  At their first
meeting (Minutes detailed at Appendix 1 to the report), the CRSG
considered proposed amendments to Part 5-6 (Hybrid Protocol for
Formal Committee Meetings) and Part 5-4 (Member / Officer Protocol)
of the Council’s Constitution. 
The Audit Committee (AC) was responsible for overseeing and
recommending changes to the Constitution.
 
A review by the
Monitoring Officer confirmed that Part 5-6 was unlawful regarding
Member attendance and required amendment.  The proposed amendments were set out in Appendix
1A to the report.  Minor revisions to
Part 5-4 were also proposed, as detailed at Appendix 1B to the
report.  It was agreed that the Member /
Officer Protocol should be reinforced through officer networks,
including incorporation into staff induction and discussion at a
forthcoming Manager’s Forum.
 
Members raised
concerns that junior officers may not necessarily feel empowered to
advise them that enquiries should be raised with Heads of Service
or Team Leaders rather than themselves, often leading to delayed
responses. Training was therefore required for both parties and
expectations managed.
 
The AC agreed to
recommend to full Council the amendments to Part 5-6 (Hybrid
Protocol for Formal Committee Meetings) and Part 5-4 (Member /
Officer Protocol) as outlined in Appendices 1A and 1B, respectively
to the report.  
           
RECOMMENDED:
That the amendments to Part 5-6 (Hybrid Protocol for Formal
Committee Meetings) and Part 5-4 (Member / Officer Protocol)
detailed within Appendices 1A and 1B, respectively to the report be
approved and adopted.
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to recommend the approval and adoption of amendments to the Council's Constitution regarding Member and Officer protocols.

purpose:
To consider the updated Corporate Risk
Register
content:
Members received
the report of the Head of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood
Services, which provided a position update on risk management
processes and the key strategic risks currently facing the
Council.
 
The Audit Committee
approved a new Risk Management Policy (RMP) in September
2022.  The RMP was reviewed annually,
including updates to the risk appetite statements where necessary
to ensure they remained aligned with the Council’s
requirements.  The most recent review
was completed by the Audit Committee in March 2025.  Cabinet subsequently reviewed the Corporate Risk
Register (CRR), the RMP and risk appetites in February 2026.
 
The CRR, attached
at Appendix A to the report was a live document.  Several risks had been updated, and some continued
to exceed the Council’s stated risk appetite, including the
following:
 

•     Risk 1:
Political – Local Government Reorganisation and Devolution
will impact delivery of Council services.  This score exceeded the Council’s risk
appetite, reflecting ongoing uncertainty surrounding local
government reorganisation.

•     Risk 2:
Financial – The high costs of rental accommodation, house
prices and living expenses are increasing demands for temporary
accommodation.  This score exceeded the
risk appetite due to rising homelessness and increasing costs, plus
recent events in Iran leading to an increase in borrowing costs.
Although mitigations were in place, a slowdown in house building
and reduced availability of affordable housing continued to present
challenges.

•     Risk 3:
Economic/Financial – Failure to operate within a sustainable
budget.  This score remained high,
reflecting ongoing financial pressure despite existing
mitigations.

•     Risk 5:
Significant breach of data protection (linked also to Risk 7: IT
failure).  This reflected increasing
risks to data protection and cyber security.

•     Risk 10:
Financial risk concerning the Rother DC Housing Company (RDCHC).
The Council were now at a critical point in terms of borrowing and
with the risk of increased cost of borrowing, the Council was
reliant on homes being sold at the required prices. Mitigations
were in place with an agreed 130 homes being sold to a registered
provider (RP).

•     Risk 11: The
Strategic Asset Management Programme may not be delivered before
local government reorganisation and before benefits are
realised.  This involved a significant
number of assets to be devolved and was delayed due to legal
processes, posing a risk to the overall delivery of the
project.
 
Members were given
the opportunity to ask questions, and the following points were
noted during the discussions:
 

•     any increase
in interest rates would lead to an increase in the income received
on the Council’s investments, therefore offsetting some
borrowing costs;

•     car park
income, council tax debts and applications for homelessness were
likely to be affected by a rise in the cost-of-living;

•     delivery of
completed houses and house sales were likely to be affected also;
and

•     RDCHC’s
scheme would soon be reaching its peak debt position of £35m
(currently at £30m). A small number of properties had been
handed over, with a few more due shortly; income from the RP was
likely to be received first.
 
RESOLVED:
That the report and Corporate Risk Register be noted.
 
(Councillor Coupar
declared an Other Registrable Interest in this matter in so far as
she was a Director of the Rother DC Housing Company Ltd and in
accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct remained in the
meeting during the consideration thereof.)
topline: The Audit Committee has approved a new Risk Management Policy to address high risks including political uncertainty and financial pressures.

purpose:
To report the proposed programme of Internal
Audit work for the coming year.
content:
Consideration was
given to the report of the Audit Manager (AM) on the Internal Audit
Plan for 2026/27 (IAP).  The Global
Internal Audit Standards required that the AM communicated the IAP
and resource requirements, including significant interim changes,
to senior management and the Audit Committee (AC) for review and
approval.
 
Attached at
Appendix A to the report was the assurance map which provided a
visual representation of the various sources of assurance received
by an organisation on its management of key service
areas.  Its purpose was to assist the
Council’s understanding of the assurance received, to
evaluate its adequacy, and to highlight any potential gaps in
coverage.  The assurance map was last
reported to the AC in March 2025 and updated for the current
position.  The assessment methodology
was set out in Appendix B to the report.  This year had seen significant improvement, with
Estates and Health and Safety remaining the only high and medium
risk areas, both of which were included in the IAP.
 
A risk assessment
was undertaken by the AM in February 2026, incorporating all new
and emerging risks identified through discussions with officers in
the Corporate Leadership Team.  High
risk activities were included in the new IAP, unless they had been
reviewed recently and were subject to follow-up.  Medium risk activities were typically reviewed
every two to three years, while low risk activities were excluded
to ensure efficient use of audit resources.
 
The 2026/27 IAP was
attached at Appendix C to the report. 
Additional high and medium risk areas considered but not included
in the final IAP were listed for information in Appendix D to the
report.
 
The AM prepared the
IAP in accordance with the Internal Audit Charter 2025, with
support from the Corporate Leadership Team (CLT).  The IAP allocated 512 audit days across 19
separate audit reviews / consultancy activities, including counter
fraud work.  A substantial proportion
focused on Governance Audits, as weaknesses in these areas could
affect the External Auditor’s overall opinion of the
Council’s financial statements.
 
Appendix E to the
report confirmed that the 2026/27 IAP could be delivered in full
using existing staff resources.
 
Progress against
the IAP would be monitored by the AM and reported to the AC
quarterly.  The AM, in consultation with
the CLT, would also keep the IAP under review and adjust as
necessary to ensure it remained aligned with the Council’s
priorities.
 
The IAP must
provide sufficient coverage to meet the Council’s statutory
obligations.  Internal Audit would
achieve this by prioritising high and medium risk activities across
key service areas.
 
Members approved
the IAP and expressed their appreciation for the AM’s
work.
 
RESOLVED:
That the Internal Audit Plan 2026/27 be approved.
 
(Councillor Coupar
declared an Other Registrable Interest in this matter in so far as
she was a Director of the Rother DC Housing Company Ltd and in
accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct remained in the
meeting during the consideration thereof.)
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to approve the Internal Audit Plan for 2026/27, allocating resources and focusing on key service areas.

purpose:
To report on the effectiveness of the Internal
Audit Service.
content:
Throughout 2025/26,
the Council’s Internal Audit Service operated in accordance
with the Global Internal Audit Standards [UK Public Sector]
(GIAS).  These standards required the
Audit Manager (AM) to undertake periodic self-assessments of the
effectiveness of Internal Audit, but they did not specify how
frequently these reviews should take place.  The AM considered it beneficial for annual reviews
to be carried out and for Members to receive the findings, prior to
31 March each year, so that reliance could be placed on the
effectiveness of Internal Audit when reviewing the Annual
Governance Statement.
 
The GIAS aimed to
achieve consistent standards for Internal Audit and included a
Quality Assurance and Improvement Programme which required both
internal and external assessments.
 
The AM conducted
the annual self-assessment of the Internal Audit function using a
toolkit provided by the Chartered Institute of Internal
Auditors.  A summary of the GIAS
assessment outcomes was presented in Appendix A to the
report.  Two areas were identified where
improved conformance was required (documentation of Continuing
Professional Development Activity; and feedback on the AM’s
performance by the Chair), which had been incorporated into the
Action Plan.  Progress on the 2025/26
Action Plan was set out in Appendix B to the report, and the
proposed 2026/27 Action Plan was provided in Appendix C to the
report.
 
An external peer
assessment was required at least once every five years.  The most recent review, undertaken in February
2023 by the Head of Internal Audit at Lewes District and Eastbourne
Borough Councils, was reported to the Committee in June
2023.  The review identified no
significant issues and confirmed that Rother District
Council’s Internal Audit function “generally
conformed” to the standards.  Due
to Local Government Reorganisation, no further external peer
assessments were expected during the Council’s remaining
lifetime.
 
Domain IV,
Principle 12 of the GIAS required that the AM sought input from the
Audit Committee and senior management when setting performance
objectives, and to obtain feedback on outcomes.  The AM currently reported annually on a set of
established performance measures, as identified within the
report.  It was proposed that these
measures continued for 2026/27, although Members might choose to
amend or add to them as appropriate. After some discussion, Members
chose to add a further two performance indicators from the list
provided in the report, namely: Audit Assignments – Completed
within planned time (target 90%); and Audit Recommendations –
Percentage of outstanding audit recommendations followed up each
quarter (target 100%).
 
The latest internal
assessment and the February 2023 peer review confirmed that the
Internal Audit Service continued to comply well with professional
standards, with no significant areas of partial compliance.
Accordingly, the AM concluded that the service generally conformed
to the standards, a view supported by both the Section 151 Officer
and the Monitoring Officer.
 
RESOLVED:
That:
 
1)         the
Review of Internal Audit 2025/26 be approved; and
 

2)         the
existing performance indicators be adopted for 2026/27, with the
addition of: Audit Assignments – Completed within planned
time (target 90%); and Audit Recommendations – Percentage of
outstanding audit recommendations followed up each quarter (target
100%) be agreed.
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to approve the Review of Internal Audit for 2025/26 and adopt existing performance indicators for 2026/27 with additional targets.

purpose:
To report on Internal Audit activity in the
third quarter of 2025/26 and to provide a progress update on the
implementation of audit recommendations made in earlier
periods.
content:
The Audit Manager
(AM) led Members through the internal audit report to 31 December
2025 that gave details of audit matters and any emerging issues,
not only in relation to audit but risk management and corporate
governance.  Despite several audit
delays beyond the Council’s control, the Internal Audit Team
remained on track to complete the majority of the 2025/26 Audit
Plan.
 
Three audit reviews
were completed in the third quarter of 2025/26.  Two provided substantial assurance, while the
Asset Management audit review received limited assurance due to
inaccuracies in the new property management system, including some
properties not being recorded.  These
issues had since been resolved.  A
summary of the audit findings, along with a management update on
the Asset Management review was provided in Appendix A to the
report.
 
Appendix B to the
report provided an update on progress with implementing audit
recommendations from previous meetings. 
The number of outstanding ‘Old Years’ recommendations
had reduced from 19 to 11, with three further cases nearing
completion. Two recommendations had been removed as unresolved.
 
The 2024/25 Debtors
audit identified a deteriorating trend in the recovery of sundry
debtor invoices.  In response, the Head
of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services established a
project team to improve monitoring of outstanding debt.  The project team met regularly over the past year,
and a comprehensive report detailing outstanding debts by service
area was now available.  Improved
communications between relevant teams had helped maintain focus on
debt recovery, which had led to the successful collection of
several older debts.  As a result, long
term outstanding debt had reduced by £250,000, with total
debt outstanding at approximately £400,000.
 
The audits
scheduled to take place in the first quarter of 2026/27 were yet to
be determined. They would be selected from the new Audit Plan once
it had been approved elsewhere on this agenda.
 
The Employment
Rights Act 2025 introduced additional protections, effective from 6
April 2026, for workers who reported sexual harassment, bringing
such disclosures within the scope of whistleblowing
law.  As a result, the Council’s
Whistleblowing Policy required updating and formal approval, and
the revised wording was set out in Appendix C to the report.
Members were happy to recommend the amended policy to full Council
for approval and adoption.
 
Members
congratulated officers on the successful collection of several
older sundry debts and on the progress with older
recommendations.
                       
RECOMMENDED:
That the revised Whistleblowing Policy be approved and adopted.
                       
AND
 
RESOLVED:
That the Internal Audit report to 31 December 2025 be noted.
 
(Councillor Barnes
declared an Other Registrable Interest in this matter in so far as
he was the Vice-Chair of Etchingham Parish Council and in
accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct remained in the
meeting during the consideration thereof.)
 
(Councillor Byrne
declared an Other Registrable Interest in this matter in so far as
he was a Member of Bexhill-on-Sea Town Council and in accordance
with the Members’ Code of Conduct remained in the meeting
during the consideration thereof.)
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to recommend the approval and adoption of the revised Whistleblowing Policy and note the Internal Audit report to 31 December 2025.

content:
Members
received the annual report of the Rother Community Safety
Partnership [known as the Safer Rother Partnership (SRP)] and
invited the Committee to review, scrutinise and make
recommendations to the responsible authorities of the SRP, in line
with the Council’s statutory responsibilities under the
Police and Justice Act 2006.  The
Overview and Scrutiny Committee was designated as the
Council’s Crime and Disorder Committee with responsibility
for annually scrutinising crime and disorder and community safety
matters.  The Chair welcomed Chief
Inspector Simon Yates and Inspector Simon Whiteheadto the
meeting.
 
The SRP’s responsible authorities were
Rother District Council (RDC), Sussex Police (SP), East Sussex Fire
and Rescue Service (ESFRS), East Sussex County Council, Probation
Service and NHS Sussex.
 
The SRP, along with all Community Safety
Partnerships in Sussex, received grant funding from the Office of
the Police and Crime Commissioner (OPCC) allocated according to
crime levels and population.  Funding
was subject to delivering both OPCC and local
priorities.  It was confirmed that the
allocation for 2026/27 would remain unchanged at
£35,077.
 
The Rother Joint Action Group (RJAG) (an officer
group) met monthly to oversee the delivery of the local priorities
for Rother which in 2025/26 included: business crime; anti-social
behaviour (ASB) and youth crime; and drug related harm (including
drug supply [both local and county lines] and the impact on the
local community).  Domestic abuse,
violence against women and girls and road safety remained areas of
focus for the Partnership, though they were not designed as
specific priorities.
 
The RJAG continued to support and deliver work to
address issues that were business as usual through the work of
partnership agencies and were priorities, such as cuckooing;
domestic abuse (including the White Ribbon Campaign); high and
medium risk ASB and all hate crime cases; modern slavery; safety;
professional safeguarding and case meetings and road
safety.
 
Work arising through partner agencies was also
supported, including serious and organised crime; safeguarding;
multiple and complex needs cases; community tensions and protests;
shoplifting and other business crime types; rural crime;
youth-related ASB; use of ASB powers; drug related harm; civil
parking enforcement; fly tipping; criminal damage; and fire
setting.  Two Home Office (HO)
initiatives were introduced in 2025/26 to support Police and local
authorities in delivering the “Make Town Centres Safer”
programme, aimed at reducing crime and ASB and ensuring clear
consequences for offenders.  Bexhill and
Rye were identified by the HO as priority areas, as outlined in
Appendix 2 to the report.
 
The joint Board met quarterly to review
significant crime and ASB trends across both areas and to assess
progress against agreed priorities.  The
Board was co-chaired by Councillor Stanger of RDC and his
counterpart from Hastings Borough Council.
 
Environmental Services and Licensing and
Community Safety staff, SP and partner agencies continued to
deliver effective operational and educational initiatives across
Rother and Wealden, as detailed within the report.  The Community Safety Team (CST) also collaborated
with other Council departments to meet statutory responsibilities
and addressed enquires from residents and Members including matters
relating to housing, planning and planning enforcement, customer
services, domestic abuse, travellers and unauthorised encampments,
mediation and general information requests.
 
SP recorded 5,658 crimes in Rother during the 12
months to December 2025, a decrease of 290 on the previous
year.  While crime levels varied across
Sussex, Rother experienced the largest overall decrease in the
county.
 
For 2025/26, the SRP commissioned Mediation Plus
to provide a confidential, impartial, and independent service for
Rother’s residents.  The service
supported constructive engagement between parties to help reach
mutually agreed solutions.  Further
information was available on the Council’s website, and two
related ASB case studies were included in Appendix 4 to the report.
Members were urged to encourage residents to contact Mediation Plus
if they were experiencing conflict or disputes.
 
In 2025/26, business crime remained a key
priority for the SRP.  The CST continued
to work with the Neighbourhood Policing Team to strengthen the DISC
system, which identified repeat offenders, and supported local
businesses in tackling shoplifting and related ASB.  The CST also worked with partner agencies
including substance misuse services, probation, housing, and mental
health providers to address the underlying causes of
shoplifting.  Across Sussex shoplifting
had increased by 4%.  East Sussex
recorded a 14% rise, reaching 6,168 incidents, while Rother
recorded an 8.3% decrease.
 
The
RJAG had recently agreed its priorities for 2026/27 at its March
meeting, which remained the same as the 2025/26
priorities.  In addition, the RJAG would
evaluate: Rother crime and ASB data; monitoring and evaluation
provided to the OPCC; results of future consultation with residents
and businesses as part of the violence reduction and contextual
safeguarding work being carried out; local and East Sussex Policing
priorities; East Sussex and Pan Sussex risk assessments and plans;
operational priorities in 2025/26 that continued into 2026/27; and
changes in Government legislation and guidance including additional
work around ASB, changes to the PREVENT (Counter Terrorism) agenda
and Martyn’s Law.
 
Members’ attention was drawn to Appendix 1 to the report,
which gave an outline of the projects that the SRP had funded in
2025/26. In addition to those listed, funding had recently been
allocated to the Pelham Community Hub to support their youth work
sessions.
 
Finally, Members’ attention was drawn to Appendix 3 to the
report which listed the priorities for the Safer Hastings and Rother Partnership Board. The
Board evaluated what the requirements were locally, looking at the
highest threat, harm and risk, taking into account the priorities
of the OPCC, the community and the policing
priorities.
 
Members were given the opportunity to ask
questions and the following points were noted during
discussions:
 

·      
although mentioned under Business Crime in the
report, Members were disappointed not to see more information and
statistics concerning rural crime within the report. It was
confirmed that this was a priority supported by the Rural Crime
team, funded by various sources separate to the
SRP;

·      
Members noted the increased Police visibility in Rye
over the previous year and the significant impact of the work being
done;

·      
a new team had recently been established within
Sussex Police to look at ‘Killed and Seriously Injured’
in road traffic accidents, details of which would be provided to
Members after the meeting. The portal which provided information
and data on road traffic accidents would be updated over the coming
weeks;

·      
Members raised concerns about the timescales between
reporting cases of ASB and action being taken. All contact was
logged, assessed for threat, risk and harm, and then responded to
accordingly, within a maximum of three days, if possible. The
issuing of Community Protection Warnings assisted in bridging any
gaps;

·      
residents were also encouraged to report instances
of ASB through Crime Stoppers, which was a secure and anonymous
reporting service;  

·      
neighbourhood policing had recently been remodelled
by the Government with slightly different objectives, including an
increased presence withing the community, the number of engagements
measured and a named officer for every Ward;

·      
Operation Stopwatch involved working with retailers
to educate staff around shoplifting and safety. The introduction of
DISC also assisted, with the ability to share information quickly
through instant messaging. In order to make an arrest and then be
able to prosecute, the Police required evidence, so reporting by
retailers was encouraged; and

·      
the new tagging system, funded by the OPCC, assisted
with dealing with known offenders from outside the area, with the
ability to ban from certain retailers.
 
The Cabinet Portfolio Holder for Community Safety, Councillor
Delany, who was present at the meeting, thanked officers for the
report and the SRP for the positive results achieved with the
allocated funding. Of particular note was the reduction in
shoplifting seen in Bexhill, which in turn released Police time to
address problems in the rural areas.
 
The OSC commended the work of the SRP and acknowledged the
excellent partnership approach and joined up working that was going
on behind the scenes to keep the Rother District a safe place to
live and work. The Chair thanked Chief Inspector Simon Yates
and Inspector Simon Whitehead for their attendance
and helpful contributions.
 
RESOLVED: That: 
 

1)  
the comments made by the Overview and Scrutiny
Committee be fed back to the Safer Rother Partnership;
and

 

2)  the
Council’s work in relation to Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime
Reduction and Community Safety be noted.
 
(Councillor
Maynard declared an Other Registrable Interest in this matter in so
far as he was an Executive Member of East Sussex County Council and
in accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct remained in
the meeting during the consideration
thereof.)
topline: The Rother District Council has approved recommendations for the annual review and scrutiny of the Safer Rother Partnership's responsibilities in crime and disorder matters.

purpose:
To monitor delivery of the Council’s Key
Performance
Indicators and make any necessary recommendations to
Cabinet.
content:
Consideration was given to the report of the Head
of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services on the
Performance Report of the Third Quarter (Q3) 2025/26.  Members were given the opportunity to scrutinise
progress towards corporate operations and service delivery and make
any necessary recommendations to Cabinet for future service
delivery.
 
A
summary of the Council’s performance against the selected Key
Performance Indicators (KPIs), broken down into nine service areas,
was included at Appendix A to the report.  Benchmarking data had been included where it was
available. Performance across the board was excellent, with only
five areas performing slightly below target for this quarter and
several areas exceeding targets.
 
The exceptions
(those either not meeting or exceeding targets) were detailed in
the report and highlighted to Members as follows:
 

·      
Corporate Core: 100% of Freedom of Information (FOI) requests
answered in 20 days – Q3 performance was 100%: Resources
had been increased and performance had improved significantly,
remaining strong.

·      
Customer Services: Channel shift – online versus
traditional – target 65% online – Q3 performance was
55% online: Online performance remained below target, with
customers preferring traditional contact methods for more complex
enquires.  Further promotion of the
benefits of online channels would be undertaken, but this was a
difficult target to influence as it was directly influenced by
customer choice.

·      
Housing: Number of households either prevented or relieved from
homelessness – Q3 performance was 59: 23% increase
compared with Q2 (48%) and Q1 (15%). 
The expansion of staff resources had strengthened joint working
within the Housing Team, which had contributed towards these
outcomes. Members praised officers for their work in this area,
which had resulted in significant savings for the Council.

·      
Housing: Average cost of placing a household in temporary
accommodation – target £1,200 – Q3 performance
£1,559: Several factors had contributed, including a rise
in complex homelessness cases requiring specialist accommodation,
and increased demand for temporary accommodation due to multiple
activations of the severe weather protocol.

·      
Revenues and Benefits: Percentage of council tax owed for the
year that has been collected and percentage of business rates owed
for the year that have been collected: Performance was below
target in both areas.  Work was underway
to improve collection rates and determine whether the business
rates shortfalls related to specific accounts. Staff turnover in
the department had also affected performance. Members were
concerned that the number of non-payers of Council Tax may have
increased due to affordability. Officers would circulate Council
Tax Reduction Scheme registration numbers after the meeting.
 
Members paid tribute to Biffa for the excellent performance with
the Missed Bins KPI and for the speed at which fly tips were
cleared. Also, to the Environmental Health department for the
improvement in food inspection rates, now that staffing issues had
been addressed.
 
Members congratulated officers on the overall performance of the
Council.

 
RESOLVED: That the report be
noted.

purpose:
To update Members on the Revenue and Capital
Budget Monitoring Position for Quarter 3 2025/26. This report also
summarises the position to date on delivery of the savings targets
for 2025/26.
content:
Members received and considered the report of the Director of
Resources on the Revenue and Capital Budget
Monitoring Position for Quarter 3 (Period 10) 2025/26.  The report also provided an update on progress
against the 2025/26 savings targets.  The Revenue Budget (RB) and Capital Programme (CP)
statements were summarised at Appendices A and B to the report
respectively and a review of the agreed savings targets for 2025/26
had been undertaken, contained within Appendix C to the
report.
 
The
RB was currently forecast to be £15.581m at year end,
compared to the approved budget of £15.716m.  £344,000 of this sum was anticipated to be
funded from flexible capital receipts, leaving the forecast service
underspend as £479,000.  The
agreed budget already anticipated a draw from reserves of
£694,000.  In addition to this,
adverse variances of £769,000 were anticipated which related
to financing costs and an error at budget setting on government
grants.  The combination of these
variances meant the Council was forecast to draw £1.075m from
reserves rather than the budgeted £694,000. The main
variances were summarised within Appendix A to the
report.
 
The
further review of the deliverability of the agreed savings targets
for 2025/26, outlined within Appendix C to the report, anticipated
£422,800 to be fully deliverable (green status), with
£130,400 identified as undeliverable in year (red
status).  The remaining savings target
of £531,200 was anticipated to be partially deliverable in
year (amber status).  Monitoring would
continue throughout the financial year.
 
The CP for
2025/26 and beyond was reviewed and reforecast as part of the
governance improvements led by the Corporate Development Team. The
priority was to ensure the CP remained affordable, minimising any
impact on the RB from borrowing and interest costs.  This approach supported the medium-term
sustainability of the CP whilst maximising opportunities to secure
external grant funding.
 
The updated CP
totalled £191m, including prior year expenditure.  Projected spend from 2025/26 to 2028/29 was
approximately £124m.  For 2025/26,
planned expenditure of £48m was now forecast at around
£45m due to re-phasing.  The
phasing to the CP had been adjusted as part of the 2026/27 budget
process to reflect the amendments outlined within the report.
 
General Reserves
(GR) stood at £5.00m, plus £5.54m in Earmarked
Reserves.  If the projected revenue
outturn was achieved, the GR would reduce by £1.075m to
£3.925m.
 
As previously
reported, the Council might need to draw on reserves to cover
losses from the Hermes Property Fund investment and to meet costs
arising from changes to capital schemes that required charging
expenditure to revenue.  These potential
transactions were not expected to exceed £1.057m.  Should they materialise, the GR was forecast to
reduce to £2.87m by year end.
 
Financing costs
excluded the anticipated interest receivable in respect of the
loans made to the Housing Company (forecast to be £1,868,500
for 2025/26), as the Council would not receive this until the
Housing Company could commence repaying the loans provided to it.
It was proposed that the surplus generated from allowing for this
interest payable within the Council’s accounts was moved to
an Earmarked reserve until realised in cash terms, at which point
it would be transferred to the General Reserve. 
 
Members were
asked to note the recent announcement that Elected Members would be
eligible to join the Local Government Pension Scheme from 1 April
2026.  As this had not been know at the
time of budget setting for 2026/27, it had not been incorporated
within the budget set, therefore officers would undertake an
analysis of this cost pressure and report it to a future committee.
Joining the scheme was optional for Members, but Members over the
age of 75 would not be eligible.
 
Members raised
concerns about the impact any non-budgeted increase in staff
salaries would have on the budget now that the Council was part of
the National Conditions; incremental salary increases plus a 3%
uplift had been included in the budget only. The Council’s
Savings Programme was therefore critical.
 

 
RESOLVED: That:

 

1)   
the report be noted; and

 

2)   
the Committee note the changes
anticipated for 2026/27 in respect of Elected Members’
eligibility to join the Local Government Pension Scheme.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations on the Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Position for Quarter 3 (Period 10) 2025/26.

content:
1066
Country Marketing was the Destination Management Organisation
responsible for promoting tourism in Hastings, Rother and
south-east of Wealden.  Established in
the early 1990s as a public / private sector partnership, it
managed and marketed the areas to support growth in the visitor
economy and delivered positive local benefits.  The organisation covered 378 square miles,
including the main settlements in Rother.  Recent performance data was detailed in Appendix A
to the report.
 
Historically, 1066 County was funded jointly by Hastings Borough
Council (HBC), Rother District Council (RDC) and Wealden District
Council (WDC).  Following HBC’s
withdrawal in 2023/24, RDC became the accountable body, with WDC
contributing a small amount; Members noted that whilst HBC made no
contribution, the businesses within Hastings were still supported
through the organisation.  The current
constitution was detailed at Appendix B to the report.
 
RDC
contributed £50,000 annually and directly employed the 1066
Project Officer.  While 1066 Country
aimed to become self-sustaining, the Council was required to
balance the need for savings with the importance of supporting
local infrastructure organisations, particularly given the
challenges of Local Government Reorganisation.  The organisation also required stability to
benefit from any future Sussex-wide initiatives arising from the
Strategic Mayoral Authority (May 2028 onwards).
 
It
was proposed that RDC entered into a 2-year grant funding agreement
with 1066 County, providing £50,000 in 2026/27 and
£45,000 in 2027/28.  The Chair of
1066 Country had been working closely with officers in developing
this proposal. 
 
After deliberation, as with the decision for the Rother
Voluntary Action Service Level Agreement [see Minute CB25/72
above], Cabinet agreed to the recommended funding levels for
2026/27 and 2027/28, subject to review at budget setting time for
the 2027/28 budget to enable consideration of reinstating the
current level of funding in light of other savings that might have
been made.  This guaranteed the levels
as set out in the report as the minimum funding 1066 would receive,
over the next two years, with the potential for funding to be in
increased to the current level, if the Council’s financial
position allowed it. 
 
Cabinet agreed to the continued employment of the 1066 Project
Officer, and the provision of financial, procurement, contracting
and management support.  Cabinet also
agreed that delegated authority be granted to the Head of
Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services, in consultation
with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder for Neighbourhood Services,
Tourism and Joint Waste Contract, to finalise the
agreement.
 
Cabinet reaffirmed that tourism was a major employer and a
significant contributor to both the district’s economy and
residents’ quality of life.  1066
Country Marketing also played a role in attracting potential
residents to relocate to the 1066 area and contributed to the
economic development and regeneration of the area.  
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)    
a grant funding agreement be entered into with 1066
Country Marketing for promotion of Rother businesses to visitors
and stimulation of the tourism economy across the area with a value
of £50,000 for 2026/27 and £45,000 for
2027/28;
 

2)    
a review takes place at budget setting time for the
2027/28 budget to enable consideration of reinstating the current
level of funding in 2027/28;   
 

3)    
the Council continues to offer support in kind to
1066 Country Marketing in the form of employment of the 1066
Project Officer, financial, procurement, contracting and management
support for the period 2026/27 and 2027/28; and
 

4)    
delegated authority be granted to the Head of
Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services, in conjunction
with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder for Neighbourhood Services,
Tourism and Joint Waste Contract to finalise the funding
agreement.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to provide funding to 1066 Country Marketing to support tourism in the Hastings, Rother, and south-east Wealden areas.

content:
Rother Voluntary Action (RVA) was the primary infrastructure
organisation supporting communities across Rother through capacity
building within the voluntary, community, and social enterprise
sector (VCSE) and by working in partnership with the
Council.  The current Service Level
Agreement (SLA) with RVA required review and the Council’s
current budgeted annual contribution was £38,000.
 
RVA
continued to be an essential partner in supporting the VCSE sector
across the district.  RVA provided
strong value for money, consistently exceeded its targets, and
secured significant external investment, enhancing the impact of
the Council’s contribution and helped to reduce long-term
demand on statutory services.  RVA was
accredited by the National Association of Voluntary and Community
Action. 
 
Given the current financial climate, it was essential that the
Council strengthened its partnership approach with the VCSE and
supported it sustainability through means other than direct
funding.  RVA was best placed to co-lead
this collaborative work, and its system wide infrastructure role
was vital to help the Council achieve its objectives and to sustain
the sector throughout this challenging period, particularly amid
the uncertainties associated with Local Government Reorganisation
(LGR). 
 
RVA
would also be working with the Council and its partners to
establish and co-ordinate a new Rother Age Friendly Network, funded
by East Sussex County Council with an additional £30,000 for
2026/27 and 2027/28, complementing the existing and proposed SLA
for VCSE infrastructure support. 
 
It
was proposed by officers that the Council entered into a 2-year SLA
funding agreement with RVA, providing £38,000 in 2026/27 and
£34,200 in 2027/28; this reflected the 10% savings that were
required across all budgets to meet the Council’s challenging
financial position.
 
After discussion, Cabinet agreed to the recommended funding
levels for 2026/27 and 2027/28, subject to review at budget setting
time for the 2027/28 budget to enable consideration of reinstating
the current level of funding in light of other savings that might
have been made.  This guaranteed the
levels as set out in the report as the minimum funding RVA would
receive, over the next two years, with the potential for funding to
be in increased to the current level, if the Council’s
financial position allowed it. 
 
It
was also agreed that delegated authority be granted to the Head of
Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood Services, in consultation
with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder for Neighbourhood Services,
Tourism and Joint Waste Contract to finalise the
agreement. 
 
The
new SLA would help to protect RVA’s sustainability during the
challenging phase of transition into LGR.  RVA’s Chief Executive had been working
closely with officers in developing the SLA and they had also
developed a business plan for income diversification over the
5-year period from April 2026, including income generation
opportunities.
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)    
Rother District Council enters into a new Service
Level Agreement with Rother Voluntary Action for infrastructure
support to the Voluntary, Community and Social Enterprise sector
across Rother, with a value of £38,000 for 2026/27 and
£34,200 for 2027/28; 
 

2)    
a review takes place at budget setting time for the
2027/28 budget to enable consideration of reinstating the current
level of funding in 2027/28;   
 

3)    
the Service Level Agreement is further enhanced by
£30,000 for 2026/27 and 2027/28 to deliver the Rother Age
Friendly Network, funded by East Sussex County Council, against a
specific set of deliverables agreed by the County; and
 

4)    
the Head of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood
Services be the granted delegated authority to finalise the
agreement, in conjunction with the Cabinet Portfolio Holders for
Corporate Policy, Communications, Improvement, Devolution, Human
Resources and Strategic Issues; and Finance and
Governance.
 
(Councillor Delany declared an Other Registerable Interest in
this matter as the Council appointed representative to Rother
Voluntary Action, and in accordance with the Members’ Code of
Conduct remained in the meeting for the consideration
thereof.)
topline: The Cabinet has decided to enter into a new Service Level Agreement with Rother Voluntary Action to support the Voluntary, Community and Social Enterprise sector in Rother.

purpose:
To present to Cabinet those Council-owned
assets that officers recommend are transferred to respective town
and parish councils on a freehold basis, following the Council's
invitation for expressions of interest as part of the Services and
Assets Devolution Framework.
content:
The
Service/Asset Devolution Framework enabled the Council to assess
proposals for transferring or disposing of Council-owned assets to
community-based organisations. 
Expressions of interest (EOI) had been invited for this
purpose.  Asset transfers to
participating Parish and Town Councils (P&TCs) would be
progressed in accordance with the Council’s Asset Disposal
Policy (ADP), using the Community Asset Transfer (CAT) criteria and
procedures set out in Appendix D of the ADP.
 
All
assets had been assessed to determine the community value and
whether they fell within the scope of asset devolution, using the
matrix detailed at Appendix A to the report.  The Council’s Property and Service
Investment and Disposal Panel (PSIDP) reviewed each asset against
the required criteria and identified some that required further
consideration due to potential development
opportunities.  The assets listed at
Appendix B to the report met the criteria and were therefore
proposed for CAT.  The terms of the
proposed transfers would not be open for detailed negotiation but
transferred on face value to prevent any delays to the
transfer.
 
P&TCs were invited to submit Business Cases, which were
evaluated by the PSIDP, resulting in 71 assets being recommended
for CAT.  Legal advice confirmed that
the transfer process was compliant, and all transfers were expected
to be completed within 12-months.  Due
to the volume of work, an external legal firm was appointed to
provide additional capacity and support.  Assets not transferred within the agreed timescale
would not be processed.
 
External planning consultants advised that 15 of the 71 assets
had no realistic prospect of securing planning consent.  These assets were therefore referred back to the
relevant P&TCs with a request for a full Business
Case.  Once received, officers would
progress them through the CAT process.
 
To
ensure compliance with legislation, a RICS Red Book Valuation would
be obtained for each asset to establish market value and, where
relevant, to identify and quantify any proposed
undervaluation.  The PSIDP would be kept
abreast of progress and would implement the delegated actions set
out in the report. 
 
As
at March 2025, the estimated cost of delivering this work was
£394,000 over two years.  The
project team was forecast to spend £149,000 in 2025/26, with
the projected cost of £248,000 in 2026/27.  The process might extend beyond current estimates,
which could increase overall costs. 
Budget approval would be sought once revised estimates were
available.
 
When
transferring assets to P&TCs, the Council might require them to
take on a proportionate share of the existing parks
contract.  The amount would reflect the
assets being transferred and would be a condition of the process to
ensure maintenance standards were maintained.  The assets listed represented an estimated
contract cost of approximately £1m, with an income reduction
of £300,000, mainly from Bexhill and Rye
cemeteries.  The Council was working
with the relevant P&TCs and the parks contractor to agree the
most suitable way forward, subject to further financial and legal
due diligence.  Those who did not agree
to share the contract would be referred back to the PSIDP and
advice would be sought.  Some recreation
grounds and sports facilities were currently leased to sports clubs
and these would transfer to the new authority as part of the CAT,
but licensed arrangements would need to be reviewed and agreed to
ensure they continued after the transfer.
 
Cabinet agreed that approving the recommendations would allow
the Council to progress the devolution project effectively,
ensuring that suitable local assets were transferred to
organisations best placed to manage them for community benefit,
whilst maintaining strong governance, legal compliance, and
appropriate risk-mitigate measures. 
 
Members therefore approved the 71 assets proposed for CAT to the
respective P&TCs, subject to further financial and legal due
diligence.  They also agreed to delegate
authority to the Head of Housing and Strategic Assets, in
consultation with the Section 151 Officer, Cabinet Portfolio Holder
for Regeneration and Economic Development and the PSIDP, to arrange
the necessary transfers or agreements and to approve the CAT of any
additional Council assets.  Cabinet
would receive periodic progress updates from the PSIDP and thanked
the officer team for the extensive work undertaken thus far on this
project.
 
The
Director of Resources confirmed that until such times as assets in
Bexhill and Rye were devolved, Rother District Council would
continue to levy an appropriate special expense on the residents of
Bexhill and Rye.  Should assets transfer
before the 31 March 2027 and there was time to evaluate the special
expense levied and collected, appropriate adjustments would be
made.  It was further confirmed that
special expenses were unlikely to be removed completely as some
related to assets / services that would not be
transferred.
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)    
the 71 assets proposed for Community Asset Transfer
to respective Parish and Town Councils at Appendix B to the
report  be approved, subject to further
finance and legal due diligence;
 

2)    
delegated authority be granted to the Head of
Housing and Strategic Assets, in consultation with the Section 151
Officer to:
 

a.  conduct appropriate
due diligence, including the obtaining of legal, financial and
valuation advice as appropriate; and

b.  agree the terms of
any associated transfers.
 

3)    
delegated authority be granted (in respect of the 71
assets) to the Head of Housing and Strategic Assets in consultation
with the Portfolio Holder for Regeneration and Economic Development
and the Property and Services Investment and Disposal Panel
to:
 

a.  approve, and enter
into Community Asset Transfers, subject to the agreed terms and due
diligence; and

b.  agree and enter into
the related agreements and associated documents to execute the
transfer.
 
(The
Chair of the Overview and Scrutiny Committee had agreed that this
Key Decision could be taken, without the prerequisite 28 clear
days’ notice on the Forward Plan in accordance with the Local
Authorities (Executive Arrangements) (Meetings and Access to
Information) (England).)
 
(Councillor Timpe declared an Other Registerable Interest in
this matter as a Member of Bexhill-on-Sea Town Council and a
Director of Old Town Occasions Limited, trading as The Manor Barn,
Bexhill-on-Sea, and in accordance with the Members’ Code of
Conduct remained in the meeting for the consideration
thereof.)
 
(When it first became apparent, Councillor McLaren declared an
Other Registerable Interest in this matter as a Member of Battle
Town Council, and in accordance with the Members’ Code of
Conduct remained in the meeting for the consideration
thereof.)
topline: The Cabinet has decided to transfer 71 Council-owned assets to Parish and Town Councils for Community Asset Transfer, subject to further financial and legal due diligence.

purpose:
To consider the Risk Register and Risk
Appetite prior to consideration by the Audit Committee
content:
Consideration was given to the report of the Head of Corporate,
Strategic and Neighbourhood Services on the updated Corporate Risk
Register (CRR) and review of the Risk Management Policy (RMP),
including risk appetites.
 
Maintaining a robust approach to risk management remained
essential for ensuring sound governance, particularly in the
context of significant financial pressures.  The RMP, originally approved in 2022 and updated
following reviews in 2023 and 2025, was attached at Appendix B to
the report. 
 
External Auditors had recommended that the Council strengthened
its risk oversight arrangements by ensuring that Cabinet reviewed
the CRR annually.  The CRR, attached at
Appendix A to the report, had been reviewed by the Corporate
Leadership Team, with no formal changes required.  Several risks were identified relating to Local
Government Reorganisation and Devolution, particularly the transfer
of assets to parish and town councils and community
groups. 
 
All
Heads of Service and Service Managers also documented and monitored
their own operational and project risks as part of normal service
planning.  It was noted that whilst some
risk scores appeared to be low, particularly around asset
transfers, the scores were considered post mitigation measures,
hence lower than the perceived risk without any mitigation measures
in place.
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)    
the revised Risk Management Policy be approved and
adopted; and
 

2)    
the report and Corporate Risk Register be
noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve and adopt the revised Risk Management Policy and note the Corporate Risk Register.

purpose:
To vary the previously agreed NHS Option
Agreement.
content:
Cabinet considered the confidential report of the Head of
Housing and Strategic Assets that proposed to remove the Buy Back
Option on Mount View Plot 2, which would enable the potential
extension of important medical facilities which were essential for
the replacement of aging facilities elsewhere in the
district. 
 
Members agreed that a Deed of Surrender of the Buy Back Option
be approved and the Option Agreement amended to include a new
covenant within the Deed of Variation, ensuring that any uplift in
value arising from a disposal of the site by the NHS within the
next 80 years was shared equally (50/50) with the Council or its
successor in title. 
 
It
was also agreed that the Chief Executive be authorised to approve
any further amendments, in consultation with the Cabinet Portfolio
Holder for Regeneration and Economic Development and the Section
151 Officer. 
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)    
a Deed of Surrender of the Buy Back Option be
approved and the Option Agreement be varied with a new covenant
inserted into the Deed of Variation, such that should the NHS
dispose of the site in the next 80 years any uplift in value will
be shared 50/50 with Rother District Council or its successor in
title; and 
 

2)    
the Chief Executive be authorised to approve further
amendments on terms to her satisfaction in consultation with the
Cabinet Portfolio Holder for Regeneration and Economic Development
and Section 151 officer.
 
(This matter was considered exempt from publication by virtue of
paragraph 3 of Schedule 12A of the Local Government Act 1972, as
amended).
topline: The Cabinet has decided to remove the Buy Back Option on Mount View Plot 2 to enable the extension of important medical facilities.

purpose:
To provide the Human Resources Committee with
an update on progress with policy reviews.
content:
Members received
the report of the Head of Corporate, Strategic and Neighbourhood
Services which brought forward the first set of new Human Resources
(HR) policies for the Committee’s approval, to replace
historical policies.
 
All matters
relating to the policy development had been considered and the
initial draft documents had been circulated to the Corporate
Leadership Team (CLT), before being shared with the Colleague
Engagement Group and UNISON for comments. The policies had then
been amended, where possible, to reflect the views of UNISON and
staff.
 
The policies
brought forward were attached at Appendices A to F to the report.
Members were advised that the Disciplinary and Dismissal Procedure
for Statutory Officers had since been withdrawn, in order to fully consult with the Council’s
Statutory Officers and would be brought to a future meeting of the
Committee. 
 
The report included
one policy for recommendation to full Council (Pay Policy Statement
2026/2027) and a further four for approval by the HR Committee, as
follows:
 

•     Managing
Sickness Absence Policy;

•     Hybrid Working
Policy (HWP);

•     Dignity at
Work Policy; and

•     Organisational
Change Policy.
 
A Change Toolkit
was also included at Appendix G to the report, as it was referenced
within the Organisational Change Policy.
 
Officers summarised
the main changes and Members were given the opportunity to ask
questions. The following points were noted during the
discussion:
 

•     the amended
sickness absence trigger of six days within six months initiated a
support stage, during which the manager would meet with the
employee to review any adjustments needed to support them in the
workplace;

•     concerns had
been raised within the feedback regarding the application of
sickness absence procedures to employees with chronic, disability
or pregnancy?related illness. Officers
confirmed that while triggers were applied consistently, they were
not applied in these circumstances;

•     Managers
received initial training when hybrid working was introduced, and
further training would be provided following the launch of the new
HWP;

•     the ability to
measure productivity for home?working staff
varied by service area, as some were set Key Performance Indicators
whilst others required assessment against appraisal objectives
which were aligned with the Council Plan;

•     the
recommended requirement for staff to work 20% of their hours in the
office (equivalent to one day per week) was agreed in consultation
with the CLT, though operational needs meant this might vary
between service areas; and

•     work had been
undertaken with the Estates Team to assess the Town Hall buildings
alongside development of the HWP, and this would continue to ensure
adequate workspace provision. Specific desk banks had been
allocated to teams on designated days in the Amherst Road building,
although further planning was still required.
 
Further policies
and procedures would be brought to the HR Committee for approval in
April and October 2026.
 
Members recommended
the Pay Policy Statement 2026/27 for approval by full Council and
approved the accompanying new and revised policies.
 
Members
congratulated the Human Resources Manager and her team for
preparing the revised policies, which strengthened the
Council’s HR procedures and better positioned the
organisation and its staff for Local Government Reorganisation.
 

RECOMMENDATION: That the Pay Policy Statement 2026/27 be
approved and adopted.
 
AND
 
RESOLVED:
That the following updated policies be approved:
 
 

•     Managing
Sickness Absence Policy

•     Hybrid Working
Policy

•     Dignity at
Work Policy

•     Organisational
Change Policy

•     Change Toolkit
For references within the Organisational Change Policy
topline: The Human Resources Committee has decided to approve new HR policies, including Managing Sickness Absence, Hybrid Working, Dignity at Work, and Organisational Change policies.

In
accordance with Council Procedure Rule 13, consideration was given
to the Motion moved by Councillor Burton (in the absence of
Councillor McGurk) and seconded by Councillor Gordon on East Sussex
County Council – Repairs and Upgrade of National Cycle Route
2 / Gibbert’s Marsh to Float Lane
Bridlepath.

was declared CARRIED as follows:

formally to East Sussex County Council, urging it to:

clarity on how its active travel and transport
funding allocations will be used within Rother District.

content:
Members received the report of the Director of Resources which
updated the Committee on the recruitment for an Independent Person
(IP) to the Audit Committee following the recruitment and interview
process.
 
Although not a legal requirement, the appointment of independent
co-opted Members was considered good practice.  Independent Members with appropriate skills and
experience supplemented those of the elected Members and improved
the effectiveness of an Audit Committee. 
 
The
role was first advertised in April 2025 and again in September
2025. 
Following the interviews in December 2025, it was proposed that
the Council appoint Gwilym (known as Tom) Davies.  Mr Davies had held the role of Head of Internal
Audit, Investigations, Risk Management & Procurement in a
similar local authority to Rother District Council for over 15
years and therefore had a range of related skills applicable to the
person specification for the IP role. 
Additionally, Mr Davies had also served as an IP for Rushmoor
Borough Council, so had a good understanding of the requirements of
the role.
 
It
was proposed that the appointment was to be made initially for a
one-year term, with the option to extend the role, depending on
performance.  The one-year term will
provide flexibility to the Council given the pending changes from
Local Government Reorganisation. 
 
Members of the Audit Committee were supportive of the
recommendation to appoint Mr Davies to the role of Audit IP and
recommended full Council ratify the appointment at their meeting in
May 2026.
 
RECOMMENDED: That Gwilym (Tom) Davies
be appointed to the Audit Committee for a period of one year, as
Audit Independent Person with the option for the Audit Committee to
extend this appointment for up to a further three years, up to the
point a successor authority is in place.
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to appoint Gwilym (Tom) Davies as the Audit Independent Person for a one-year term, with the option to extend for up to three years.

Thornton's Audit Findings Report for 2024/25. The committee
