Day Room - Drawing No. 2022-1321v2-Day Room - Dated 22 May
2025
Existing
Block Plan - Drawing No. 2022-1321v2-ExistBlock - Dated 22 May
2025
Reason: For
the avoidance of doubt and in the interests of proper
planning.

 

3.      The site shall be laid out
in accordance with the Block Plan (2022-1321v1-PropBlock, dated 4
October 2022) approved under the original planning permission,
reference: RR/2022/2791/P.
Reason: To
protect the ancient woodland adjacent to the site, including any
protected species that may be present, from increased disturbance,
lighting from the caravans and compaction of the ground where the
touring caravans would be stored in accordance with Policies EN1
(vi) and EN5 (viii) (ix) of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy,
Policy DEN4 (ii) of the Rother Development and Site Allocations
Local Plan, Policy EN2 of the Battle Civic Neighbourhood Plan,
Paragraph 186 of the National Planning Policy Framework, together
with standing advice produced by the Forestry Commission and
Natural England relating to ancient woodlands.

 

4.      The implemented
landscaping scheme approved under the 'Application for
Approval of Details Reserved by Condition' (reference:
RR/2024/1168/DC), shall be retained in place. If within the
temporary period of this permission any tree or plant is removed,
uprooted, destroyed or defective, another tree or plant of the same
species and size as originally planted shall be planted at the same
place, unless the Local Planning Authority gives its written
consent to any variation.
Reason: To
enhance the setting of the development in the interests of
conserving the natural beauty of the High Weald National Landscape
in accordance with Policies EN1(i) and
LHN6 of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy, Policy DEN2 of the
Rother Development and Site Allocations Local Plan and Policies HD5
and EN3 of the Battle Civic Neighbourhood Plan.

 

5.      The implemented foul and
surface water strategy approved under the 'Application for
Approval of Details Reserved by Condition' (reference:
RR/2024/1168/DC), shall be retained in place. Any variation to
the approved scheme shall be submitted to and approved in writing
by the Local Planning Authority and only the approved details shall
be implemented and thereafter retained.
Reason: To
ensure the satisfactory drainage of the site and to prevent water
pollution in accordance with Policies OSS4 (iii) and EN7 of the
Rother Local Plan Core Strategy.

        
 

6.      The visibility splays
measuring 2.4m by 95m to the northwest and 2.4m x 155m to the
southeast shall be retained and thereafter be maintained and kept
free of all obstructions over a height of 600mm.
Reason: To
ensure the safety of persons and vehicles entering and leaving the
access and proceeding along the highway in accordance with Policy
CO6 (ii) of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy and Policy IN4 of
the Battle Civic Neighbourhood Plan.

 

8.      The use hereby permitted
shall be occupied only by Ms Sherri McCallister and Ms Susan Smith
and their current resident dependants (as listed in the Planning
Statement received 16 March 2023) and shall be for a limited period
expiring on 30 May 2027. When the site ceases to be occupied by Ms
Sherri McCallister or Ms Susan Smith or their named resident
dependants, or at the end of that period, at which time the use
shall cease and all caravans, day room, structures, materials and
equipment brought on to or erected on the site, and/or works
undertaken to it in connection with the use, shall be removed and
the site restored in accordance with a scheme and timetable which
shall be approved in writing by the Local Planning
Authority.  This scheme and timetable
shall be submitted within one month of 30 May 2027 or when the site
is vacated, whichever is the soonest.
Reason: The
proposed development is only acceptable on a temporary basis due to
the personal circumstances of the Applicant and their way of life,
which mean that they meet the definition of a "gypsy or traveller".
The residential use of the site is not considered suitable on a
permanent basis in this location due to the harm it causes to the
landscape and scenic beauty of the High Weald National Landscape
which is an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty but is permitted on
a temporary basis due to current lack of local provision of Gypsy
and Traveller sites. There is also no alternative accommodation for
the occupiers to move to, and the personal circumstances of the
occupiers mean it is in their best interests to remain on the site
at the current time. A temporary permission will time limit the
harm to the landscape and natural beauty of the High Weald National
Landscape in accordance with Policies EN1(i) and LHN6 of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy,
Policy DEN2 of the Rother Development and Site Allocations Local
Plan and Policies HD5 and EN3 of the Battle Civic Neighbourhood
Plan.

        
 

9.      There shall be no more
than two pitches and one day room (which shall serve both pitches)
within the site. On each of the two pitches hereby approved no more
than two caravans shall be stationed at any one time, of which no
more than one shall be a mobile home or a static caravan as defined
in the Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960 and the
Caravan Sites Act 1968.
Reason: To
conserve the natural beauty of the High Weald National Landscape in
accordance with Policies EN1(i) and
LHN6 of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy, Policy DEN2 of the
Rother Development and Site Allocations Local Plan and Policies HD5
and EN3 of the Battle Civic Neighbourhood Plan.

 

11.    Any
static caravans and day room present on the site shall not exceed
the dimensions annotated on the approved Proposed Block Plan -
Drawing No. 2022-1321v2-PropBlock - Dated 22 May
2025.
Reason: To
limit the temporary harm to the landscape and scenic beauty of the
High Weald Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty in accordance with
Policies EN1(i) and LHN6 of the Rother
Local Plan Core Strategy.
 
Condition 10 is retained to ensure continued
compliance:
 

10.    No
vehicles over 3.5 tonnes shall be stationed, stored or parked on
the site and no commercial activities, including burning, shall
take place on the land, including the storage of materials, plant
or waste.
Reason: To
preserve the amenities of the locality, in accordance with Policy
OSS4(ii) of the Rother District Local Plan Core
Strategy.
        
 
Condition
7, requiring construction of the access to East Sussex County
Council (Highways) standards, has been satisfied and is therefore
removed.
 
Additional Conditions:
 

12.    The day
room hereby approved shall not be used at any time for sleeping or
overnight accommodation.
Reason: To
ensure the day room functions solely as an ancillary amenity
building serving the two existing temporary pitches.  Temporary permission is granted for the day room
to meet the needs of the current Gypsy and Traveller (G&T)
incumbents, having regard to the context within which the original
temporary permission was granted i.e. because of the current lack
of local G&T site provision, the absence of alternative
accommodation, and the personal circumstances of the occupiers,
which make it in their best interest to remain on the site at this
time. Limiting the permission to a temporary period will reduce
long-term harm to the HWNL, in line with Policies EN1(i) and LHN6 of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy,
Policy DEN2 of the Rother Development and Site Allocations Local
Plan, and Policies HD5 and EN3 of the Battle Civic Neighbourhood
Plan.
 

13.    No
floodlighting or other external means of illumination shall be
provided, installed or operated at the site until full details of
any external lighting scheme has been submitted to and approved in
writing by the Local Planning Authority. Any lighting shall then be
carried out in accordance with the approved details and thereafter
retained.
Reason: To
safeguard the special character of the rural area within the High
Weald National Landscape, in accordance with Policies
EN1(i) of the Rother Local Plan Core
Strategy, Policies DEN2 and DEN7(ii) of the Rother Development and
Site Allocations Local Plan and Policies HD5 and EN3 of the Battle
Civic Neighbourhood Plan.
 

14.    Details
of the external colour treatment to the day room shall be submitted
to the Local Planning Authority for written approval within two
months from the date of this decision. 
The approval works shall then be carried out in full accordance
with the agreed details and within two months of the date of the
details being approved.
Reason: To
preserve the special character of the rural area within the High
Weald National Landscape, in accordance with Policies OSS4(ii) of
the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy and Policies HD5 and EN3 of the
Battle Civic Neighbourhood Plan.
 
NATIONAL PLANNING POLICY FRAMEWORK: In accordance with Paragraph 39 of the National Planning
Policy Framework (2024), the Council has worked in a positive and
pro-active way and has imposed planning conditions to enable the
grant of planning permission.
 
(When it first became apparent, Councillors J. Barnes and Mrs
Barnes each declared a Non-Registerable Interest in this matter in
so far as they had known the objector for many years, had not
discussed the application with him and in accordance with the
Members’ Code of Conduct remained in the meeting during the
consideration thereof.)
 
(At the commencement of the meeting,
Councillor Mrs Cook declared an Other Registerable Interest in this
matter in so far as she was a Member
of Battle Town Council (BTC), had attended a BTC meeting where

made.  However, Councillor Mrs Cook had already left the
meeting prior to this application being
considered.)
 
(Councillor McLaren declared an Other Registerable Interest in

content:
This
application was presented to the Planning Committee as it was a
Council application.
 
Members of the Planning Committee had visited the site and heard
a representation from the Applicant.  It
was the Council’s statutory duty to deliver a Waste
Collection service across the district. 
It was noted that no ‘objections’ had been received
from local residents.  Consideration was also given to the comments made
by the statutory and non-statutory bodies as detailed within the
report.
 
The
site was formerly used as a vehicle depot by East Sussex County
Council and consisted mainly of hardstanding (tarmac).  It was bordered by residential properties, Combe
Valley Way (A2690), and commercial units.  The proposal included the on-site storage of nine
vehicles, but these would be empty of food waste.  The new building had a smaller footprint than the
original building but was taller to accommodate vehicle maintenance
and cleaning.  It would be positioned
approximately 20m from the nearest dwelling.  Noise mitigation measures were secured through
Condition 7, restricting noisy operations to specified
hours.  The development would create
additional local employment.  To achieve
10% Biodiversity Net Gain, off-site units would be purchased,
however, Members were particularly keen for on-site measures to
also be implemented, where feasible.  It
was requested that landscaping included planting suitable native
species, such as hawthorn or silver birch, to enhance screening and
that the colour of the building’s external finish be designed
to blend with its surroundings.
 
Councillor Stanger moved the motion to GRANT (Full Planning Permission) subject to
conditions, including landscaping (planting native species) and the
colour palette used to mitigate the impact of this relatively tall
building; wording to be delegated to officers in consultation with
the Chair of the Planning Committee. 
This was seconded by Councillor Chowdhury.  The motion was declared CARRIED (7 for /
unanimous).
 
DECISION: GRANT (FULL PLANNING
PERMISSION)
 
SUBJECT TO
CONDITIONS:
 

1.      The development hereby
permitted shall be begun before the expiration of three years from
the date of this permission.
Reason: In
accordance with section 91 of the Town and Country Planning Act
1990 (as amended by section 51 of the Planning and Compulsory
Purchase Act 2004).

 

2.      The development hereby
permitted shall be carried out in accordance with the following
approved plans and details:
Drawing No.
(BA2528.01B) As Existing Site Location Plan, dated
(11.25)
Drawing No.
(BA2528.02B) As Existing Block Plan., dated (11.25)
Drawing No.
(BA2528.03B) As Proposed Site Plan., dated (11.25)
Drawing No.
(BA2528.09 B) As Proposed Welfare Buildings., dated
(11.25)
Drawing No.
(BA2528.11A) As Proposed Block Plan (Dimensioned)., dated
(11.25)
Drawing No.

Brochure
(Wardale® Cycle Shelter ref BXMW/WAR), undated
Drawing No.

Drawing No.
(BA2528.07) As Proposed Front Elevation Long Section, dated
(September 2025)
Drawing No.
(BA2528.08) As Proposed Rear Elevation Long Section, dated
(September 2025)
Reason: For
the avoidance of doubt and in the interests of proper
planning.

 

3.      Pre-commencement condition: Prior to the
commencement of the development hereby approved, a Biodiversity
Gain Plan (BGP) and Metrics shall be submitted to and approved in
writing by the Local Planning Authority. The BGP shall demonstrate
how the development will achieve the minimum required Biodiversity
Net Gain (BNG) in accordance with the Environmental Act 2021. The
BGP shall include but not be limited to:

a)   
the completed statutory biodiversity metrics
calculations showing pre-and post-development biodiversity values;
and

b)   
full details of the off-site biodiversity units to
be secured (including but not limited to location of the off-site
land, Biodiversity Unit Certificate, units reference number from
Natural England BNG Register).
The
development shall thereafter be carried out in full accordance with
the approved details.

         Reason: To
ensure that the development delivers a measurable and legally
secured BNG in accordance with Section 98 of the Environmental Act
2021, and the National Planning Policy Framework.

 

4.      No development above
ground level shall take place on any part of the site until full
details of the soft landscaping along the site boundaries
(north-west and south-west) have been submitted to and approved in
writing by the Local Planning Authority. The details shall
include:

a)   
indications of all existing trees and other
vegetation on the land within the blue line, including details
of those to be retained, together with measures for their
protection during the course of
development;

b)   
planting plans;

c)   
written specifications (including cultivation and
other operations associated with plant and grass
establishment);

d)   
schedules of plants, noting species (which must be
native), plant sizes, and proposed numbers/densities;
and

e)   
an implementation programme.
The
approved scheme shall be implemented in accordance with the agreed
programme and maintained thereafter.
Reason: To reinforce and intensify the existing
vegetation to provide effective screening, in
order to mitigate the impact of development on neighbouring
residents and to enhance the appearance of the development, in
accordance with Policy OSS4(iii) and EN3 of the Rother Local Plan
Core Strategy and DEN1 of the Development and Site Allocation Local
Plan.

 

5.      If within a period of five
years from the date of the planting of any tree that tree, or any
tree planted in replacement for it, is removed, uprooted, destroyed
or dies, (or becomes, in the opinion of the local planning
authority, seriously damaged or defective) another tree of the same
species and size as that originally planted shall be planted at the
same place, unless the local planning authority gives its written
consent to any variation.

Reason: To ensure the
ongoing enhancement of the development in accordance with Policies
OSS4 (ii) (iii) and EN3 (ii) (e) of the Rother Local Plan Core
Strategy.

 

6.      No development above
ground level shall take place until details of the external
materials to be used in the construction of the buildings
hereby permitted, including their colour have been submitted to and
approved in writing by the Local Planning Authority. Development
shall be carried out in accordance with the approved details and
thereafter retained

         Reason: To
ensure that the development is of a satisfactory appearance and to
preserve the visual amenities of the area in accordance with Policy
OSS4(iii) of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy. 

 

7.      Prior to the first use of
the development hereby permitted, the noise mitigation measures set
out in Section 5 of the Noise Statement dated 1 December 2025 shall
be fully implemented and thereafter maintained for the lifetime of
the development. Specifically:

a)   
Wash-down operations shall only be undertaken
between the hours 08:00–18:00 (Monday–Friday) unless
otherwise agreed in writing with the Local Planning
Authority.

b)   
No radios to be used onsite before 08:00 or after
18:00.

c)   
Refuelling shall not take place between 19:00 and
07:00 the following day, unless otherwise agreed in writing with
the Local Planning Authority.

d)   
All vehicles and private staff cars shall be shut
down when not in use.

e)   
Workshop doors shall remain closed before 07:00 and
after 18:00

f)    
No grinding or other noisy machinery operations to
take place outdoors or with workshop shutters open.

g)   
Operative induction and Toolbox Talk to reinforce
quiet working practices and ‘good neighbour’ behaviours
shall be undertaken by the site operator regularly.
Reason: To
safeguard the amenities of nearby occupiers and ensure compliance
with relevant environmental standards, in accordance with Policy
OSS4(ii) of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy.

 

8.      Prior to commencing
construction of the development hereby approved, the
recommendations set out within the Arboricultural Report authored by The Mayhew
Consultancy Ltd, dated September 2025, in relation to tree
protection measures shall be fully implemented and adhered to for
the duration of the development until completion of the
constructions works.
Reason: To
ensure the protection of existing trees and vegetation during
construction, in accordance with Policy OSS4 (iii) of the Rother
Local Plan Core Strategy and DEN1 of the Development and Site
Allocation Local Plan.

 

9.      The surface water drainage
scheme for the site shall be wholly implemented in accordance with
the approved details prior to the first use and thereafter,
the approved system shall be maintained and managed wholly in
accordance with the approved maintenance and management plan
(Paragraph 8.8 of Flood Risk Assessment & Drainage Strategy
authored by (BP Civils D2408/FRA1.1 September
2025).
Reason: The
full implementation of the approved scheme and its long-term
management is to prevent the increased risk of flooding, to improve
and protect water quality in accordance with Policies DEN5 of the
Development and Site Allocation Local Plan, SRM2 (iii) and EN7
(iii) of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy and the National
Planning Policy Framework.

 

10.    The
development shall be carried out in accordance with the
precautionary working method for reptiles as set out in the
submitted ecological details, including the following
measures:

a)   
vegetation shall be maintained at a short sward
(approximately 5cm) throughout construction to discourage
reptiles;

b)   
any excavations shall be covered overnight or fitted
with a ramp to allow trapped animals to escape;

c)   
best practice pollution prevention measures shall be
implemented to minimise impacts on nearby habitats;

d)   
all chemicals and pollutants used or created during
the development shall be stored and disposed of in accordance with
COSHH regulations;

e)   
if reptiles are encountered, they shall be allowed
to disperse naturally or, if at immediate risk, moved by hand to a
sheltered, vegetated area away from disturbance; and

f)    
in the event a reptile is identified, works shall
cease immediately and advice sought from a suitably qualified
ecologist.
Reason: To
protect reptiles and ensure compliance with biodiversity
requirements in accordance with Policy EN5 of the Rother Local Plan
Core Strategy and the National Planning Policy
Framework.

 

11.    Prior to
the completion of development, a biodiversity enhancement scheme
shall be implemented to improve habitat opportunities for reptiles.
The scheme shall include:

a)   
installation of log piles created from felled
materials within suitable areas of the site; and

b)   
planting of native shrub species to provide shelter
and foraging opportunities.
The
approved enhancements shall be retained and maintained for the
lifetime of the development.

         Reason: To
enhance biodiversity and provide suitable habitat for reptiles in
accordance with Policy EN5 of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy
and Development and Site Allocations Local Plan and the National
Planning Policy Framework.

 

12.   The
development shall not be occupied until the parking
area has been provided in accordance with the approved plans
and shall thereafter be retained for that use and shall not be
used other than for the parking of motor vehicles.

        
Reason: To ensure the safety of persons and vehicles entering
and leaving the access and proceeding along the highway in
accordance with Policy TR4 of the Rother Local Plan Core
Strategy.

 

13.    The
proposed parking spaces shall measure at least 2.5m by 5m (add an
extra 50cm where spaces abut walls).

         Reason: To
provide adequate space for the parking of vehicles and to ensure
the safety of persons and vehicles entering and leaving the access
and proceeding along the highway in accordance with Policy TR4 of
the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy.

 

14.    The
proposed disabled parking spaces shall measure at least 3.6m by 5m
(add an extra 50cm where spaces abut walls).

         Reason: To
provide adequate space for the parking of vehicles and to ensure
the safety of persons and vehicles entering and leaving the access
and proceeding along the highway in accordance with Policy TR4
of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy.

 

15.    The
development shall not be occupied until cycle parking area(s) has
been provided in accordance with the approved plans and shall
thereafter be retained for that use and shall not be used other
than for the parking of cycles.

         Reason: In
order that the development site is accessible by non-car modes and
to meet the objectives of sustainable development in accordance
with Policy TR3 of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy.

 

16.    The
development shall not be occupied until a turning space for
vehicles has been provided and constructed in accordance with the
approved plans and the turning space shall thereafter be retained
for that use and shall not be obstructed.

         Reason: To
ensure the safety of persons and vehicles entering and leaving the
access and proceeding along the highway in accordance with Policy
TR3 of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy.

 

17.    No
external lighting shall be installed until full details of any
external lighting scheme have been submitted to and approved in
writing by the Local Planning Authority. The works shall then be
carried out in accordance with the approved details and thereafter
retained. Any variation to the approved scheme shall require prior
approval of details and subsequent compliance.

         Reason: To
safeguard the amenity of adjoining residents in accordance with
Policy OSS4(ii) of the Rother Local Plan Core Strategy.
        
 

BIODIVERSITY NET GAIN
CONDITION:
 

A.     The
effect of paragraph 13 of Schedule 7A of the Town and Country
Planning Act 1990 is that planning permission granted for the
development is deemed to have been granted subject to the condition
(“the biodiversity condition”) that development may not
begin unless:

a)   
Biodiversity Gain Plan (BGP) has been submitted to
the Local Planning Authority; and

b)   
the Local Planning Authority has approved the BGP.
The Local Planning Authority, for the purposes of determining
whether to approve a BGP if one is required in respect of this
permission would be Rother District Council.
As such,
the development granted by this planning permission is subject to
the Biodiversity Gain Condition, which requires a BGP to be
submitted to and approved in writing by the Local Planning
Authority before development commences. A BGP template is available
on the Government website:

https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/biodiversity-gain-plan,
and this should be completed and submitted to the Local Planning
Authority to demonstrate how the development will achieve 10%
Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG).  Advice on how BNG may be
delivered is also available on the Government website: 
https://www.gov.uk/guidance/understanding-biodiversity-net-gain.
          
NATIONAL PLANNING
POLICY FRAMEWORK: In accordance with
Paragraph 39 of the National Planning Policy Framework (2024), the
Council has worked in a positive and pro-active way with the
Applicant and has negotiated amendments to the application to
enable the grant of planning permission.

content:
At
the last meeting, Cabinet granted delegated authority to the
Section 151 Officer, in liaison with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder
for Finance, to approve the first Bexhill Neighbourhood
Board’s (BNB) 4-year Regeneration Investment Plan (RIP) to
meet the Government’s submission deadline of 28 November
2025. 
 
The
RIP of the BNB was based on extensive community, business and
Voluntary, Community and Social Enterprise (VCSE)
engagement.  A summary of the RIP was
provided to Members at Appendix A to the report; it aligned with
existing strategic plans and strategies of Rother District Council
(RDC) and East Sussex County Council and had been specifically
developed to meet identified economic development and community
cohesion needs of Bexhill. 
 
The
detailed summary set out the vision, spatial targeting, strategic
case for change, match funding and leveraged investment, community
and stakeholder engagement, governance and assurance.  The Bexhill Town Board and Partnerships Manager
advised that community engagement had been strong, as well as with
the business community, including the Bexhill Chamber of Commerce
and several high street businesses who were actively
engaged.  Continued engagement was a
commitment over the 10-year lifetime of the programme and not a
one-off exercise. 
 
The
total grant allocation for the programme delivery over the 10-year
period of Pride in Place (Phase 1) was £19.51m across revenue
and capital.  The funding would be used
mainly to deliver capital projects which contributed to
transformational regeneration within Bexhill.
 
The
submitted RIP for the first four years of its 10-year life,
represented a significant opportunity to transform Bexhill in terms
of its identity, economic and social resilience and its shared
prosperity, alongside a reduction in social and health
inequalities. It was noted that whilst RDC was not the
decision-making body for how the funding would be allocated, it was
the accountable body as well as being a likely project delivery
partner, roles that would likely pass to any successor Unitary
Authority under Local Government Reorganisation.  The Interim Director of Resources agreed to
consider the governance relationship between the BNB and the
Council, as accountable body, and how this would be monitored,
through the Audit Committee, if appropriate. 
 
RESOLVED: That the contents of the
first Regeneration Investment Plan of the Bexhill Neighbourhood
Board Pride in Place (2026 2030) plan, as submitted to the Ministry
of Housing, Communities and Local Government on 28 November 2025
and the extensive community, business and Voluntary, Community and
Social Enterprise engagement underpinning the development of the
plan, be noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the first Bexhill Neighbourhood Board's 4-year Regeneration Investment Plan to transform Bexhill's identity and economic resilience.

To confirm the result of the recent
Neighbourhood Plan Referendum for the parish of Hurst
Green.
content:
Following an affirmative local Referendum result in relation to
the use of the Hurst Green Neighbourhood Plan (HGNP) to help the
determination of planning applications in the Parish Neighbourhood
Area, Cabinet was requested to recommend to Council that the HGNP
be formally adopted and become part of the statutory Development
Plan for the area.
 
On 6
October 2025, Rother District Council (RDC) resolved that the HGNP
(as amended in line with the Examiner’s proposed
modifications) should proceed to local Referendum. This decision,
together with a revised version of the Plan, was published on the
Council’s website.  Following the
due legal process, and in accordance with the Neighbourhood Plan
legislation, a local Referendum was held on 20 November
2025. 
 
Following a turnout of 19%, 83% were in favour of RDC using the
HGNP for Hurst Green to help it decide planning applications; 17%
were against.
 
Following this result, it was incumbent on RDC under paragraph
38A(4)(a) of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004 to
‘make’ a Neighbourhood Plan within eight weeks of the
referendum result.  The principal effect
of making the Neighbourhood Plan was that it would become part of
the statutory ‘development plan’ for the area. Hence,
planning applications within Hurst Green Parish would be determined
against the HGNP, alongside relevant Local Plan policies, also
having regard to the National Planning Policy
Framework.  It was noted that the
development boundary for Hurst Green, as contained in the HGNP,
superseded the development boundary and related site allocations in
the 2006 Rother District Local Plan.
 
The
decision to make the HGNP would be publicised together with a
statement setting out how the environmental considerations had been
integrated into the Plan.  Cabinet was
pleased to recommend to Council that the HGNP be “made”
with immediate effect, which would bring it into legal
force.  This would take place at the
next scheduled meeting of full Council due to be held on 15
December 2025. 
 
Cabinet and the local Member paid tribute to officers and the
dedicated volunteer Neighbourhood Plan Steering Group at Hurst
Green Parish Council for all the hard work and efforts. 
 
RECOMMENDED: That the Hurst Green
Neighbourhood Plan 2021 - 2028 incorporating the Examiner’s
modifications, as presented to local Referendum, be
‘made’ with immediate effect and form part of the
Council’s Development Plan.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to formally adopt the Hurst Green Neighbourhood Plan as part of the Development Plan for the area.

purpose:
To approve the East Sussex Housing Partnership
Strategy and note the action taken preparing for Devolution and
Local Government Re-Organisation
content:
The
East Sussex Housing Partnership (ESHP) was a multi-agency network,
led by the five housing authorities in East Sussex, which included
local housing providers, professional bodies from the housing
sector and health, adult social care, children’s services,
criminal justice and the voluntary and community
sector.  Michael Courts, East Sussex
Housing Partnership Lead, Public Health, Adult Social Care and
Health, was welcomed to the meeting.
 
The
ESHP had developed the strategy to guide their work over the coming
years to sit alongside and complement the individual strategies in
each of the housing authorities.  The
draft strategy, attached at Appendix A to the report, built on a
strong history of partnership working locally and, since the
announcement of devolution and Local Government Reorganisation
(LGR), the ESHP was keen to maintain momentum to address local
housing needs and ensure capacity, resources and that expertise was
retained in the sector and strengthened cross sector working during
a time of change.
 
The
Cabinet Portfolio Holder for Housing endorsed the draft ESHP
strategy as a vital step in strengthening collaboration across the
county. The strategy set out clear priorities namely, preventing
homelessness, improving housing standards, and delivering the homes
needed, while addressing critical challenges such as health
inequalities and climate change. It reflected extensive engagement
with partners and residents, ensuring that local voices shaped the
approach. By endorsing this strategy and supporting the action
plan, the ESHP would work collectively to make the best use of
resources and deliver meaningful outcomes for communities during a
time of significant change.
 
The
draft ESHP strategy had been developed through a process of
system-wide collaboration, identifying shared objectives and
strategic outcomes that provided a long-term vision for the sector
and its place in the wider system. The strategy was designed to
form the basis for future business cases across the system, to
encourage greater levels of pooled resources, shared commissioning
and improved service coordination between sectors. The ESHP, and
its strategy, was well placed to provide the infrastructure to
continue to lead the development of the housing sector during
devolution and LGR.
 
The
action plan would be updated annually and reported back to Members
on progress; Members were particularly interested to see the number
of empty homes reduced, the prospect of modular housing that could
be constructed quickly and the development of council- owned social
rented housing.
 
RESOLVED: That
 

1)       
the East Sussex Housing Partnership Strategy be
endorsed; and
 

2)       
the outline draft action plan be supported for the
coming year, which the East Sussex Housing Partnership will
continue to update.
 
(Councillor McCourt declared an Other Registerable Interest as a
Board Member of Bexhill Community Land Trust and in accordance with
the Members’ Code of Conduct remained in the meeting for the
consideration thereof).
topline: The Cabinet has decided to endorse the East Sussex Housing Partnership Strategy and support the outline draft action plan for the coming year.

purpose:
To present the annual findings of the Rother
District Council residential accommodation complaints and tenant
satisfaction measures
content:
Consideration was given to
the report of the Head of Housing and Strategic Assets which
presented the findings of the Council’s owned accommodation
complaints and tenant satisfaction measures.  From 2020, the Council was a Registered Provider
(RP) for housing.  As an RP, the Council
was required to follow the Housing Ombudsman’s complaint
handling code.  Tenants were asked to
provide feedback on their tenancy via Tenants Satisfaction Surveys
(TSS); a copy of the data was detailed at Appendix 2 to the
report.
 
Between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2025, the Council received one
complaint, which was resolved at Stage 1.  Service requests were received, and these were
completed in a timely manner.  The TSS
achieved a 50% response rate (an increase from the previous year)
with 100% of tenants confirming that their property was
well-maintained.  Feedback was
overwhelmingly positive, with tenants highlighting prompt issue
resolution and strong communication from staff.  One tenant reported dissatisfaction due to
anti-social behaviour in the surrounding area.  Whilst this fell outside of the Council’s
direct control, these matters would be monitored and referred to
the relevant authorities, where appropriate.  Tenants’ feedback was detailed at Appendix 1
to the report.
 
Members were advised that as of 30 November 2025, all statutory
compliance checks were up-to-date and satisfactory, and all housing
management staff had completed legionella and asbestos awareness
training.  The Council narrowly avoided
a compliance failure when an internal warning email was
missed.  Existing safeguards ensured
that the estate’s compliance check was still completed on
time.  To prevent future issues, more
staff would receive alerts, and a new housing compliance system
would automate notifications, track due dates, and improve
oversight across all compliance areas.
 
In
response to Awaab’s Law, which mandated urgent action on
damp, mould and other hazards, the Council’s monitoring
systems and been enhanced and Damp and Mould Policy
updated.  This included trialling
environmental sensors and gateways that detected humidity,
CO2 levels and fire alarm tampering.
 
Members were pleased to note that tenant satisfaction was
good.  Congratulations were extended to
the Housing Management Team on the excellent results and for their
hard work in maintaining the Council’s residential
properties.
 
RESOLVED: That the
report be noted and the Housing Management Team be congratulated on
the results of the annual satisfaction survey.
topline: The Standards Committee has decided to approve recommendations based on positive feedback from Council tenants in the annual satisfaction survey.

purpose:
To advise the Committee on the Government's
response to the consultation on Strengthening the Standards and
Conduct Framework for councils in England
content:
At
the last meeting, Members were advised that between December 2024 and February 2025, the Government published
a consultation “Strengthening
the standards and conduct framework for local authorities in
England.”  2,092 responses were received. 
 
As a
result, the Government planned to legislate and reform the current
system as set out in the Localism Act 2011.  The new statutory regime would include the
introduction of a mandatory minimum Code of Conduct (CoC) for local
authorities; requirement that councils had Standards Committees;
that support be offered to both the complainant and the subject
Member during CoC investigations; introduction of a ‘right of
review’ for both the complainant and subject Member (might
necessitate establishing a new Standards Sub-Committee Hearing,
which could present operational challenges); powers to suspend
elected Members for a maximum of six months, with the option to
withhold allowances during the suspension period; police
investigations for serious offences; a new disqualification
criteria; and creation of a new national appeals
function. 
 
The
Council, or any future unitary authority (UA), would be required to
implement any legislative changes to the Localism Act 2011 and / or
any new legislation to its standards framework. 
 
During the discussion, the following comments were
made:
 

·      
The new UA might oversee up to 93, if not more,
Parish and Town Councils (P&TCs) across East Sussex. Guidance
would be sought from existing authorities on managing complaints at
this scale.

·      
A new Public Code of
Ethical Conduct (PCEC), incorporating the seven Nolan Principles,
was expected to be enacted in 2026.  It
was unclear whether this would occur before Local Government
Reorganisation.  The PCEC would no doubt
partially overlap with the existing Standards CoC (Strengthening
the Standards and Conduct Framework) and once adopted, was likely
to fall under the remit of the Standards Committee to introduce and
implement.

·      
The definition of a ‘serious breach’ and
‘non-serious breach’ had not yet been established;
statutory national criteria / guidance from the Government was
expected when they proceeded with legislating the changes they had
endorsed.  Once known, the criteria /
guidance would be formally adopted / replicated by the Council and
forwarded to P&TCs.  Members were
advised that any preliminary process to be adopted by P&TCs
through Rother Association of Local Councils was scheduled to be
discussed at the next meeting of East Sussex
Association of Local Councils (week commencing 8 December
2025).  Any
suggestions of the definition of a ‘serious breach’
should be submitted by Members of the Standards Committee to the
Monitoring Officer for onward referral.

·      
It was essential that
clear, standardised national guidelines were issued to all local
authorities and P&TCs. 
 
RESOLVED:
That:
 

1)   
the Government’s response to the consultation
on strengthening the Standards and Conduct Framework for Council in
England and the proposed legislative changes be both noted and
welcomed; and

 

2)   
Members of the Standards Committee to forward any suggestions of
the definition of a ‘serious breach’ to the Monitoring
Officer for onward referral.
topline: The Standards Committee has decided to approve recommendations for new legislative changes to the standards and conduct framework for local authorities in England.

purpose:
To receive an update on the number of Local
Government and Social Care Ombudsman complaints received since the
last report on 01 July 2025.
content:
Members considered the report of the Head of Digital and
Customer Services that set out details of the four complaints made
to the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman (LGSCO) which had
been determined since the Committee’s last meeting.
Complaints related to Parking and Other Penalties, Planning
Enforcement, Housing and Land.  One was
upheld (fault by the Council) and three were not investigated
(insufficient evidence, no fault found in the Council’s
actions, and / or not in the public interest to pursue
further).  A glossary of the terminology
was detailed at Appendix 2 to the report.
 
Key learning from LGSCO complaints included strengthening
governance in planning enforcement through adherence to policy,
accurate record-keeping and providing clear, well-reasoned
responses to complaints.  The Head of
Planning would be meeting with the Ombudsman to address enforcement
concerns.  Implementation of the Idox
Planning System, a new Planning Enforcement Policy, and additional
resources for the Enforcement Team were expected to strengthen
compliance and reduce complaints.   
 
As requested at the last meeting, Appendix 1 to the report
provided a comparative analysis of East Sussex councils’
LGSCO complaints, which showed that complaint volumes were broadly
consistent across authorities.
 
For the period from 8 May 2025 to 5 November 2025, Rother had
received 140 non-ombudsman complaints. 
Of these, 34 were non-complaints and treated as service requests,
40 were signposted to the Judicial Review Process, 13 were
non-council matters, two were resolved by Customer Services, 41
were Stage 1 complaints and 10 were Stage 2 complaints.  None were treated as vexatious.  Of the total 41 Stage 1 complaints, 10 were
resolved at the initial stage, eight were upheld, 17 were not
upheld, two were fast-tracked to Stage 2, and four were currently
under investigation.  Of the total 10
Stage 2 complaints (responded to formally by the Head of Service),
one was upheld, five were not upheld, one was referred as a Stage 1
complaint, and three were currently under review.  Details of both Stage 1 and 2 complaints,
including the average response times, were detailed within the
report.
 
Complaints provided the Council with an opportunity to learn and
improve processes and procedures to enable continuous improvement
in the services provided to residents.
 
RESOLVED: That the report be
noted.
topline: The Standards Committee has decided to note complaints made to the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman regarding Parking, Planning, Housing, and Land.

purpose:
To receive an update on the number of
complaints received and processed and other standards related
matters since the last report in July 2025.
content:
Consideration
was given to the regular (six-monthly) report of the Monitoring
Officer (MO) which set out details of the complaints received and
concluded, and other standards related matters arising since the
last meeting.
 
13 Code of Conduct (CoC) complaints involving
five District Councillors and eight Parish and Town Councillors had
been considered, nine of which had been concluded, three might
require a Standards Sub-Committee Hearing and one was on hold
pending the outcome of a related complaint.  Whilst most cases had been dismissed at an early
stage or not upheld, there had been remedial suggestions to improve
conduct and relationships.  The views of
one of the Council’s Independent Persons (IPs) was sought and
concurred with the proposed action in each case; brief details of
each case were provided at Appendix A to the report.  The triage stage continued to be effective and had
reduced the call on resources to consider minor and repetitive
complaints; monitoring would be ongoing.  In addition, five non-valid complaints had been
received and dismissed. 
It was noted that there were no
financial implications at this stage, however where complaints had
been referred to an external independent investigator, costs would
be incurred.
 
Support and guidance on dealing with conduct
matters had been provided to several Parish and Town Clerks where
persistent complaints between Members had been
experienced.  The MO had also delivered
a presentation on Governance, Standards and Member Conduct at the
Annual Parish Conference on 15 October 2025, at which 27 attendees
were present.  Going forward, support
and guidance on complaints issues / processes would be communicated
with the Parish and Town Councils (P&TCs), where
applicable.
 
A part-time Deputy Monitoring Officer, Mark
Watkins, had been appointed to assist the MO and oversee the
complaints process.
 
As reported in June 2024, the Arrangements for
Dealing with Member Complaints (ADMC) had been reviewed due to a
high volume of trivial or vexatious cases being
received.  A triage system was
introduced on a trial basis to manage these complaints more
efficiently. The system had proven effective and was now
incorporated into the ADMC.  Details
were also incorporated concerning the procedure to be followed
should a complaint progress beyond the triage stage; the MO might
seek informal resolution before initiating a formal investigation.
Where informal resolution was declined, the MO, in consultation
with the IP, would determine whether a formal investigation was
necessary or if the matter should proceed directly to a Hearing
Panel.  This would only occur where
further investigation would add little value and a hearing was in
the public interest.  It was confirmed
that references to the former Audit and Standards Committee had
been replaced with ‘Standards Committee,’ throughout
the document.  Members agreed the
proposed amendments to the ADMC as detailed at Appendix B to the
report.
 
The MO advised that the new unitary authority
would be overseeing a larger number of Members. Parish and Town
Clerks would be encouraged to play a greater role in supporting
smooth Council operations.  It was
important that Members exercised heightened awareness of their
conduct and responsibilities.
 
During the discussion, the following comments
were made:
 

·      
It was understood that Trevor Leggo, Chief Executive
of East Sussex Association of Local Councils, had developed a
mediation scheme for P&TCs to deal with complaints, which was
scheduled to be implemented in West Sussex.  The Rother Association of Local Councils (RALC)
would be seeking further details on the scheme, which could be
implemented in East Sussex.

·      
RALC had formed a working group, which included the
Chief Executive, relevant Council officers and Councillor Prochak,
to review and propose recommendations on the role of P&TCs
within the new unitary structure.

·      
Parish and Town Clerks
should have a clear understanding of the complaints process to
ensure issues were addressed appropriately from the
outset.  It would be helpful if Parish
and Town Clerks supported the MO in the initial stages of the
complaints process to assist with resolving issues internally
before escalation.  The MO agreed to
pause consideration of complaints, where appropriate, to allow
Parish and Town Clerks time to do this.

·      
The ADMC applied to all
complaints.

·      
The MO confirmed support, as appropriate, would be
provided to Councillors facing threats or harassment, particularly
online or via social media. Serious incidents would be referred to
the Police.
 
The MO expressed
appreciation to the IPs for their prompt handling of complaints and
to Democratic Services for their support in reducing the backlog
along with RALC for their positive commitment to supporting the
process at an early stage.
 
RESOLVED: That the:
 

1)   
report be noted; and

 

2)   
amendments to the Arrangements for Dealing with
Member Complaints, as highlighted within Appendix B, with the
approved insertion of the triage procedure at Appendix 1 to the
Arrangements and the inclusion within the arrangements of not
having to undertake a formal investigation, as appropriate, in
consultation with the Independent Person along with noting the
other changes as set-out in paragraphs 8 to 11 of the
report.
topline: The Standards Committee has decided to approve recommendations for handling Code of Conduct complaints involving District and Parish Councillors.

purpose:
To report on Internal Audit activity in the
second quarter of 2025/26 and to provide a progress update on the
implementation of audit recommendations made in earlier
periods.
content:
The Audit Manager
led Members through the internal audit report to 30 September 2025
that gave details of audit matters and any emerging issues, not
only in relation to audit but risk management and corporate
governance.
 
Five audit reviews
were completed in the second quarter of 2025/26. All provided
substantial assurance on the governance arrangements apart from the
Cyber Security review, which only provided limited assurance and
the reason for this was explained in confidential Appendix C. An
overview of the findings arising from the other four audits was
given in Appendix A to the report. 
 
Appendix B to the
report updated Members on progress made on implementing the audit
recommendations reported at the previous meetings. The number of
recommendations in the ‘Old Years’ section had almost
doubled this quarter due to the addition of the recommendations
still outstanding from 2024/25. In total, there were now 19
recommendations in this section, made up of eight longstanding
recommendations and 11 recommendations relating to 2024/25. Whilst
there had been some movement on many of these recommendations in
recent months, overall progress remained slow. In the
‘Current Year’ section, only one recommendation was
made in the first quarter of 2025/26, and this had since been
implemented.
 
The audits
currently scheduled to take place in the fourth quarter of 2025/26
were:
 

•     Creditors

•     Grounds
Maintenance

•     Payroll

•     Treasury
Management
 
Members were given
the opportunity to ask questions and the
following points were noted during the discussions:
 

•     Members were
grateful to the Senior Leadership Team (SLT) for monitoring the
outstanding recommendations;

•     professional,
external companies with the relevant expertise tested the
Council’s IT system;

•     all the
outstanding recommendations had been agreed with management at the
time the audit reports were issued and it was frustrating that
progress was so slow;

•     the Estates
Team’s outstanding recommendations were complicated,
compounded by a poor system in place previously. Major issues were
now being focused on and tracked weekly rather than the minor
issues which did not generate much income. The team also met with
agents every three weeks. The spreadsheets used to monitor progress
were shown to the Chair and the Audit Manager prior to the
meeting;

•     Members were
reassured that progress was being made by the Estates Team and as
the Council was receiving an uplift in income of approximately one
fifth on some of the larger rent reviews, some delays could be
tolerated. It was important that the Estates Team was not put under
pressure to negotiate too quickly, which could result in lower
rental income;

•     a metric would
be developed over the coming months with the Audit Manager to
measure the Estate Team’s progress. Internal tolerance levels
would be agreed with SLT in the first instance and then exception
reports  to
the Audit Committee;

•     Members
requested information concerning the level of accrued debts by the
Estates Team to be written off, both as a
result of the COVID-19 pandemic and since, and a summary of
the approach taken. Some debts were being recouped by adding a
premium to rental charges. A report would be brought to the
additional Audit Committee meeting scheduled to be held on 19
January 2026;

•     the Financial
Procedure Rules in the Council’s Constitution gave details of
the relationship between the Council and Internal Audit and the
roles of senior management. Members were encouraged to read through
the document for their information;

•     a review of
the Financial Procedure Rules would be conducted in due course and
brought to the Audit Committee for consideration; and

•     the Chair
could request to meet with relevant officers to discuss outstanding
recommendations and ask them to report to the Audit Committee, if
necessary.
 
Members discussed
the Cyber Security audit in confidential Appendix C to the report
in private session and recommended to SLT that non-IT backups of
the Council data be made and stored for use in the event of the
Council’s network being inaccessible. Members congratulated
officers on the progress made.
Members thanked the
Audit Manager and his team for their work and were happy to note
the report.
 
RESOLVED:
That:
 

1)   the Internal Audit report to
30 September 2025 be noted; and

 

2)   non-IT backup systems be put
in place for use in the event of the Council’s network being
inaccessible.
 
(Appendix C was
considered exempt from publication by virtue of paragraph 7 of
Schedule 12A of the Local Government Act 1972, as amended).
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to approve internal audit recommendations and implement non-IT backup systems for the Council's network.

purpose:
To consider the updated Corporate Risk
Register.
content:
Members received
the report of the Head of Corporate and Strategic Services, which
provided a position update on Risk Management processes and the key
strategic risks currently facing the Council.
 
A new Risk
Management Policy was approved by the Committee in September 2022,
was reviewed on an annual basis and the risk appetite statements
within it revisited and amended each year (where appropriate) to
ensure that they continued to meet the Council’s
requirements. The last review was undertaken by the Audit Committee
in March 2025, and the next review would take place at the Cabinet
meeting scheduled to be held on 2 February 2026.
 
The Corporate Risk
Register (CRR), attached at Appendix A to the report, had been
reviewed and updated by the Senior Leadership Team (SLT). Several
existing risks had been amended, one new risk had been added, and
some continued to exceed the risk appetite score (as stated on the
register), most notably:
 

•     Risk 1 –
Political – Local Government Reorganisation and Devolution
will impact delivery of Council services. This score exceeded the
risk appetite and reflected the uncertainty of local government
reorganisation.

•     Risk 2 –
Financial – The high costs of rental accommodation, house
prices and living expenses are increasing demands for temporary
accommodation. This score exceeded the risk appetite due to
increased levels of homelessness and escalating costs. Although
mitigations were in place, there was a general slow-down in house
building and the availability of affordable housing.

•     Risk 3 –
Economic/Financial – Failure to operate within a sustainable
budget. This score remained extremely high and reflected the
financial pressure that the Council was under, even with
mitigations in place.

•     Risk 5 –
Significant breach of data protection (linked also to risk 7
– IT failure). This reflected the ever-increasing threats to
data protection and cyber security.

•     Risk 10
– Financial risk concerning the Rother DC Housing
Company.

•     Risk 11
– The Strategic Asset Management Programme may not be
delivered before local government reorganisation and before
benefits are realised. This was a new risk about delivery of the
Strategic Asset Management Plan.
           
Service Plans
required all Heads of Service/Service Managers to record and
monitor their operational risks in a CRR. Performance and risk were
discussed regularly at Corporate Management Team meetings, which
was improving the identification and mitigation of the day-to-day
risks in the service areas and escalation of corporate level
risks.
 
Members were given
the opportunity to ask questions and the following points were
noted during the discussions:
 

•     Members raised
concerns regarding Risk 3, Economic/Financial, in light of the
disappearance of Central Government grants and the Local Government
Fair Funding Review, which was likely to redistribute funding to
the north of the country. Members agreed that this was scored
correctly;

•     Members raised
concerns that Risk 2, Financial, might be affected by the recent
Budget in terms of increased taxation on rental income, which could
either result in landlords leaving the rental market or passing on
increases to tenants, therefore potentially increasing
homelessness. It was hoped that the Council could purchase further
property for use as temporary accommodation and therefore continue
the success of the programme and minimise the cost of
homelessness;

•     it was hoped
that the Renters Rights Bill, to be enacted in due course, would
mitigate any resulting effects of the increased taxation on rental
income;

•     Members raised
concerns about the current reorganisation of management
responsibilities in terms of the Waste Contract and securing the
food waste depot. It was confirmed that, due to changes made within
the management structure and the fact that the food waste depot was
currently on track and regularly monitored by the Corporate
Programme Board, there was no need to escalate the risk;

•     concerns were raised regarding Risk 9, the Council’s
inability to deliver its housing building targets, which was being
monitored closely. The national planning system was working well,
but the problem lay with the time taken for houses to be built-out
following approvals; there were approximately 1.25m houses with
permission unbuilt nationally. The Council’s draft Local Plan
was going out to consultation shortly;

•     it was hoped
that the Registered Providers sector would become more active in
response to the £39 billion rent convergence announced by
Government earlier in the year, as well as the 10-year rent
settlement for social housing providers, which would help unlock
stalled sites;

•     the Council
was actively pursuing sites to come forward for development,
including Council-owned sites; and

•     the cyber
security risk should be highlighted to Cabinet.
 
Members recommended
and agreed to bring the CRR to Cabinet’s attention,
highlighting in particular the financial situation, house building
and cyber security risks and requested that the position be
reviewed.
 
RESOLVED:
That:
 

1)   the report and Corporate Risk
Register be noted; and

 

2)   the Corporate Risk Register be
brought to Cabinet’s attention, highlighting in particular
the financial situation, house building and cyber security risks
and that Cabinet review the position.
 
(Councillor Thomas
declared an Other Registrable Interest as Chair of Rother DC
Housing Company Ltd, and in accordance with the Members’ Code
of Conduct remained in the meeting for the consideration
thereof.)
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to review and update the Risk Management Policy and Corporate Risk Register to address key strategic risks facing the Council.

That the press and public be excluded whilst matters containing
exempt information, as prescribed by Part 1 of Schedule 12A of the
Local Government Act 1972, as amended and relating to Minutes

purpose:
This report summarises the findings of Grant
Thornton's Annual Audit Report for 2024/25. The
Annual Report provides commentary and
recommendations on the authority's arrangements for achieving value
for money across financial sustainability, governance and securing
economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of
resources.
content:
Members received
the report of the Interim Director of Resources which summarised
the findings of the Council’s External Auditor’s, Grant
Thornton, Audit Findings and Annual Audit Report for 2024/25. The
Annual Auditor’s Report (AAR) provided commentary and
recommendations on the authority's arrangements for achieving value
for money across financial sustainability, governance and securing
economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.
 
Ade Oyerinde, Grant
Thornton, led Members through the AAR, which was attached at
Appendix A to the report and covered three main areas:
 

a.   Opinion on the financial
statements (this work was pending the outcome of the main external
audit);

b.   Value for Money arrangements;
and
c.
  where relevant, other matters related
to the Auditor’s wider powers.
 
In line with the
previous year, the Auditors had found no significant weaknesses in
the Value for Money arrangements assessment for Financial
Sustainability, Governance and Improving Economy and Efficiency and
Effectiveness, but had identified improvement recommendations for
both Governance and Financial Sustainability. This year, only two
new improvement recommendations had been identified, which were
outlined on page 33 of the appendix, alongside management
responses. Insights for the Committee to consider were also
outlined within the respective commentary on arrangements sections
for the three criteria. There were no matters in relation to the
Auditor’s wider powers to report upon.
 
The AAR also
included a follow up on previous recommendations made; 10 of the 15
recommendations had been addressed or did not require any further
action, with four recommendations partially addressed and one
outstanding.
 
The Auditor’s
work on reviewing the financial statements for 2024/25 was well
progressed and was anticipated to be reported to the additional
meeting of the Audit Committee scheduled to be held on 19 January
2026 through the Audit Findings Report and updated draft financial
statements.  
 
Members were given
the opportunity to ask questions and the
following points were noted during the discussions:
 

•     recommendation
IR5 from the previous year, to take the Risk Register to Cabinet
annually, would be addressed when discussed elsewhere on the
agenda;

•     Members
congratulated officers for their work on rebuilding reserves since
the COVID-19 pandemic and for embracing technology, providing
greater visibility for the Council; and

•     Members noted
the need for Cabinet to continue to rebuild reserves to take into
the new unitary authority. 
                       
Members thanked
Grant Thornton for a comprehensive and valuable report, which they
were happy to note.
 
RESOLVED:
That the Annual Auditor’s Report presented by Grant Thornton,
be received and noted.
 
(Councillor Thomas
declared an Other Registerable Interest in this matter in so far as
he was Chair of the Rother DC Housing Company Ltd and in accordance
with the Member’s Code of Conduct, remained in the room
during the consideration thereof.)
topline: The Audit Committee has decided to receive and note the Annual Auditor's Report presented by Grant Thornton.

purpose:
To approve the draft local plan for
consultation purposes.
content:
Members received the report of the Head of Planning, the Rother
Draft Local Plan Regulation 18 document and the Development
Strategy and Site Allocations document, ahead of Cabinet approval
in December for  public consultation in
January 2026.
 
The
new Rother Local Plan (LP) would be a key planning document for
Rother, setting out the Council’s strategy for land use and
contributing to the achievement of all of the Council’s
Corporate Priorities. It was progressing in accordance with the
timetable agreed, which provided for a second “Regulation
18” consultation, in early 2026, to be focused on proposed
site allocations. Once adopted, the new LP would update and replace
Rother’s Core Strategy (2014) and Development and Site
Allocations (2019) Plans and would be supported at the local level
by Neighbourhood Plans.
 
The
draft Rother LP published for consultation in April 2024 contained
proposed policies and policy approaches relating to many different
topic areas, including housing, the economy and environmental
management. It also included a proposed Development Strategy.
However, it did not include proposed sites for development
(“site allocations”). The Regulation 18 document
attached at Appendix A to the report did not repeat those policies
and chapters but took forward the overall priorities and sub-area
approach.
 
It
was intended that the new LP would cover the period 2025–2042
(previously 2020-2040), as the National Planning Policy Framework
(NPPF) required local planning authorities to have an up-to-date
plan with strategic policies that covered a period of at least 15
years from the date it was adopted.
 
As
the current document was for public consultation, the proposed site
allocations were in draft form, requiring further evidence to
determine if all the site allocations were appropriate. Final
decisions on the site allocations to be included in the submission
LP, would be informed by this further work and the public
consultation.
 
The
report outlined the key considerations within the Regulation 18
document, including housing needs and supply, the Housing and
Economic Land Availability Assessment, the proposed site
allocations, the duty to cooperate actively and on an ongoing basis
with neighbouring authorities, county councils and other prescribed
bodies, employment floorspace and gypsy and traveller pitches,
infrastructure and spatial strategy. 
 
The
proposed public consultation on the LP would last eight weeks, be
widely promoted and would seek to inform and receive comments from
the widest possible range of people, organisations and stakeholder
groups. The Council would publicise the consultation through press
releases, social media and ‘My Alerts’. An online
consultation platform would be used to both display and provide an
opportunity to comment on the consultation document in an
accessible and engaging format, as well as a number of in-person
consultation events.
 
It
was intended to also publish an interim Consultation Statement with
the January 2026 consultation, providing an update on progress with
reviewing the policies and policy approaches in the light of
comments received in the first public consultation, which had been
continuing in parallel to the work on the Development Strategy,
site allocations and area-specific policies, presented in the
Regulation 18 document.
 
The
comments received in response to the January 2026 public
consultation would help officers pull together the 'Proposed
Submission version' of the LP, which would also go through a formal
public consultation process, known as the 'Regulation 19' stage,
scheduled for Summer 2026. It would then be submitted to the
Government, who would assign a Planning Inspector to carry out an
‘Examination in Public’. If found “sound”
and judged to have met other legal requirements by the Planning
Inspector, the Council would be able to adopt the new
LP.
 
Members had the opportunity to ask questions and the following
points were noted during the discussions:
 

·     
the new unitary authority must understand what was
important to Rother;

·     
Government targets were unrealistic, the development
of housing was a long process with many problems that prevented
progress, e.g. increased cost of materials, labour etc.;

·     
page 28 of the pack, point 2, Members suggested
adding ‘in particular reference to the rights of rivers and
trees, as agreed by this Council’;

·     
page 76 of the pack, point 6.23, Members suggested
adding ‘with a high priority to explore brownfield sites
first’, although Rother’s housing need could not be met
through brownfield sites alone;

·     
Rye and the eastern settlements cluster’s
strategic attempt to become a hub of transport and industry had
been well articulated. It was hoped that Community Land Trusts be
engaged to explore building social housing on brownfield
sites;

·     
Members suggested that the Rye Area Cycle and
Accessibility Master Plan be included in the LP, however this
suggestion would be submitted during the consultation
process;

·     
Community Infrastructure Levy funding could be
allocated to improve cycle paths;

·     
the disparity between income and house prices meant
that houses were not selling, therefore discouraging developers
from building out sites;

·     
unsold homes in Rother were being bought by London
boroughs for use as social housing. Members would prefer to see the
Council buying these properties for rental purposes;

·     
the importance of rivers and trees should be
stressed rather than stated as rights, as this was not a nationally
recognised policy;

·     
more emphasis should be placed on the protection of
the HWNL, which should remain as an area of scattered settlement,
rather than development eating into greenfield spaces;

·     
identifying more sites in Northern Rother than Rye
and Eastern Rother, which was not in the HWNL, sent the wrong
message. Officers confirmed that all areas of the district had been
considered equally, but the Council was reliant on the availability
of sites;

·     
page 76 of the pack, point 6.22, Members suggested
modifying as the Council needed to be more proactive about the
requirement of a bypass in western Bexhill, to improve east-west
communication across Rother, release more land for development and
remove heavy traffic from the roads of Bexhill, therefore this
should still be of the highest priority;

·     
Members suggested that the notion that diesel and
petrol cars were still the predominant car choice for those reliant
on private transport and therefore not in alignment with the
Council’s Climate Strategy should be modified on page 101 of
the pack, as more electric vehicles were being
purchased;

·     
there were sites proposed for Flimwell and Hurst Green which crossed the proposed
A21 bypass, therefore these should be given further
consideration;

·     
the principle of ‘windfall development’
(sites of less than five dwellings that were not planned for) or
‘infilling’ was supported within settlements and a
policy had been developed and considered in the previous
consultation to look at such opportunities where they could be
appropriate in the countryside;

·     
the importance of preserving the wetlands should be
emphasised. It was noted that relevant organisations would have the
opportunity to respond to the consultation;

·     
the Council worked closely with the Neighbourhood
Plan (NP) groups. Once the new LP had been adopted, the new set of
NPs could come forward and be in general conformity with
it;

·     
corroboration between the Parish and Town Councils
to work on NPs together should be encouraged;

·     
Parish Priority Statements were an option, but there
were currently none in Rother. They did not carry the same weight
as NPs, but could be a useful tool in setting out and consulting on
priorities, which would be taken into account when making planning
decisions;

·     
the HELAA was an evolving document, with new sites
being added;

·     
if a site was included in the final submission of
the LP to Government which then became unavailable, the Council
would not be open to legal challenge, but the Inspector would be
unlikely to allow it to be included. The consultation would gather
further information on site availability; and

·     
the up-to-date IDP was currently being prepared and
providers would be contacted during and after the consultation to
ensure the LP could be provided for.
 
Members thanked officers for their work in producing the
document and urged all residents and stakeholders to take part in
the consultation, to help shape the future of the district. It was
important to ensure that a high level of engagement was
generated.
 
The
Committee was happy to recommend the Rother Draft Local Plan
(Regulation 18) document to Cabinet for approval and formal
consultation, with the above comments of the Committee to be taken
into consideration. The Committee were also in support of the Head
of Planning being authorised by Cabinet to make any minor
amendments and editorial changes required prior to public
consultation, in consultation with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder for
Planning.
 
RESOLVED: It be recommended to Cabinet
that:
 

1)    
the Rother Draft Local Plan Regulation 18 document
be approved for formal public consultation;
 

2)    
the comments of the Overview and Scrutiny Committee
be considered; and
 

3)    
the Head of Planning be authorised to make any minor
amendments and editorial (including presentational) changes
required to the Regulation 18 document prior to public
consultation, in consultation with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder for
Planning.
 
(Councillor Coupar declared an Other Registerable Interest in
this matter in so far as she was a Director of Rother DC Housing
Company and in accordance with the Member’s Code of Conduct,
remained in the room during the consideration thereof.)
 
(Councillor Maynard declared an Other Registerable Interest in
this matter in so far as he was an Executive Member of East Sussex
County Council and in accordance with the Member’s Code of
Conduct, remained in the room during the consideration
thereof.)
 
(Councillor Thomas declared an Other Registerable Interest in
this matter in so far as he was Chair of Rother DC Housing Company
and a member of the Pevensey and Cuckmere Water Level Management
Board and in accordance with the Member’s Code of Conduct,
remained in the room during the consideration thereof.)
topline: The Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve the Rother Draft Local Plan Regulation 18 document for formal public consultation, with considerations for housing, environmental management, and infrastructure planning.
