purpose:
To update Members on the Revenue and Capital
Budget Monitoring Position for Quarter 2 2025/26. This report also
summarises the position to date on delivery of the savings targets
for 2025/26.
content:
Members received and considered the report of the Interim
Director of Resources on the Revenue and Capital Budget monitoring
position for Quarter 2 2025/26. The report also summarised the
position to date on delivery of the savings targets for 2025/26.
The Revenue Budget (RB) and Capital Programme (CP) statements were
summarised at Appendices A and B to the report respectively and a
review of the agreed savings targets for 2025/26 had been
undertaken, contained within Appendix C.  
 
The
RB (Total Cost of Services) was currently forecast to be
£16.172m (£15.966m forecast at quarter 1) at year end,
compared to the approved budget of £15.716m.  Members were asked to note that £265,000 of
this sum was anticipated to be funded from flexible capital
receipts, leaving the forecast service overspend as
£191,000.  The agreed budget
already anticipated a draw from Reserves of
£694,000.  In addition to this,
there was anticipated to be adverse variances of £296,000
related to financing costs and an error at budget setting on
government grants.  The combination of
these variances meant the Council was forecast to draw
£1.181m from reserves rather than the budgeted
£694,000. The report detailed the main variances, which were
summarised at Appendix A to the report.
 
The
further review of the deliverability of the agreed savings targets
for 2025/26, outlined within Appendix C to this report, anticipated
£398,200 to be fully deliverable (green status), with
£120,500 having been identified as undeliverable in year (red
status).  The remaining savings target
of £565,700 was anticipated to be partially deliverable in
year (amber status).  Work would
continue to be undertaken to monitor this position as the in-year
monitoring progressed. 
 
The
CP for 2025/26 and beyond remained under review and was being
constantly updated and reforecast as part of the governance
improvements introduced by the Corporate Development Team (CDT).
The focus was on the affordability of the overall Programme and
ensuring that any negative impact on the RB due to borrowing and
interest costs was minimised. This would ensure the medium-term
affordability of the CP, maximising the use of external grant
funding opportunities wherever possible.
 
The
updated CP totalled £183m, including prior year spend, with
the projected spend from 2025/26 through to 2028/29 totalling
c£115m and the anticipated spend for the 2025/26 budget
projected at £51m, illustrated in a table and pie chart
within the report. The phasing to the CP had been further revised
and updated as part of the period 2 budget monitoring process and
reflected the amendments outlined in the report, also shown within
the ‘Proposed 2025/25 Budget Change’ column of the
updated CP at Appendix B to the report.
 
The
Council had £5.00m in General Reserves not earmarked for any
specific purpose (plus a further £5.54m in Earmarked
Reserves).  If the revenue outturn
reported was realised, the General Reserve would reduce by
£1.181m to £3.819m. 
 
As
previously reported, the Council had some anticipated requirements
to draw from reserves for losses on investments (Hermes Property
Fund) and also where capital schemes had
changed direction and there might be a requirement to charge those
costs incurred to revenue.  The total of
these transactions was not anticipated to exceed £1.32m and
if these were to materialise, the General Reserve would be forecast
to be £2.5m at year end.
 
Members were given the opportunity to ask questions and the following points were noted during
the discussion:
 

·     
although Planning income was down against the
target, income had actually increased
compared to 2024/25, but the budget had also increased;

·     
business rates due to voids in
the area of Strategic Asset Management (SAM) had been
creating additional costs. Commercial agents were advertising the
properties for rent, but the market was less buoyant. Members
suggested that these assets be disposed of if income could not be
improved. This process was already underway, with five properties
being actively disposed; and

·     
the use of consultancy and interim staff in SAM had
also contributed to the deficit.
 
Members were supportive of the proposed amendments to the CP as
outlined within Appendix B to the report, with the additional
£310,000 for the Fairlight Coastal Defence Scheme. Members
welcomed the disposal of assets.
 
RESOLVED: It be recommended to Cabinet
that:
 

1)    
the proposed amendments to the Capital Programme, as
outlined in Appendix B to the report, with the additional
£310,000 for the Fairlight Coastal Defence Scheme, be
supported; and
 

2)    
the disposal of assets continue.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to recommend amendments to the Capital Programme and continue asset disposal in response to the forecasted overspend in the Revenue Budget for Quarter 2 2025/26.

content:
Cabinet received and considered Minute OSC25/34 arising from the
meeting of the Overview and Scrutiny Committee (OSC) held on 13
October 2025 that had considered the draft Budget Challenge
Proposals 2026/27, prior to public consultation.  The Chair of the OSC addressed Cabinet and
highlighted the concerns of the OSC, as contained within the Minute
extract, and in particular with regard
to the proposed removal of the conservation grant of
£1,050 to Sussex Wildlife Trust (SWT).    
 
The
report set out the challenging financial landscape facing the
Council, the process which had been followed and the need to
identify further savings ahead of setting the budget for
2026/27.  All Heads of Service
(HoS) had been requested to identify
sufficient savings to offset any growth that would be unavoidable,
the impact of inflationary pressures and to meet the base budget
shortfall for 2025/26 of £694,000.
 
HoS had been
tasked to identify 10% savings on their gross budgets and proposals
had been RAG (Red, Amber and Green) rated, for deliverability and
reputational impacts.  The proposals
were considered by the Budget Challenge Panel, consisting of the
Leader, Deputy Leaders (or their substitute) and the Portfolio
Holder for Finance and Governance, in late July. Draft proposals
were then considered by Cabinet Members at an informal
meeting.
 
Proposals were summarised in Appendix A (Savings) and Appendix B
(Growth) to the report for Cabinet’s consideration ahead of
public consultation, together with proposals for discretionary fees
and charges at Appendix C to the report. 
 
Additional growth items totalling £248,600 had been
identified since the start of the budget process and the OSC
meeting, relating to: Camber Welcome Centre cleaning and
maintenance, Deputy Monitoring Officer cover, permanent Information
Governance resource, Emergency Rota payments and a reduction in
baseline Planning Income due to volume of applications
received.  It was also anticipated
provision for the costs of Local Government Reorganisation would
need to be made, including management support changes, training
etc., but would be met either from grant funding (if available) or
using Flexible Capital Receipts where possible. 
 
With regard to the grant to SWT, whilst Members were minded to remove it from the proposed savings, it was
agreed to keep the proposed removal in the consultation and draw
specific attention to it.  As an aside,
it was advised that East Sussex County Council (ESCC) and the
Environment Agency also made contributions (£5,000 from ESCC)
and SWT had total reserves of £3m in 2023/24.  Members would reconsider whether to remove the
grant following the outcome of the consultation. 
 
Members were asked to note that additional savings from the base
budget would need to be identified beyond those outlined within the
paper, to ensure a balanced budget could be set and the Council
remained financially stable.  The
Finance team would be working alongside the Senior Leadership Team
and HoS to seek to identify further
savings during the Autumn and early Winter.
 
Public consultation on the proposals would commence in November
and December 2025 and those organisations that had been identified
as potentially losing funding would be proactively targeted.
Members requested that plain English principles be applied to the
consultation documents together with an increased use of
graphics.   Consultation results
and an update on the financial position would be reported to the
OSC on 26 January 2026.  It was likely
that a Member Briefing would be arranged in the new year, following
confirmation of the Council’s three-year settlement figure
from Government which was expected just before
Christmas.
 
RESOLVED: That the:
 

1)    
proposals, including the schedules within Appendix
A, B & C to the report be approved for inclusion in the public
consultation for the 2026/27 Budget, together with the additional
growth items totalling £248,600; and
 

2)    
contents of the report, including the challenging
financial position and need to identify further savings ahead of
setting the budget for 2026/27, be noted.
 
(Councillor Barnes, J declared an Other Registerable Interest as
a Member of Sussex Wildlife Trust and Friends of Rye Harbour Nature
Reserve, and in accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct
remained in the meeting for the consideration thereof.)
 
(Councillor Maynard declared an Other Registerable Interest as
an Executive Member of East Sussex County Council, and in
accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct remained in the
meeting for the consideration thereof.)
 
(Councillors Prochak and Rathbone Ariel each declared an Other
Registerable Interest as a Member of Sussex Wildlife Trust and in
accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct remained in the
meeting for the consideration thereof.)   
 
(Councillor Timpe declared an Other Registerable Interest as a
Member of Bexhill-on-Sea Town Council and a De La Warr Pavilion
Trustee, and in accordance with the Members’ Code of Conduct
remained in the meeting for the consideration thereof.)
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve budget proposals for 2026/27, including the removal of a conservation grant to Sussex Wildlife Trust.

purpose:
To approve the Data Protection
Policy
content:
A
new draft Data Protection Policy (DPP), attached at Appendix A to
the report had been developed in response to evolving legislation
and increased public expectations regarding data
privacy.  The DPP ensured the Council
maintained compliance with the Data Protection Act 2018 and UK
General Data Protection Regulations (GDPR).  It also reflected best practices in data
governance and security.
 
It
was reported that local government was among the most at risk for
data beaches and findings from the Information Commissioner’s
Office found that from 2023 until March this year, there were
around 1,956 GDPR breaches impacting councils. 
 
The
Council handled a wide range of personal and sensitive data in the
delivery of its services; therefore, it was essential that data was
managed responsibly.  The DPP was based
on six core data protection principles, over which
‘accountability’ was the primary theme.  The DPP improved focus on data governance, aligned
with key themes within the Council Plan and would aid readiness for
Local Government Reorganisation.
 
Cabinet was supportive of the new DPP and agreed it ensured that
the Council met is legal obligations under current legislation and
supported operational efficiency by defining roles,
responsibilities and procedures for managing data
security.  It was also recommended that
delegated authority be granted to the Data Protection Officer, in
consultation with the relevant Senior Information Risk Owner and
Head of Digital and Customer Services to make any minor amendments
to the DPP, as required, as well as implementation and overseeing
staff training and awareness.   
 
RECOMMENDED: That:
 

1)    
the proposed Data Protection Policy at Appendix A to
report, be approved and adopted;
 

2)    
delegated authority be granted to the Data
Protection Officer, in consultation with the relevant Senior
Information Risk Owner and Head of Digital and Customer Services,
to authorise minor amendments to the Data Protection Policy as
required by legislative or other procedural changes; and
 

3)    
delegated authority be granted to the Data
Protection Officer, in consultation with the relevant Senior
Information Risk Owner and the Head of Digital and Customer
Services to implement the Data Protection Policy and oversee staff
training and awareness.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve and adopt a new Data Protection Policy to ensure compliance with data protection regulations and best practices.

purpose:
To approve the Freedom of Information Policy /
Framework
content:
The
Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOI) and Environmental Information
Regulation 2004 (EIR) Policy ensured that the Council had a
comprehensive framework to manage requests for information, which
were compliant with statutory obligations and promoted transparency
across all services.  FOI / EIR requests
provided a statutory right of access to information held by public
authorities and the Council was required to respond to requests for
information in accordance with these laws.
 
The
updated Policy, attached at Appendix A to the report formalised the
Council’s procedures for handling FOI / EIR requests,
replaced current processes and aligned with best practice guidance
from the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO).  It focused on data governance, improved the
Council’s current position, aligned with key themes within
the Council Plan and would aid readiness for Local Government
Reorganisation.
 
Cabinet was pleased to note that because of new procedures being
introduced by the Data Protection Officer, improvements had been
made to the Council’s response times which would be reflected
in the next set of Key Performance Indicator data.  A new FOI software package was also being rolled
out that would further improve processing, coupled with a
publication scheme that could reduce the number of FOIs
further.  
 
Cabinet was supportive of the new Policy and agreed it would
reduce the risk of reputational damage, complaints and enforcement
action from the ICO.  It was also
recommended that delegated authority be granted to the Data
Protection Officer, in consultation with the relevant Senior
Information Risk Owner and Head of Service, to make any minor
amendments to the Policy, as required.  
 
RECOMMENDED: That:
 

1)    
the proposed Freedom of Information Act 2000 and
Environmental Information Regulation Policy 2004 at Appendix A, be
approved and adopted; and
 

2)    
delegated authority be granted to the Data
Protection Officer, in consultation with the relevant Senior
Information Risk Owner and Head of Service, to authorise minor
amendments to the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and Environmental
Information Regulation Policy 2004, as required by legislative or
other procedural changes.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve and adopt a new Freedom of Information Act 2000 and Environmental Information Regulation Policy 2004.

content:
Cabinet received and considered Minute OSC25/33 arising from the
meeting of the Overview and Scrutiny Committee (OSC) held on 13
October 2025 that had considered the Council’s Housing
Renewal Financial Assistance Policy 2026-2028 (HRFAP).  The OSC had considered the HRFAP in detail and
were pleased to recommend it to Cabinet for onward approval and
adoption by full Council.
 
The
Council only received sufficient funding from HM Government
(through the Better Care Fund paid to East Sussex County Council
(ESCC) and distributed to the Council) to mainly provide mandatory
Disabled Facilities Grants (DFGs) in accordance with the Housing
Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996. DFGs were available
to disabled people when works to adapt their home were assessed as
necessary and appropriate to meet their needs, and when it was
reasonable and practicable to carry them out having regard to the
age and condition of the dwelling. Elements of the grant were
mandatory, and others could be provided at the discretion of the
Council (discretionary grants).
 
The
main change in the Council’s proposed policy (attached at
Appendix A to the report) was increasing the discretionary grant
from £30,000 to £40,000, to reflect the costs of more
complex cases.  The mandatory maximum of
£30,000 was set in 2008 and was no longer adequate in many
cases. In such cases, funds from other bodies were sought,
including registered social landlords and ESCC.
 
Members were supportive of the proposed change to the policy and
recognised the valuable contribution adaptations made to
residents’ lives.  It was
requested that information and case studies be provided to Members
on a regular basis to raise the profile of the availability and
success of these grants. 
 
RECOMMENDED: That the Housing Renewal
Financial Assistance Policy 2026-2028 at Appendix A to the report

content:
Consideration was given to the comprehensive report of the Head
of Corporate and Strategic Services that updated Members on the
Bexhill Neighbourhood Board Regeneration Investment Plan, that was
required to access the Pride in Place Programme (PiPP) funding allocated by the Ministry of Housing,
Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) to Bexhill.  The total grant allocation for the programme
delivery over the 10-year period of PiPP was £19.51m across revenue and
capital.
 
The
decision-making body for how the funding would be spent was the
Bexhill Neighbourhood Board (BNB), which was established in May
2025 as the Bexhill Town Board under the previous planned Long-Term
Plan for Towns programme. The first four tranches of funding would
be released by MHCLG subject to successful assessment of a 10-year
vision statement and 4-year investment plan.
 
The
BNB and Partnerships Manager and Project Officer, supported by
Council colleagues, Members and other partners and stakeholders,
had worked with the BNB to commission a specialist agency to
develop an inclusive Place Plan for Bexhill, drawn from extensive
stakeholder and community engagement, which had been highly
commended.  This work had directly
informed the BNB Regeneration vision and plan, which required
formal BNB approval at its meeting on 21 November 2025, prior to
its submission by 28 November 2025.
 
Whilst the Council was not the decision-making body for the
PiPP, it was the Accountable Body for
the spend and the overall programme and was likely to be a delivery
partner for some projects.  To meet the
prescribed timescales, delegated authority was sought for the
Section 151 Officer in liaison with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder
for Finance and Governance to approve the BNB’s Plan, prior
to the submission deadline of 28 November.  The full submitted plan would then be reported to
Cabinet at the meeting scheduled to be held on 8 December
2025.
 
Cabinet was pleased to approve the recommendation and
acknowledged the commitment by MHCLG to grant more than £19m
over 10 years for Bexhill, which represented much needed
investment. It was a significant opportunity to transform the town
in terms of its identity, its economic and social resilience and
its shared prosperity, alongside reduction in social and health
inequalities.
 
RESOLVED: That
 

1)    
delegated authority be granted to the Section 151
Officer in liaison with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder for Finance
and Governance, to approve the details of the first 4-year
investment plan of the Bexhill Neighbourhood Board in order to meet
the submission deadline of 28 November 2025;
 

2)    
within the Councils’ role as the accountable
body for the Pride in Place Programme, delegated authority be
granted to the Section 151 Officer, in liaison with the Finance and
Governance Portfolio Holder, to approve the governance arrangements
when finalised;
 

3)    
delegated authority be granted to the Head of
Corporate and Strategic Services to enter into relevant agreements
with third party entities, as agreed by the Bexhill Neighbourhood
Board and for the purposes of delivering the programme, in
consultation with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder for Finance and
Governance; and
 

4)    
a full report, including the Bexhill Neighbourhood
Plan first 4-year investment intentions and details of underpinning
engagement, be received by Cabinet at the meeting scheduled to be
held on 8 December 2025.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Bexhill Neighbourhood Board Regeneration Investment Plan to access funding for a 10-year programme.

purpose:
To consider whether or not to convene the IRP
to consider Member Allowances for the remainder of the current
administration, in light of LGR and budget constraints
content:
In
accordance with the Members Allowances Regulations 2003, before the
Council could make any amendments to its allowance scheme, the
Council had to have regard to the recommendations made by an
Independent Remuneration Panel (IRP). 
In February 2025, the Council set its allowances to apply for the
current civic year 2025-26 and agreed a 3% increase to the Basic
Allowance (BA) and all Special Responsibility Allowances which was
in line with the staff pay award.
 
In
2024-25, it was agreed by Council that the IRP would meet annually
until Autumn 2026 to review the BA and consider any
increase.  If the IRP did not meet, the
current allowances would continue, without any annual uplift,
representing a budget saving.  It was
noted that the Members’ Allowances currently paid at Rother
were not out of keeping in comparison with neighbouring East Sussex
district and borough councils and varied by only
£200-£300. 
 
Members were acutely aware of the Council’s challenging
financial position and having consulted with all Group Leaders /
Deputies on this matter, it was a shared view that there should be
no increase on the current Members’ Allowances for the
remainder of the life of Rother District Council (RDC), for Members
to directly contribute to budget savings.  It was therefore proposed that the IRP was not
convened, and the current Members’ Allowances remain in place
until May 2027 or the demise of RDC, whichever was the later,
as a result of Local Government
Reorganisation (LGR).  It was noted that
should LGR not proceed or be significantly delayed beyond 2028, the
Chief Executive would convene an IRP to review the Members’
Allowances at that time. 
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)    
the Independent Remuneration Panel not be convened and the current 2025/26
Members’ Allowances remain as the allowances, with no annual
increase for the remainder of the current administration (May 2027)
or until the demise of Rother District Council, subject to Local
Government Reorganisation, whichever was the later; and
 

2)    
should it become clear that the Local Government
Reorganisation not proceed or is significantly delayed beyond 2028,
the Chief Executive will convene an Independent Remuneration Panel
to review the Members’ Allowances.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to freeze Members' Allowances until 2027 or the potential demise of Rother District Council, with a provision for review in case of Local Government Reorganisation delays.

purpose:
To update on the progress of the Services and
Assets Devolution framework and introduce the draft Services and
Assets Evaluation Matrix for approval.
content:
Members received the report of the Deputy Chief Executive that
provided an update on the progress of the Services and Assets
Devolution Framework (SADF) and introduced a draft Services and
Assets Evaluation Matrix (the Matrix) for approval (Appendix B to
the report). 
 
The
SADF was adopted by Cabinet in March 2025 and provided the criteria
the Council would apply when considering whether to dispose of
services and assets, governed by the Council’s adopted Asset
Disposal Policy (ADP).  It was likely
that in certain circumstances, some assets would not be eligible
for devolution, including those that generated significant income,
were held to fulfil strategic priorities, projects or future
capital realisation.
 
Between March and the 30 September 2025 deadline, the Council
had received Expressions of Interest (EOI) for 131 assets within
the district from 25 different organisations; none had been made in
relation to services beyond those associated with repairing and
maintaining an asset.  Events, workshops
and individual meetings had been held with community groups and
parish and town councils to explain the criteria of the SADF and
listen to any concerns raised, as well as discuss the legislative
constraints that applied to public bodies when meeting their
statutory obligations.
 
To
inform the process, the Council had also reviewed and made a
high-level assessment of some 200 of its land assets to ensure that
it had up to date information and understood the existing and
future values, as well as identifying assets that were likely to be
excluded from the SADF criteria.    
 
The
Matrix would support the Council to deliver the objectives of the
SADF openly and transparently by demonstrating the rationale of its
decision making.  The Matrix weighed the
financial value of an asset above others, supporting the
Council’s Fit for the Future priority within the Council
Plan. In addition, other less tangible values, would also be
considered, including community benefit, environmental and economic
values, and supporting the key Council Plan priorities of Live Well
Locally, A Thriving Local Economy and Green to the Core.
 
The
SADF criteria would be applied to each EOI and authority sought
from the Property and Service Investment and Disposal Panel (PSIDP)
to invite a full business case from applicants to demonstrate
capability and affordability to manage and maintain the asset
lawfully and responsibly.  Once a
business case was received, assessed and recommended by the PSIDP,
it would be recommended to Cabinet that the service and asset be
devolved to the applicant.
 
An
internal project team would be formed to oversee the process,
including colleagues from the Estates team as well as Finance and
Legal teams. The project was already monitored by the
Council’s internal Corporate Programme Board and the Board
would continue to monitor progress as well as project risks and its
communication approach.  Members were
supportive of the Matric being used to complement and aid decision
making and reiterated that the ADP and supporting SADF should be
flexible and applied on a case by case basis, in light of local
information. 
 
RESOLVED: That
 

1)    
the progress of the implementation of the Services
and Assets Devolution Framework and next steps be noted;
 

2)    
the draft Services and Assets Evaluation Matrix be
considered and approved for use in the next phase of the
implementation of the Services and Assets Devolution Framework;
and
 

3)    
the Property and Services Investment and Disposal
Panel be authorised to make amendments to the Services and Assets
Evaluation Matrix criteria as may be required, noting that any
final approval to devolve or dispose an asset remains with
Cabinet.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the draft Services and Assets Evaluation Matrix for the implementation of the Services and Assets Devolution Framework.

purpose:
To seek approval to the letting of the new
Kiosk at Camber
content:
An
open marketing campaign had been undertaken to find a takeaway food
and beverage operator for the kiosk space within the new
development of the Coastal office, public conveniences and showers,
new public meeting space and Royal National Lifeboat Institution  operations
space at Camber Central Car Park.
 
Three acceptable offers had been received for the premises and
scored to ensure the successful candidate aligned with the
Council’s values and commitment to collaborate with its
communities, add maximum value to the local economy and promote a
sustainable business model as well as providing a quality fit out
and food and beverage proposal.  Details
were set out within the Confidential Appendices A and B to the
report. 
 
Following the scoring exercise, the operator referred to as
candidate ‘C’ within Confidential Appendix A was
recommended for approval due to a broader market appeal, community
and sustainability as opposed to simply accepting the highest base
rent payable.  It was noted that whilst
the base rent proposed was not the highest offered, the agreement
included a turnover element, which was likely to exceed the rent
offered by the other candidates.
 
Cabinet accepted the recommendation and agreed that the proposed
operator demonstrated a strong branding and design proposal, as
well as a high-quality food and beverage offer and desire to work
with and support the local community.
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)    
the newly developed Kiosk at Camber Central Car Park
be leased to candidate ‘C’ on the terms detailed in
Confidential Appendix A to the report; and
 

2)    
delegated authority be granted to the Chief
Executive, in consultation with the Cabinet Portfolio Holder for
Regeneration and Economic Development and Section 151 Officer, to
make amendments to the final lease contract terms as
required.
 
(Appendices A and B were considered exempt from publication by
virtue of paragraph 3 of Schedule 12A of the Local Government Act
1972, as amended).
topline: The Cabinet has decided to lease the kiosk at Camber Central Car Park to candidate 'C' based on their community engagement and sustainability focus.

purpose:
To provide the Human Resources Committee with
an update on progress with the People Strategy Action Plan and
general Human Resources update.
content:
Members received
the report of the Head of Corporate and Strategic Services that
provided an update on progress with the People Strategy Action Plan
(PSAP) and general Human Resources (HR) update, covering the period
April 2024 to March 2025. The PSAP was attached at Appendix A to
the report and Members were asked to note that most actions had now
been delivered or were in progress.
 
Appraisals had
commenced in March 2025; the mid-year review phase commenced in
September and would continue throughout October 2025. Recruitment
activity had remained stable during the reporting period, the
annual staff turnover rate had increased to 17.8%, compared to
13.6% in the previous year, however, there had been an overall
improvement in staffing trends in the current year, with an
increase in new starters and a reduction in the number of
leavers.
 
Recruiting to
professional posts remained an area of concern and the Council was
working collaboratively with partner authorities across East and
West Sussex, as well as with South East
Employers. Key senior appointments had now been successfully made,
resulting in the Senior Leadership Team now being fully in place.
The HR team was also now fully resourced, and Belinda Collins had
been appointed as the new HR Manager.
 
The Corporate
Induction Programme had been refreshed
and a new Welcome Pack gave new starters all essential information
in one place. Quarterly induction sessions were also planned, to
include presentations from the Senior Management Team and
representatives from a range of services.
 
An Employee
Engagement Group (Colleague Engagement Group) had recently been
introduced, bringing together staff representatives from each
department, to discuss upcoming changes and to share suggestions
and ideas. Other employment relations activities included stable
relations with Employee and Trade Unions, a Staff Survey resulting
in a number of actions having been
implemented, including the opening of a new staff canteen area
which had been well received, and refurbishment of the Town Hall
Villas, which were being redesigned to accommodate staff meetings
and collaborative working.
 
The Apprenticeship
Scheme (AS) continued to perform strongly, with two apprentices
having completed their programmes this year and secured permanent
roles with the Council. There were currently 15 apprentices across
a range of services, focusing on higher-level apprenticeships (up
to Level 5) to support recruitment and retention to professional
posts. Since the scheme’s inception, 22 apprentices had
successfully completed their programmes, and further growth was
planned for the following year.
 
Seven students had
completed work experience placements across various services and two further placements were scheduled
within Environmental Health and Planning. One earlier placement
with Environmental Health had subsequently been interviewed and
appointed to a permanent role within the Council.
 
The HR team had
recently participated in several job fairs, including the event
hosted at the De La Warr Pavilion. These events saw strong
attendance and generated significant interest in career
opportunities at the Council.
 
The majority of training had continued to be
delivered online and training requests from appraisal reviews had
been logged. Together with information from service plans, this
would inform a corporate training plan. New legislation required
senior Housing Managers to attain a Level 4 or 5 apprenticeship
qualification, and work was being carried out with managers to
deliver this mandatory training.
 
A new suite of
iHASCO courses had been added and uptake of optional courses
continued to increase. Cyber Security training had been prioritised
across the workforce and a Carbon Literacy training programme
introduced to support the Council’s sustainability goals; the
Council had achieved a Bronze Carbon Literate Organisation status
in June 2024 and a Silver accreditation in September 2025. The ILM
Level 5 Management course had also been launched, as part of the
Council’s commitment to developing strong and effective
leadership across the organisation.
 
Each business area
managed its own training budget and the overall training budget
remained similar to the previous year.
The Sussex Training Consortium and iHASCO continued to be the
Council’s primary HR training providers, and a significant
portion of the budget was allocated to their services. The year
ahead would focus on developing staff and supporting them through
organisational change.
 
One minor staff
accident was reported during the period, representing a reduction
on the previous year and refresher training was being provided as
first-aid qualifications expired. Health and Safety processes and
policies were being updated to ensure compliance and appropriate
staff support. The HR Health and Safety Equipment budget continued
to fund Display Screen Equipment assessments and any resultant
equipment required. The Council had four trained Mental Health
First Aiders and general mental health training for staff had been
expanded via iHASCO. Staff could access support through the
Employee Assistance Programme (EAP), with referrals to Occupational
Health and counselling services where appropriate.
 
One new policy to
allow flexible retirement had been brought forward and the Council
was in the process of updating all HR policies, with a suite of
policies to be made available to all staff.
 
In April 2025, it
was agreed that all staff would receive a £1,000 pay award
and it had been confirmed that from April 2026 onwards, pay awards
would be determined nationally through the NJC (National Joint
Council) pay negotiations. Market supplements for roles where there
was clear evidence of recruitment difficulties had begun to be
implemented and the Gender Pay Gap Report, attached at Appendix B
to the report, demonstrated continued improvement compared to
previous years. An Employee Monitoring Dashboard was also found at
Appendix C to the report, providing further data for Members’
information.
 
Members were given
the opportunity to ask questions and the
following points were noted during the discussion:
 

•     cyber security
and data breaches had both been raised as high corporate risks to
the Council. Training courses in both were mandatory for all staff
and Members and work was being carried out to ensure completion;

•     the EAP
offered advice and guidance covering a wide range of issues;

•     the reviewed
Absence Policy and Recruitment and Retention Policy would be
amongst the first to be brought to the Committee for approval;

•     the AS was
open to all ages, was job specific and funded through a levy taken
through the salary budget of 3%. A paper could be brought to the
Committee at a later date, providing
further information on the scheme, such as retention rates; and

•     the Council
was having to look further afield for suitable candidates for
professional posts that were difficult to fill; there was a skills
shortage nationally. Consideration was being given to how the AS
could also assist in these areas, particularly in the light of
successes in the Environmental Health and Planning departments.
 
The Chair and Chief
Executive thanked the HR Manager and her team for an excellent
report, which clearly highlighted the key messages of employee
relations, initiatives and training and development, with the use
of graphics in the Dashboard to illustrate key data. The Chair
encouraged all Members of the Council to read the report.
 
The Local
Government Reorganisation process would be challenging, and the
Council was looking to develop a Change Programme to include
leadership development, skills development and managing change,
in order to equip staff to thrive in the
new unitary authority. This would be brought to the Committee for
approval.
 
RESOLVED:
That the 
progress made with the People Strategy Action Plan and
general Human Resources update be noted.
topline: The Human Resources Committee has decided to note the progress made with the People Strategy Action Plan and general Human Resources update.

content:
Members received
the report of the Chief Executive which outlined the
Council’s approach to Market Supplements and Retention
Payments and proposed an update to the Pay Policy accordingly.
 
The Human Resources
(HR) Committee had approved the Market Supplement Policy Statement,
as set-out in the Pay Policy, the previous year and the proposed
revised Interim Market Supplement wording included an additional
section as detailed in paragraphs 6 to 8 of the report. In
addition, there was the introduction of an Interim Policy
Statement, to be included in the Pay Policy, at paragraphs 9 to 11
of the report, which began to address the issues of
retention. 
 
Turnover had risen
in the current year, which could result in service delivery
difficulties in some areas. The Retention Payment Policy needed to
be considered within a wider recruitment and retention strategy,
which would be brought forward to the next HR Committee
meeting.
 
The HR department
had identified some cases where retention payments were essential
now however, longer term, there would need to be other initiatives
to support retention. The management of market supplements and
retention payments would be tightly controlled and any expenditure would go through the
Spending Review Panel before any payments would be made.
 
The proposed
protocol for the application of market supplement payments was
outlined in paragraph 3 of the report. Payments would be offered,
in the first instance, at a rate of c30% of the difference between
the highest Council package value and the highest package in the
market for directly comparable roles, rounded down to the nearest
£500. Initial market rate analysis indicated the service
areas of Planning, Estates/Evaluation, Accountancy and Housing that
might have roles eligible for payments c£2-3k, where the
criteria was met. Further research was required to determine if
there might be a business case for similar value market supplements
to be paid to specialist roles in Revenues and Benefits and
Digital, where the criteria was met.
 
The Council had so
far identified that there were three categories of roles that were
being impacted by both recruitment and retention: Surveyors,
Environmental Health Officers and Project and Programme Managers.
Although not an exhaustive list, the Council had a pressing need to
recruit to and retain the posts identified and there did appear to
be local movement in the market of local authorities in advance of
Local Government Reorganisation. It was proposed that a double
market supplement be added to the roles identified and the market
tested urgently where those vacancies were waiting to be filled;
some roles had been advertised three times, including the usual
market supplement, without success. The maximum payments would be
based on the grades that had previously been agreed, but would be twice that amount where the
Council was finding it extremely difficult to recruit.
 
The Council had
identified a number of areas where there
was a “flight risk.”  In
advance of the Policy, special permission was reached to make a
retention payment to a surveyor to reduce that risk; this policy
was only to be approved by the Senior Leadership Team and would
require a MORI to be approved. The criteria for a retention payment
was outlined in paragraphs 10 and 11 of
the report.
 
Members were
supportive of the proposed amended wording to the Council’s
Pay Policy and agreed that the Policy be updated.
 
RESOLVED:
That:
 

1)   the Council’s Pay Policy
be updated with the following wording: 
 
From
time to time, it may be necessary to take account of the external
pay market to attract and retain employees with the required
experience, skills, and capabilities. Where necessary, the Council
will ensure the requirement for such is objectively justified by
reference to clear and transparent evidence of relevant market
comparators, using appropriate data sources. This does not affect
the Council’s in-house approach to managing equality of
opportunity and does not affect the overarching responsibilities of
the Council to manage pay through job evaluation or the internal
job ranking linked to pay. Any additional payments linked to work
and salaries will need to have a MORI approved if the cost will be
more than £500. The only other way that approval can be
granted, where time is vital, will be via the Senior Leadership
Team (SLT);
 

2)   the updated element of the Pay
Policy October 2025, as detailed in Appendix A, be agreed;

 

3)   the Interim Policy Statement,
as detailed in Appendix A, be included in the Pay Policy; and

 

4)   the proposed Rother District
Council protocol for the application of market supplement payments,
as detailed in Appendix A, be agreed.
 
(The Chair had
accepted this item onto the Agenda as an Additional Agenda Item to
enable the HR Committee to consider this matter which could not
wait until the next scheduled meeting of Committee in April
2026).
topline: The Human Resources Committee has decided to approve recommendations on market supplements and retention payments to address turnover and recruitment challenges within the council.

purpose:
To present the performance of the housing
company
content:
Consideration was given to the report of the Deputy Chief
Executive that set out the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) that
had been agreed between Rother DC Housing Company (RDCHC) and
Rother District Council (RDC) officers and provided the latest
performance update in respect of RDCHC performance.  
 
The
report set out the notable highlights in respect of progress, as
follows:
 

-    
progress was currently out of sequence compared to
the Contract Programme contained within the Joint Contracts
Tribunal contract, however there were no overall issues, with some
elements of work being ahead of schedule while others delayed, but
were not likely to cause a delay to the overall
programme;
 

-    
whilst the first phase of completions were expected
by March 2026 the Chief Operating Officer for RDCHC updated at the
meeting to say these were now expected at the end of January. The
whole scheme was expected to be completed by September 2027, to
include delivery of 130 affordable homes (20% of the overall RDCHC
Business Plan target (2022 to 2025), towards the delivery of 1,000
new homes by 2037).
 

-    
latest cashflow position included a reduction in the
estimated peak debt of c£0.34m and this was expected to
reduce further to c£1.12m over the coming months, with
finance costs anticipated to reduce accordingly by
c£0.15m
 
The
KPIs included a mix of financial and non-financial indicators and
covering cost, profit, debt and revenue metrics, which had been
discussed and agreed with officers of RDCHC and signed off by the
Housing Company Board.  Council officers
had applied a red, amber, green (RAG) status to the KPI data
provided by RDCHC, to consider current risks against overall
progress of the Blackfriars programme, to include performance
monitoring in accordance with the Development Finance Agreement
(DFA).
 
The
KPIs which would be considered and reported against
were:
 
a.         Approved
Main Contractor Costs vs Forecast Main Contractor Costs
b.         Main
Contractor Costs Per Unit
c.        
Development Progress (Costs incurred vs Expected costs)
d.        
Development Profit Margin
e.        
Operating Profit Margin
f.         
Tasking (savings identified)
g.         Peak
Debt (value and date)
h.         Debt
incurred
i.         
Funding Drawdown Efficiency
j.         
Weighted Average Interest Rate
k.         Units
Delivered by Contractor (against programme)
l.         
Contractor Delivery (weeks delay/improvement)
m.        Sales
Completed (%age against target)
n.         Sales
Completed (weeks delay/improvement)
o.         Sales
Revenue
 
Officers were working with RDCHC on agreeing both suitable
tolerances for the measurement of the KPIs, as well as which
indices would be considered commercially sensitive and reported
confidentially; this would be completed ahead of the next
meeting.  Further detail on the proposed
KPIs was included at Confidential Appendix A, to the
report.
 
The
Council remained responsible for complying with the terms of the
Grant Funding Agreement that secured the c£17m Housing
Infrastructure Fund received relating to delivery of the road and
infrastructure project, completed in May 2025, which was
conditional on the delivery of 200 new homes. 
 
Since March 2025, under the terms of the DFA, RDCHC now reported
monthly, with the latest monitoring information included within the
confidential appendix.  The £40m
loan provision represented a significant financial risk to the
Council and represented the single largest item of expenditure
within the Council’s £183m Capital Programme. The
monitoring of the DFA agreement would ensure that, as far as
possible, delivery remained on track and any unforeseen issues were
raised and mitigated at an early stage.
 
The
report included a schedule of the current legal agreements in place
between RDC and RDCHC, which provided a robust governance framework
that was understood by all parties.
 
There were several risks associated with both the delivery of
the housing and the provision of the loan to RDCHC, with the two
issues being fundamentally connected. 
The key risks highlighted in the report related to the delivery of
the programme, cashflow and peak debt, sales and contractor
performance.  RDCHC had supplied their
Contract and Corporate Risk Register and it was recommended that
these items were added to the Work Programme for detailed
consideration at the next meeting scheduled to be held on 21
January 2026 in line with best practice.
 
During the discussion on this item the Shareholder Executive
Committee moved into confidential session and a number of concerns
were raised with RDCHC. 
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)    
the proposed Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) be
approved;
 

2)    
a review of the Rother DC Housing Company Contract
and Corporate Risk Register be added to the Work Programme for
consideration in more detail by the Committee at the next meeting
scheduled to be held on 21 January 2026 in line with best practice;
and

To determine the Premises Licence application

9QT
content:
Consideration was
given to the report of the Head of Environmental Services,
Licensing and Community Safety that gave details of an application
for a Premises Licence for Battle Brewery, Woodman’s Yard,
Penhurst Lane, Battle, TN33 9QT. The application was to add off
sales to enable retail customers to collect orders directly from
the Brewery as an alternative to the High Street location, where
parking could be challenging, from Monday to Saturday 10:00 to
19:00hrs and Sunday 12:00 to 18:00hrs. No other Licensable
Activities had been applied for.
 
One representation
had been made in relation to the application, concerned with the
licensing objectives of prevention of public nuisance, public
safety, and prevention of crime and disorder, reproduced at
Appendix F to the report.
 
No representations
or objections were received from the responsible bodies. Sussex
Police had agreed conditions with the Applicant with relation to
the four licensing objectives, which superseded those offered by
the Applicant; these were reproduced in Appendix E to the
report.
 
The Council’s
Planning Service did not make a formal representation, however did provide comments detailing a planning
decision from July 2022, the conditions of which were detailed in
the report.
 
The Chair welcomed
all who were present and gave general advice in
regard to the Hearing. The Panel then proceeded to hear the
case following the adopted procedure and all parties present at the
Hearing were invited to address the Panel.
 
The Panel heard
from the Licensing Assistant, who presented the report detailing
the application and then from Michael Corfield, Corfield 1066
Limited, (the Applicant) and Jack Hance (Brewery Manager and
Designated Premises Supervisor), who presented the case for the
application.
 
The Panel
gave full consideration to the report,
the written submission from the Representor and verbal statements
given at the Hearing.
 
The Panel
deliberated the application, which was determined having regard to
the licensing objectives, together with the Guidance under section
182 of the Licensing Act and the local Licensing Policy, and retired to make their decision in
private session. 
 

RESOLVED:  That the application
for a Premises Licence be granted as set out in Appendix 1.
 
(Councillor Field
declared an Other Registerable Interest as Ward Member for North
Battle, Netherfield and Whatlington and Member of East Sussex
County Council for Battle and Crowhurst Division and in accordance
with the Members’ Code of Conduct, remained in the meeting
for the consideration thereof.)

content:
Members received
the report of the Head of Environmental Services, Licensing and
Community Safety which recommended the Housing Renewal Financial
Assistance Policy 2026 (Disabled Facilities Grants) to Cabinet for
approval and onward recommendation for adoption by full
Council.
 
The Council
received sufficient funding from the Government (through the Better
Care Fund paid to East Sussex County Council (ESCC) and distributed
to the Council) to mainly provide mandatory Disabled Facilities
Grants (DFGs) in accordance with the Housing Grants, Construction
and Regeneration Act 1996. The Government was consulting on
changing the funding arrangements; the formulae being proposed to
allocate funding was logical and reasonable.
 
DFGs were available
to disabled people when works to adapt their home were assessed as
necessary and appropriate to meet their needs, and when it was
reasonable and practicable to carry them out having regard to the
age and condition of the dwelling. Elements of the grant were
mandatory, and others could be provided at the discretion of the
Council (discretionary grants). The Housing Assistance Policy, at
Appendix A to the report, set out situations where the Council
might provide assistance in addition to
DFGs, and Appendix B to the report gave details of DFGs awarded in
2024/25.
 
The main change in
the Council’s proposed policy was increasing the
discretionary grant from £30,000 to £40,000, to reflect
the costs of more complex cases. The mandatory maximum of
£30,000 was set in 2008 and was no longer adequate in many
cases. In such cases, funds from other bodies were sought,
including registered social landlords and ESCC. Officers had fed
back to the Government, through the current consultation, the need
to increase the maximum mandatory amount of £30,000. Other
changes to the Policy were highlighted in yellow.
 
Members were given
the opportunity to ask questions and the
following points were noted during the discussion:
 

•     Members
suggested that the sentence under ‘Dementia Assistance’
concerning eligibility in Appendix A to the Policy be amended to
read ‘Anyone diagnosed with Dementia by a
professional’;

•     there was no
service user feedback provided in the report and Members were
advised that the East Sussex Occupational Therapy team were
considering ways to gather this;

•     grant funding
awarded to the Council reflected the previous year’s
spending; and

•     information
concerning the performance of the DFG was available at a county
level, which illustrated how it compared to other authorities and
could be made available for Members if necessary.
 
Members were
supportive of the changes proposed and recommended that Cabinet
approve the Policy including the suggested amendment to Appendix A,
as detailed above for onward approval and adoption by full
Council.
 
RESOLVED:
That the Housing Renewal Financial Assistance Policy 2026,
including the suggested amendment to Appendix A, be recommended to
Cabinet for onward approval and adoption by full Council.
topline: The Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to recommend the approval of the Housing Renewal Financial Assistance Policy 2026 to Cabinet for adoption.

purpose:
This report summarises the work undertaken to
date on the proposed growth and savings proposals for 2026/27 for
consideration by Members ahead of public consultation.
content:
Members received
the report of the Deputy Chief Executive which summarised the work
undertaken to date on the proposed growth and savings proposals for
2026/27 for consideration by Members ahead of public
consultation.
 
The report set out
the challenging financial position facing the Council and the need
to identify further savings ahead of setting the budget for
2026/27.
 
In the previous
year, the budget challenge exercise identified savings which were
approved by Members of £1.1m and this was offset by essential
growth of £540,000. All Heads of Service (HoS) were issued
guidance in mid-June outlining the process for the budget challenge
sessions and the wider budget setting for 2026/27. This guidance
included the need to identify sufficient savings to offset any
growth that would be unavoidable, the impact of inflationary
pressures and to meet the base budget shortfall for 2025/26 of
£694,000.
 
HoS were asked to
identify 10% savings on their gross budget (excluding where
expenditure was directly funded from earmarked grants or subsidy).
Proposals were RAG (Red, Amber and Green) rated by HoS, where they
evaluated the deliverability and the reputational impacts of the
proposals and were considered by the Budget Challenge Panel (BCP),
consisting of the Leader, Deputy Leaders (or their substitute) and
the Portfolio Holder for Finance and Governance, in late July.
Draft proposals were then considered by Cabinet Members at an
informal meeting.
 
Proposals were
summarised in Appendix A (Savings) and Appendix B (Growth) to the
report for the Committee’s consideration ahead of public
consultation, together with proposals for discretionary fees and
charges at Appendix C to the report.
 
Members were asked
to note that additional savings from the base budget would need to
be identified beyond those outlined within the paper, to ensure a
balanced budget could be set and the Council remained financially
stable.  The Finance team would be
working alongside the Senior Leadership Team and HoS to seek to
identify further savings during the Autumn and early Winter.
 
Cabinet would
formally consider the proposals, with the Committee’s
comments or recommendations, at their meeting on 3 November 2025.
The Council would commence public consultation on the proposals
during November and December, returning to the January Committee
meeting to report back on both the findings and update to the
financial position.
 
Members were given
the opportunity to ask questions of the HoS and Cabinet Portfolio
Holders present at the meeting, and the following points were noted
during the discussions:
 

•     the Revenue
and Benefits department was currently supported by an external
agency providing skilled staff, as benefits officers took
approximately 18 months to train. It was proposed to reduce
dependency on the agency and attempt to recruit externally.
Although this would result in a reduction in costs, the potential
risk to the Council was a reduction in skills and therefore
processing times;

•     Members raised
concerns about the proposed removal of the conservation grant to
Rye Harbour Nature Reserve of £1,050, payable to Sussex
Wildlife Trust (S12) and questioned whether the effect would be
disproportionate. Members agreed to recommend that the Chief
Executive review savings proposal S12;

•     the percentage
range of bulky waste charge increases related to the different
charges paid for the number of items to be collected. These were
benchmarked, and were to cover the removal costs and encourage
residents to use the service, rather than fly-tip;

•     the Government
had discussed retrospective planning applications attracting a
higher charge than normal planning applications, but this had not
been implemented at the current time;

•     the cost of
the proposed new Housing Enforcement Officer, detailed in Appendix
B to the report, reflected the net cost and related to the new
private sector housing legislation;

•     there was
currently no option in the Council’s fees and charges
schedule for sponsored walks on Council land; the not-for-profit
event charge of £84 was applied in such cases, which often
discouraged event organisers. Members suggested that the wording be
amended to include fund raising walks;

•     a detailed
study had been undertaken to consider the effects of an earlier
summer season start in Camber car park summer charges with an
interim payment, and a longer season end with an interim payment,
but this would result in the Council losing money. Therefore it was proposed that the summer season
tariffs in Camber remain the same;

•     charging for
filming in the district was administered by the 1066 Country Film
Office, a partnership between Hastings Borough and Rother District
Councils. The risk of any increase in charges was that film
companies would go elsewhere;

•     additional
resources were required in the Human Resources department to expand
the historically very small team, in order
to resource the challenges of Local Government Reorganisation;

•     Members raised
concerns about farmers being paid by developers to take soil from
building developments, which could spoil parts of the Area of
Outstanding Natural Beauty. Some occasions required planning
permission, but not all caused harm and were assessed on a
case-by-case basis; and

•     Members
welcomed the efforts that had been made to identify budget savings,
as this was a substantial step towards achieving a balanced
budget.
 
RESOLVED:
That the:
 

1)   proposals, including the
schedules within Appendix A, B & C to the report, subject to
reviewing Sussex Wildlife Trust S12, be recommended to Cabinet for
inclusion in the public consultation for the 2026/27 Budget;

 

2)   contents of the report,
including the challenging financial position and need to identify
further savings ahead of setting the budget for 2026/27, be noted;
and

 

3)   efforts that had been made to
identify budget savings be welcomed.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations for growth and savings proposals for the 2026/27 budget, which will be included in the public consultation.

content:
In February 2024,
Cabinet approved a 3-year extension of its funding agreement to the
De La Warr Pavilion Charitable Trust (DLWPCT), with an annual
review of the funding amount. This allowed the DLWPCT to
concentrate fund raising activities on the Levelling Up Fund (LUF)
capital refurbishment project and to help support the DLWPCT while
it reviewed its business planning with the Council beyond March
2025 and while the LUF funded project was underway. The Council was
currently reviewing the funding agreement collaboratively with the
DLWPCT to feed into the Council’s general budget setting
process for 2026/27.
 
The core grant was
£477,000 per annum, with an additional planned maintenance
grant of £59,139. The percentage increase to the maintenance
grant, together with the community grant, were removed in the
current funding round to effectively reduce the level of funding
provided. The level of grant awarded by the Council enabled the De
La Warr Pavilion (DLWP) to draw down an additional £517,785
of revenue funding annually from Arts Council England (ACE)
National Portfolio Organisation (NPO), as part of its prestigious
NPO funding. This funding had been extended until March 2028 to
account for the uncertainty provided by Government spending reviews
and Devolution/Local Government Reorganisation.
 
The Chair welcomed
Stewart Drew, Director and Chief Executive Officer, Patricia
Lochans, Director of Operations and Sally Ann Lycett, Director of
External Relations of the DLWPCT to the meeting, who proceeded to
present the annual report to the Overview and Scrutiny Committee
(OSC). Members had been in receipt of a written report that updated
the Council on its financial position and operating performance
during the financial year 2024/25, as well as its successes and the
challenges it faced, alongside the main risks. In addition, the
report provided an opportunity for the DLWP to demonstrate to
Members the community value generated by the funding the Council
provided, as well as the benefits to the wider economy of the
Rother district.
 
Following the
presentation, Members asked a number of
questions and the following key points
were noted during the discussion:
 

•     ACE provided
critical matched funding, alongside the Council and the Lottery
Grant, which ran in three to four year
cycles, the last round having been extended to five years, to 2028.
The uncertainty of further funding posed a considerable risk to the
DLWPCT;

•     ACE provided
strategic support to the DLWP;

•     the Member for
Rye and Winchelsea thanked the DLWP for their outreach programme in
the Ward;

•     it was not
clear from the report if there had been much engagement with the
Battle area. As Chair of 1066 Country for the previous 10 years,
the Chief Executive Officer advised that he had spent a
considerable amount of time in Battle and the DLWP was very mindful
of the rural areas of the district;

•     the DLWP had a
large volunteer programme through the National Heritage Fund and
tended not to use additional volunteers, but paid staff
members;

•     the DLWP aimed
to provide a balanced and varied programme of events, exhibitions
and learning, which they would continue to adapt throughout the
building programme;

•     Members
expressed concern that visitor numbers were taking some time to
recover to pre-pandemic levels;

•     a new unitary
authority (UA) was unlikely to be able to provide the level of
support and funding currently received from the Council, therefore
the DLWP would need to commence negotiations with the new Mayoral
Authority and UA as soon as possible so as not to undermine the
current funding or business model;

•     social media
was becoming increasingly more important as a
way to promote and communicate, especially in order to reach the younger generation. Rural
communities often communicated news via e-bulletins, which would be
a good way to promote the DLWP across the northern Rother parishes
and the High Weald;

•     securing
funding into the future for the DLWPCT was a huge priority for the
Council and options were being considered; and

•     it was
essential for the DLWPCT and the Council to work together to
protect the DLWP as an essential asset to the community.
 
Members
congratulated Stewart Drew on the 2024/25 successes of the
DLWP and the Chair gave thanks, on
behalf of the OSC, for his informative and interesting
presentation.
 
RESOLVED:
That the performance report of the Chief Executive Officer of the
De La Warr Pavilion Trust be welcomed.
topline: The Council has decided to approve a 3-year extension of funding for the De La Warr Pavilion Charitable Trust.

purpose: To approve the Data Breach Policy
content:
Consideration was given to the report of the Deputy Chief
Executive that outlined a new Data Breach Policy independent from
the Council’s ICT Policy, which followed national best
practice.   The Council had a very
good track record for its data management and the new policy, set
out at Appendix A to the report, was designed to build on this and
strengthen the use and guardianship of the Council’s customer
information.
 
The
Data Breach Policy aimed to mitigate the risks of non-compliance
with data protection legislation and reinforced and supported a
culture of accountability and transparency and reduced the
likelihood of data breaches through early detection and
response.
 
Cabinet was pleased to recommend the Policy to Council that was
a critical step in strengthening the Council’s resilience
against data security incidents.  It was
noted that by establishing clear procedures for identifying,
reporting, responding and recovery to breaches, the Council ensured
compliance with legal and regulatory obligations but also
reinforced public trust in the Council’s commitment to
safeguarding personal and sensitive information.  It was noted that following adoption of the
Policy, the Head of Digital and Customer Services would ensure
staff were aware and trained, where necessary.
 
RECOMMENDED: That:
 

1)         the
proposed Data Breach Management Policy at Appendix A to the report,
be approved; and
 

2)        
delegated authority be granted to the Head of Digital and Customer
Services to implement the policy and oversee training and
awareness.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve a new Data Breach Policy to strengthen data management and compliance with data protection legislation.

content:
Members received the report of the Deputy Chief Executive and
Section 151 Officer, which provided an update on the Revenue and
Capital Budget Monitoring Position for Quarter 1 2025/26. The
report also summarised the position to date on delivery of the
savings targets for 2025/26.  This
report had been considered by the Overview and Scrutiny Committee
at its meeting on 8 September 2025. 
 
The
Revenue Budget (RB) and Capital Programme (CP) statements were
summarised in Appendices A and B to the report, respectively.
Whilst it was an early stage in the financial year, a comprehensive
review had been undertaken and Appendix C to the report outlined
the current position regarding the agreed savings targets for
2025/26.
 
The
RB (Total Cost of Services) was currently forecast to be
£15.966m at year end, compared to the approved budget of
£15.716m.  The agreed budget
already anticipated a draw from Reserves of £694,000, and
this position would increase that to £944,000. The main
variances were discussed within the report and summarised in
Appendix A to the report. 
Members’ attention was drawn to the forecast reductions in
planning application fee income, increase in parking income due to
good weather over the summer period and garden and bulky
waste. 
 
An
early review of the deliverability of the agreed savings targets
for 2025/26 had also been undertaken and the outcome of this was
outlined within Appendix C to the report.  In summary, £380,000 was anticipated to be
fully deliverable (green status), with £109,000 having been
identified as undeliverable in year (red status).  The remaining savings target of £567,000 was
anticipated to be partially deliverable in year (amber
status).  Work would continue to be
undertaken to monitor this position as the in-year monitoring
progressed.
 
The
CP for 2025/26 and beyond remained under review and was being
constantly updated and reforecast as part of the governance
improvements introduced by the Corporate Development Team
(CDT).  The total CP was £183m,
including prior year spend, with the projected spend from 2025/26
through to 2028/29 totalling c£115m. The phasing to the CP
had been further revised and updated as part of the period 3 budget
monitoring process and also reflected the further amendments
outlined in paragraphs 12 to 17 of the report. The updated CP was
at Appendix B to the report.
 
The
Council had £5.00m in General Reserves not earmarked for any
specific purpose (plus a further £5.54m in Earmarked
Reserves).  If the revenue outturn
reported here was realised, the General Reserve would reduce by
£944,000 to £4.056m. 
 
It
was likely that abortive costs in relation to two recent capital
schemes (Town Hall Renaissance and King Offa) no longer being
pursued would be written off, potentially as high as
£900,000.  Additionally, the
Council had now received the final valuation for the Hermes
Property Fund investment, and this gave rise to a loss being
written off in year in the region of £420,000, although
income received over the lifespan of the investment was more than
the loss, so had been a good investment. 
 
These factors would bring the forecast General Reserve level to
around £2.7m to £3m by the end of the year and budget
reports in the coming months would consider whether this was a
sustainable position for the next two years or whether the Council
needed to take further action to increase the Reserves.  
 
RESOLVED: That the report be
noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to note the update on the Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Position for Quarter 1 2025/26.

content:
Cabinet received and considered Minute OSC25/21 arising from the
meeting of the Overview and Scrutiny Committee (OSC) held on 8
September 2025 that had considered the Council’s draft
Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy (HRSS).  The OSC had considered the Strategy in detail and
were pleased to recommend the HRSS to Cabinet for onward approval
and adoption by full Council; the Council had a statutory
obligation to have a 5-year Homeless Strategy in place.
 
The
HRSS set out the Council’s approach to preventing
homelessness in the district, by providing advice and support for
people in the district who were, or might become, homeless. The
HRSS had been developed with the support of a service review led by
Shelter, enabled by a successful grant application to the Ministry
for Housing, Communities and Local Government. In addition, the
Council had developed the HRSS in partnership with the national
homeless charity Homeless Link. This approach allowed the Council
to develop a strategic response based on an objective assessment of
its current service performance, as well as ensuring that the HRSS
was informed by the latest national and international best
practice.
 
The
Cabinet Portfolio Holder for Housing outlined the issues facing the
housing service, highlighted the key themes within the Strategy and
commended its adoption to Cabinet and Council.  It was agreed that the Strategy would stand the
Council in good stead in light of Local Government Reorganisation
and would be used to steer the direction of the Housing Service
over the next five years (2025-30). 
Members were particularly pleased to see the clearer focus on
community collaboration between service users and support services
to overcome housing issues in a more coordinated way.
 
RECOMMENDED: That the Homelessness and
Rough Sleeping Strategy 2025-2030 be approved and
adopted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve and adopt the Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy 2025-2030.

purpose:
To recommend approval of the request by Rye
Chamber of Commerce to seek a ballot in February 2025 for the
creation of a Business Improvement District in Rye.
content:
Consideration was given to the report of the Head of Corporate
and Strategic Services concerning the Rye Business Improvement
District (BID) Business Proposal.  The
proposal had been developed over the past year, drawing together a
wide range of businesses and public bodies within the BID area and
was attached as Appendix 1 to the report.
 
A
BID was a defined area in which a levy was charged on all eligible
business rate payers in addition to the business rates bill. This
levy was used to develop projects which would benefit businesses in
the local area.  There was no limit on
what projects or services could be provided through a BID, the only
requirement was that it should be something that was in addition to
services provided by local authorities. Improvements could include,
but were not limited to, extra safety/security, cleansing and
environmental measures.
 
The
Council had supported the development of the Rye BID through the
provision of £57,000 of funding, as the accountable body for
the Levelling Up Partnership funding.
 
The
Council was responsible for the payment of business rates for nine
hereditaments that were located within the BID area and every
eligible hereditament had the opportunity to cast a ballot, as
required by BID Regulations of 2004. The Council would therefore
receive a total of nine votes (out of a total of approximately 295
eligible voters currently in the BID Ballot), which represented 3%
of the number of votes, the others being from
businesses. 
 
The
Council’s contribution through the BID levy, if successful,
would be in the order of £3,200 per annum over five
years.  The BID income would be
ring-fenced for use only in the BID area, for initiatives directed
at increasing footfall and spend by residents and visitors.
Businesses in the BID area would be represented and have a say in
identifying key issues to be addressed.
 
A
ballot was only successful if a majority (51% or more) on two
counts was achieved, namely, the number of businesses voting for
and rateable value of businesses voting for.  The overall number of rateable properties in the
proposed BID area was c.295, with a total rateable value of circa
£4m.  It was noted that only those
businesses that were registered and charged business rates would be
included within the ballot and, if successful, pay the additional
levy. The Council would manage the collection and enforcement of
BID Levy charges delivered through an Operating Agreement between
Rye BID and Rother District Council, including recovery of the BID
billing and enforcement.
  
Cabinet agreed that the Rye BID Proposal did not conflict to a
material extent with the Council’s adopted, published
policies, nor did it warrant the use of veto for any other reason
under regulation 12 of the BID Regulations 2004
(England).
 
Cabinet was supportive of the BID ballot as it would improve the
area for the benefit of residents, businesses and tourists and
agreed that the Returning Officer be instructed to hold the ballot
no later than 12 February 2026, should the final decision by the
Rye BID steering group be to proceed. 
Whilst it was noted that not all businesses in Rye were supportive
of the proposal, there had been wide-spread consultation within the
business community, and the outcome of the BID would be determined
by a democratic vote. 
 
RESOLVED: That:
 

1)         the
content of the Business Improvement District (BID) proposals does
not conflict with any existing Council policy, nor propose a
disproportionate burden on businesses in the proposed BID
area;
 

2)         it is
agreed that the submitted Business Improvement District Proposals
meet the regulations;
 

3)         the
potential financial implications of a positive Business Improvement
District Ballot be noted; and
 

4)         the
Returning Officer be instructed to hold a ballot, with the final
day of the ballot being 12 February 2026, subject to final
confirmation being received from the Rye BID Task Group.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Rye Business Improvement District (BID) Proposal, despite some opposition from local businesses, in order to benefit the area's residents, businesses, and tourists.

purpose:
To approve the revised vexatious complaints
policy
content:
The
Council’s current Vexatious Complaints Policy had remained
largely unchanged since 2015 and required revision to provide an
improved structured approach to identifying and managing complaints
that were persistent, unreasonable, or abusive, while safeguarding
the rights of individuals to raise legitimate concerns.  The Policy aligned with good practice from the
Local Government Ombudsman and the Information Commissioner's
Office.
 
The
revised policy would also promote transparency and accountability
in how complaints were handled and improve complaint management to
protect staff and provide a clear escalation route to senior
management. 
 
The
Council’s Audit Committee (AC) had considered the Policy at
its meeting held on 29 September 2025, as it had a role to monitor
certain policies, including those in relation to the
Council’s complaints process.   The AC was supportive and appreciative of
the language and tone of the policy and the distinction made
between the complaint and the complainant to ensure that the
Council did not lose sight of the substance of genuine complaints
and was keen to ensure that the Policy was promoted widely to
stakeholders.
 
Cabinet was supportive of the Policy and agreed to recommend it
to Council, as submitted.  The
Monitoring Officer agreed to look at and provide training on how
Members could be better protected in terms of vexatious
complainants and the difficulties that Members faced because of
residents being designated as vexatious complainants.  It was noted that once the Policy had been
approved by full Council, the Head of Digital and Customer Services
would oversee training and awareness for staff and stakeholders,
including induction training for new staff, as well as including
the parish and town councils.   
 
RECOMMENDED: That:
 

1)         the
revised Vexatious Complaints Policy and Guidance at Appendix 1 to
the report be approved and adopted; and
 

2)        
delegated authority be granted to the Head of Digital and Customer
Services to implement the Policy and oversee training and
awareness.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to revise and approve the Council's Vexatious Complaints Policy to provide a structured approach to managing complaints while safeguarding individuals' rights.
